statement: Server latencies can impact web performance. If the server latency of an origin is high, it's an indication the server is overloaded or has poor backend performance. Learn more about server response time.
audit_check: Server Backend Latencies
citation: Google. Lighthouse audit network-server-latency.

author: Google Chrome team
title: Avoid non-composited animations
statement: Animations which are not composited can be janky and increase CLS. Learn how to avoid non-composited animations
audit_check: Avoid non-composited animations
citation: Google. Lighthouse audit non-composited-animations.

author: Google Chrome team
title: Ensure proper origin isolation with COOP
statement: The Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy (COOP) can be used to isolate the top-level window from other documents such as pop-ups. Learn more about deploying the COOP header.
audit_check: Ensure proper origin isolation with COOP
citation: Google. Lighthouse audit origin-isolation.

author: Google Chrome team
title: Redirects HTTP traffic to HTTPS
statement: Make sure that you redirect all HTTP traffic to HTTPS in order to enable secure web features for all your users. Learn more.
audit_check: Does not redirect HTTP traffic to HTTPS
citation: Google. Lighthouse audit redirects-http.

author: Google Chrome team
title: Avoid multiple page redirects
statement: Redirects introduce additional delays before the page can be loaded. Learn how to avoid page redirects.
audit_check: Avoid multiple page redirects
citation: Google. Lighthouse audit redirects.

author: Google Chrome team
title: Document has a valid `rel=canonical`
statement: Canonical links suggest which URL to show in search results. Learn more about canonical links.
audit_check: Document does not have a valid `rel=canonical`
citation: Google. Lighthouse audit canonical.

author: Google Chrome team
title: Links are crawlable
statement: Search engines may use `href` attributes on links to crawl websites. Ensure that the `href` attribute of anchor elements links to an appropriate destination, so more pages of the site can be discovered. Learn how to make links crawlable
audit_check: Links are not crawlable
citation: Google. Lighthouse audit crawlable-anchors.

author: Google Chrome team
title: Document has a valid `hreflang`
statement: hreflang links tell search engines what version of a page they should list in search results for a given language or region. Learn more about `hreflang`.
audit_check: Document doesn't have a valid `hreflang`
citation: Google. Lighthouse audit hreflang.

author: Google Chrome team
title: Page has successful HTTP status code
statement: Pages with unsuccessful HTTP status codes may not be indexed properly. Learn more about HTTP status codes.
audit_check: Page has unsuccessful HTTP status code
citation: Google. Lighthouse audit http-status-code.

author: Google Chrome team
title: Page isn’t blocked from indexing
statement: Search engines are unable to include your pages in search results if they don't have permission to crawl them. Learn more about crawler directives.
audit_check: Page is blocked from indexing
citation: Google. Lighthouse audit is-crawlable.

author: Google Chrome team
title: Links have descriptive text
statement: Descriptive link text helps search engines understand your content. Learn how to make links more accessible.
audit_check: Links do not have descriptive text
citation: Google. Lighthouse audit link-text.

author: Google Chrome team
title: Structured data is valid
statement: Run the Structured Data Testing Tool to validate structured data. Learn more about Structured Data.
audit_check: Structured data is valid
citation: Google. Lighthouse audit structured-data.

author: Google Chrome team
title: Document has a meta description
statement: Meta descriptions may be included in search results to concisely summarize page content. Learn more about the meta description.
audit_check: Document does not have a meta description
citation: Google. Lighthouse audit meta-description.

author: Google Chrome team
title: robots.txt is valid
statement: If your robots.txt file is malformed, crawlers may not be able to understand how you want your website to be crawled or indexed. Learn more about robots.txt.
audit_check: robots.txt is not valid
citation: Google. Lighthouse audit robots-txt.

author: Google Chrome team
title: Initial server response time was short
statement: Keep the server response time for the main document short because all other requests depend on it. Learn more about the Time to First Byte metric.
audit_check: Reduce initial server response time
citation: Google. Lighthouse audit server-response-time.

author: Google Chrome team
title: Avoids third-party cookies
statement: Third-party cookies may be blocked in some contexts. Learn more about preparing for third-party cookie restrictions.
audit_check: Uses third-party cookies
citation: Google. Lighthouse audit third-party-cookies.

author: Google Chrome team
title: Mitigate DOM-based XSS with Trusted Types
statement: The `require-trusted-types-for` directive in the `Content-Security-Policy` (CSP) header instructs user agents to control the data passed to DOM XSS sink functions. Learn more about mitigating DOM-based XSS with Trusted Types.
audit_check: Mitigate DOM-based XSS with Trusted Types
citation: Google. Lighthouse audit trusted-types-xss.

author: Google Chrome team
title: Image elements have explicit `width` and `height`
statement: Set an explicit width and height on image elements to reduce layout shifts and improve CLS. Learn how to set image dimensions
audit_check: Image elements do not have explicit `width` and `height`
citation: Google. Lighthouse audit unsized-images.

author: Google Chrome team
title: User Timing marks and measures
statement: Consider instrumenting your app with the User Timing API to measure your app's real-world performance during key user experiences. Learn more about User Timing marks.
audit_check: User Timing marks and measures
citation: Google. Lighthouse audit user-timings.

author: Google Chrome team
title: Page has valid source maps
statement: Source maps translate minified code to the original source code. This helps developers debug in production. In addition, Lighthouse is able to provide further insights. Consider deploying source maps to take advantage of these benefits. Learn more about source maps.
audit_check: Missing source maps for large first-party JavaScript
citation: Google. Lighthouse audit valid-source-maps.

author: Google Chrome team
title: WebMCP form coverage
statement: Consider adding WebMCP annotations to the forms listed below. This helps AI agents identify and interact with these forms more reliably.
audit_check: WebMCP form coverage
citation: Google. Lighthouse audit webmcp-form-coverage.

author: Google Chrome team
title: WebMCP tools registered
statement: Lists the WebMCP tools registered at the time of analysis.
audit_check: WebMCP tools registered
citation: Google. Lighthouse audit webmcp-registered-tools.

author: Google Chrome team
title: WebMCP schemas are valid
statement: Valid WebMCP schemas are required for AI agents to understand and interact with tools correctly. Please fix any errors or warnings reported by the browser.
audit_check: WebMCP schemas are invalid
citation: Google. Lighthouse audit webmcp-schema-validity.

author: Google (web.dev)
title: Largest Contentful Paint (Core Web Vital) thresholds
statement: Good: <= 2.5s; Needs improvement: 2.5-4.0s; Poor: > 4.0s, measured at the 75th percentile of page loads (mobile and desktop separately).
audit_check: Is Largest Contentful Paint (Core Web Vital) within the good threshold (2.5s) at p75?
citation: Google web.dev, "Web Vitals" (2020; INP replaced FID in March 2024).

author: Google (web.dev)
title: Interaction to Next Paint (Core Web Vital) thresholds
statement: Good: <= 200ms; Needs improvement: 200-500ms; Poor: > 500ms, measured at the 75th percentile of page loads (mobile and desktop separately).
audit_check: Is Interaction to Next Paint (Core Web Vital) within the good threshold (200ms) at p75?
citation: Google web.dev, "Web Vitals" (2020; INP replaced FID in March 2024).

author: Google (web.dev)
title: Cumulative Layout Shift (Core Web Vital) thresholds
statement: Good: <= 0.1score; Needs improvement: 0.1-0.25score; Poor: > 0.25score, measured at the 75th percentile of page loads (mobile and desktop separately).
audit_check: Is Cumulative Layout Shift (Core Web Vital) within the good threshold (0.1score) at p75?
citation: Google web.dev, "Web Vitals" (2020; INP replaced FID in March 2024).

author: Google (web.dev)
title: First Contentful Paint thresholds
statement: Good: <= 1.8s; Needs improvement: 1.8-3.0s; Poor: > 3.0s, measured at the 75th percentile of page loads (mobile and desktop separately).
audit_check: Is First Contentful Paint within the good threshold (1.8s) at p75?
citation: Google web.dev, "Web Vitals" (2020; INP replaced FID in March 2024).

author: Google (web.dev)
title: Time to First Byte thresholds
statement: Good: <= 0.8s; Needs improvement: 0.8-1.8s; Poor: > 1.8s, measured at the 75th percentile of page loads (mobile and desktop separately).
audit_check: Is Time to First Byte within the good threshold (0.8s) at p75?
citation: Google web.dev, "Web Vitals" (2020; INP replaced FID in March 2024).

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Use plain language and avoid figures of speech, idioms, and complicated metaphors.
statement: Write content at an 8th grade reading level.
rationale: WCAG 3.1.5 Reading Level
audit_check: Use plain language and avoid figures of speech, idioms, and complicated metaphors.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Make sure that button, a, and label element content is unique and descriptive.
statement: Terms like “click here” and “read more” do not provide any context. Some people navigate using a list of all buttons or links on a page or view. When using this mode, the terms indicate what will happen if navigated to or activated.
rationale: WCAG 1.3.1 Info and Relationships
audit_check: Make sure that button, a, and label element content is unique and descriptive.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Use left-aligned text for left-to-right (LTR) languages, and right-aligned text for right-to-left (RTL) languages.
statement: Centered-aligned or justified text is difficult to read.
rationale: WCAG 1.4.8 Visual Presentation
audit_check: Use left-aligned text for left-to-right (LTR) languages, and right-aligned text for right-to-left (RTL) languages.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Validate your HTML.
statement: Valid HTML helps to provide a consistent, expected experience across all browsers and assistive technology.
rationale: WCAG 4.1.1 Parsing
audit_check: Validate your HTML.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Use a lang attribute on the html element.
statement: This helps assistive technology such as screen readers to pronounce content correctly.
rationale: WCAG 3.1.1 Language of Page
audit_check: Use a lang attribute on the html element.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Provide a unique title for each page or view.
statement: The title element, contained in the document's head element, is often the first piece of information announced by assistive technology. This helps tell people what page or view they are going to start navigating.
rationale: WCAG 2.4.2 Page Titled
audit_check: Provide a unique title for each page or view.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Ensure that viewport zoom is not disabled.
statement: Some people need to increase the size of text to a point where they can read it. Do not stop them from doing this, even for web apps with a native app-like experience. Even native apps should respect Operating System settings for resizing text.
rationale: WCAG 1.4.4 Resize text
audit_check: Ensure that viewport zoom is not disabled.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Use landmark elements to indicate important content regions.
statement: Landmark regions help communicate the layout and important areas of a page or view, and can allow quick access to these regions. For example, use the nav element to wrap a site's navigation, and the main element to contain the primary content of a page.
rationale: WCAG 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value
audit_check: Use landmark elements to indicate important content regions.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Ensure a linear content flow.
statement: Remove tabindex attribute values that aren't either 0 or -1. Elements that are inherently focusable, such as links or button elements, do not require a tabindex. Elements that are not inherently focusable should not have a tabindex applied to them outside of very specific use cases.
rationale: WCAG 2.4.3 Focus Order
audit_check: Ensure a linear content flow.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Avoid using the autofocus attribute.
statement: People who are blind or who have low vision may be disoriented when focus is moved without their permission. Additionally, autofocus can be problematic for people with motor control disabilities, as it may create extra work for them to navigate out from the autofocused area and to other locations on the page/view.
rationale: WCAG 2.4.3 Focus Order
audit_check: Avoid using the autofocus attribute.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Allow extending session timeouts.
statement: If you cannot remove session timeouts altogether, then let the person using your site easily turn off, adjust, or extend their session well before it ends.
rationale: WCAG 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable
audit_check: Allow extending session timeouts.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Remove title attribute tooltips.
statement: The title attribute has numerous issues, and should not be used if the information provided is important for all people to access. An acceptable use for the title attribute would be labeling an iframe element to indicate what content it contains.
rationale: WCAG 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value
audit_check: Remove title attribute tooltips.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Make sure there is a visible focus style for interactive elements that are navigated to via keyboard input.
statement: Can a person navigating with a keyboard, switch, voice control, or screen reader see where they currently are on the page?
rationale: WCAG 2.4.7 Focus Visible
audit_check: Make sure there is a visible focus style for interactive elements that are navigated to via keyboard input.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Check to see that keyboard focus order matches the visual layout.
statement: Can a person navigating with a keyboard or screen reader move around the page in a predictable way?
rationale: WCAG 1.3.2 Meaningful Sequence
audit_check: Check to see that keyboard focus order matches the visual layout.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Remove invisible focusable elements.
statement: Remove the ability to focus on elements that are not presently meant to be discoverable. This includes things like inactive drop down menus, off screen navigations, or modals.
rationale: WCAG 2.4.3 Focus Order
audit_check: Remove invisible focusable elements.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Make sure that all img elements have an alt attribute.
statement: alt attributes (alt text) give a description of an image for people who may not be able to view them. When an alt attribute isn't present on an image, a screen reader may announce the image's file name and path instead. This fails to communicate the image’s content.
rationale: WCAG 1.1.1 Non-text Content
audit_check: Make sure that all img elements have an alt attribute.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Make sure that decorative images use null alt (empty) attribute values.
statement: Null alt attributes are also sometimes known as empty alt attributes. They are made by including no information between the opening and closing quotes of an alt attribute. Decorative images do not communicate information that is required to understand the website's overall meaning. Historically they were used for flourishes and spacer gif images, but tend to be less relevant for modern websites and web apps.
rationale: WCAG 1.1.1 Non-text Content
audit_check: Make sure that decorative images use null alt (empty) attribute values.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Provide a text alternative for complex images such as charts, graphs, and maps.
statement: Is there a plain text which lists points on the map or sections of a flowchart? Describe all visible information. This includes graph axes, data points and labels, and the overall point the graphic is communicating.
rationale: WCAG 1.1.1 Non-text Content
audit_check: Provide a text alternative for complex images such as charts, graphs, and maps.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: For images containing text, make sure the alt description includes the image's text.
statement: For example, the FedEx logo should have an alt value of “FedEx.”
rationale: WCAG 1.1.1 Non-text Content
audit_check: For images containing text, make sure the alt description includes the image's text.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Make sure that svg elements include the code focusable="false" when they are the child element of a focusable element.
statement: This prevents Internet Explorer from allowing focus to navigate through the child elements of a SVG that is meant to be decorative.
rationale: WCAG 1.3.1 Info and Relationships
audit_check: Make sure that svg elements include the code focusable="false" when they are the child element of a focusable element.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Add aria-hidden="true" to SVG that is decorative.
statement: This is equivalent to an empty/null alt value on a non-svg image.
rationale: WCAG 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value
audit_check: Add aria-hidden="true" to SVG that is decorative.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Make sure that SVG utilizing the use element has whitespace between the svg and use elements.
statement: This solves a bug in Safari which sometimes creates hidden, unanticipated tab-stops when navigating.
rationale: WCAG 2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap
audit_check: Make sure that SVG utilizing the use element has whitespace between the svg and use elements.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: It's recommended that img elements with an svg source include the role="img" attribute.
statement: VoiceOver on macOS and iOS may not correctly convey the element as an image if role="img" is not present.
rationale: WCAG 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value
audit_check: It's recommended that img elements with an svg source include the role="img" attribute.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Use heading elements to introduce content.
statement: Heading elements construct a document outline, and should not be used for purely visual design.
rationale: WCAG 2.4.6 Headings or Labels
audit_check: Use heading elements to introduce content.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Use only one h1 element per page or view.
statement: The h1 element should be used to communicate the high-level purpose of the page or view. Do not use the h1 element for a heading that does not change between pages or views (for example, the site's name).
rationale: WCAG 2.4.6 Headings or Labels
audit_check: Use only one h1 element per page or view.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Heading elements should be written in a logical sequence.
statement: The order of heading elements should descend, based on the “depth” of the content. For example, a h4 element should not appear on a page before the first h3 element declaration. A tool such as headingsMap can help you evaluate this.
rationale: WCAG 2.4.6 Headings or Labels
audit_check: Heading elements should be written in a logical sequence.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Don't skip heading levels.
statement: For example, don't jump from a h2 to a h4, skipping a h3 element. If heading levels are being skipped for a specific visual treatment, use CSS classes instead.
rationale: WCAG 2.4.6 Headings or Labels
audit_check: Don't skip heading levels.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Use list elements (ol, ul, and dl elements) for list content.
statement: This may include sections of related content, items visually displayed in a grid-like layout, or sibling a elements.
rationale: WCAG 1.3.1 Info and Relationships
audit_check: Use list elements (ol, ul, and dl elements) for list content.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Use the a element for links.
statement: Links should always have a href attribute, even when used in Single Page Applications (SPAs). Without a href attribute, the link will not be properly exposed to assistive technology. An example of this would be a link that uses an onclick event, in place of a href attribute.
rationale: WCAG 1.3.1 Info and Relationships
audit_check: Use the a element for links.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Ensure that links are recognizable as links.
statement: Color alone is not sufficient to indicate the presence of a link. Underlines are a popular and commonly-understood way to communicate the presence of link content.
rationale: WCAG 1.4.1 Use of Color
audit_check: Ensure that links are recognizable as links.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Ensure that controls have :focus states.
statement: Visible focus styles help people determine which interactive element has keyboard focus. This lets them know that they can perform actions like activating a button or navigating to a link's destination.
rationale: WCAG 2.4.7 Focus Visible
audit_check: Ensure that controls have :focus states.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Use the button element for buttons.
statement: Buttons are used to submit data or perform an on-screen action which does not shift keyboard focus. You can add type="button" to a button element to prevent the browser from attempting to submit form information when activated.
rationale: WCAG 1.3.1 Info and Relationships
audit_check: Use the button element for buttons.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Provide a skip link and make sure that it is visible when focused.
statement: A skip link can be used to provide quick access to the main content of a page or view. This allows a person to easily bypass globally repeated content such as a website's primary navigation, or persistent search widget.
rationale: WCAG 2.4.1 Bypass Blocks
audit_check: Provide a skip link and make sure that it is visible when focused.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Identify links that open in a new tab or window.
statement: Ideally, avoid links that open in a new tab or window. If a link does, ensure the link's behavior will be communicated in a way that is apparent to all users. Doing this will help people understand what will happen before activating the link. While this technique is technically not required for compliance, it is an often-cited area of frustration for many different kinds of assistive technology users.
rationale: WCAG G201: Giving users advanced warning when opening a new window
audit_check: Identify links that open in a new tab or window.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Use the table element to describe tabular data.
statement: Do you need to display data in rows and columns? Use the table element.
rationale: WCAG 1.3.1 Info and Relationships
audit_check: Use the table element to describe tabular data.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Use the th element for table headers (with appropriate scope attributes).
statement: Depending on how complex your table is, you may also consider using scope="col" for column headers, and scope="row" for row headers. Many different kinds of assistive technology still use the scope attribute to help them understand and describe the structure of a table.
rationale: WCAG 4.1.1 Parsing
audit_check: Use the th element for table headers (with appropriate scope attributes).
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Use the caption element to provide a title for the table.
statement: The table's caption should describe what kind of information the table contains.
rationale: WCAG 2.4.6 Headings or Labels
audit_check: Use the caption element to provide a title for the table.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: All inputs in a form are associated with a corresponding label element.
statement: Use a for/id pairing to guarantee the highest level of browser/assistive technology support.
rationale: WCAG 3.2.2 On Input
audit_check: All inputs in a form are associated with a corresponding label element.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Use fieldset and legend elements where appropriate.
statement: Does your form contain multiple sections of related inputs? Use fieldset to group them, and legend to provide a label for what this section is for.
rationale: WCAG 1.3.1 Info and Relationships
audit_check: Use fieldset and legend elements where appropriate.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Inputs use autocomplete where appropriate.
statement: Providing a mechanism to help people more quickly, easily, and accurately fill in form fields that ask for common information (for example, name, address, phone number).
rationale: WCAG 1.3.5 Identify Input Purpose
audit_check: Inputs use autocomplete where appropriate.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Make sure that form input errors are displayed in list above the form after submission.
statement: This provides a way for assistive technology users to quickly have a high-level understanding of what issues are present in the form. This is especially important for larger forms with many inputs. Make sure that each reported error also has a link to the corresponding field with invalid input.
rationale: WCAG 3.3.1 Error Identification
audit_check: Make sure that form input errors are displayed in list above the form after submission.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Associate input error messaging with the input it corresponds to.
statement: Techniques such as using aria-describedby allow people who use assistive technology to more easily understand the difference between the input and the error message associated with it.
rationale: WCAG 3.3.1 Error Identification
audit_check: Associate input error messaging with the input it corresponds to.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Make sure that error, warning, and success states are not visually communicated by just color.
statement: People who are color blind, who have other low vision conditions, or different cultural understandings for color may not see the state change, or understand what kind of feedback the state represents if color is the only indicator.
rationale: WCAG 1.4.1 Use of Color
audit_check: Make sure that error, warning, and success states are not visually communicated by just color.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Make sure that media does not autoplay.
statement: Unexpected video and audio can be distracting and disruptive, especially for certain kinds of cognitive disability such as ADHD. Certain kinds of autoplaying video and animation can be a trigger for vestibular and seizure disorders.
rationale: WCAG 1.4.2 Audio Control
audit_check: Make sure that media does not autoplay.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Ensure that media controls use appropriate markup.
statement: Examples include making sure an audio mute button has a pressed toggle state when active, or that a volume slider uses <input type="range">.
rationale: WCAG 1.3.1 Info and Relationships
audit_check: Ensure that media controls use appropriate markup.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Check to see that all media can be paused.
statement: Provide a global pause function on any media element. If the device has a keyboard, ensure that pressing the Space key can pause playback. Make sure you also don't interfere with the Space key's ability to scroll the page/view when not focusing on a form control.
rationale: WCAG 2.1.1 Keyboard
audit_check: Check to see that all media can be paused.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Confirm the presence of captions.
statement: Captions allow a person who cannot hear the audio content of a video to still understand its content.
rationale: WCAG 1.2.2 Captions
audit_check: Confirm the presence of captions.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Remove seizure triggers.
statement: Certain kinds of strobing or flashing animations will trigger seizures.
rationale: WCAG 2.3.1 Three Flashes or Below Threshold
audit_check: Remove seizure triggers.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Confirm that transcripts are available.
statement: Transcripts allow people who cannot hear to still understand the audio content. It also allows people to digest audio content at a pace that is comfortable to them.
rationale: WCAG 1.1.1 Non-text Content
audit_check: Confirm that transcripts are available.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Check your content in specialized browsing modes.
statement: Activate modes such as Windows High Contrast or Inverted Colors. Is your content still legible? Are your icons, borders, links, form fields, and other content still present? Can you distinguish foreground content from the background?
rationale: WCAG 1.4.1 Use of Color
audit_check: Check your content in specialized browsing modes.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Increase text size to 200%.
statement: Is the content still readable? Does increasing the text size cause content to overlap?
rationale: WCAG 1.4.4 Resize text
audit_check: Increase text size to 200%.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Double-check that good proximity between content is maintained.
statement: Use the straw test to ensure people who depend on screen zoom software can still easily discover all content.
rationale: WCAG 1.3.3 Sensory Characteristics
audit_check: Double-check that good proximity between content is maintained.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Make sure color isn't the only way information is conveyed.
statement: Can you still see where links are among body content if everything is grayscale?
rationale: WCAG 1.4.1 Use of Color
audit_check: Make sure color isn't the only way information is conveyed.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Make sure instructions are not visual or audio-only.
statement: Use a combination of characteristics to write cues, particularly the actual names of sections and elements, rather than just descriptions like location (“on the right”) or audio (“after the tone”).
rationale: WCAG 1.3.3 Sensory Characteristics
audit_check: Make sure instructions are not visual or audio-only.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Use a simple, straightforward, and consistent layout.
statement: A complicated layout can be confusing to understand and use.
rationale: WCAG 1.4.10 Reflow
audit_check: Use a simple, straightforward, and consistent layout.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Ensure animations are subtle and do not flash too much.
statement: Certain kinds of strobing or flashing animations will trigger seizures. Others may be distracting and disruptive, especially for certain kinds of cognitive disability such as ADHD.
rationale: WCAG 2.3.1 Three Flashes or Below Threshold
audit_check: Ensure animations are subtle and do not flash too much.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Provide a mechanism to pause background video.
statement: Background video can be distracting, especially if content is placed over it.
rationale: WCAG 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide
audit_check: Provide a mechanism to pause background video.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Make sure all animation obeys the prefers-reduced-motion media query.
statement: Remove animations when the “reduce motion” setting is activated. If an animation is necessary to communicate meaning for a concept, slow its duration down.
rationale: WCAG 2.3.3 Animation from Interactions
audit_check: Make sure all animation obeys the prefers-reduced-motion media query.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Check the contrast for all normal-sized text.
statement: Level AA compliance requires a contrast ratio of 4.5:1.
rationale: WCAG 1.4.3 Contrast
audit_check: Check the contrast for all normal-sized text.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Check the contrast for all large-sized text.
statement: Level AA compliance requires a contrast ratio of 3:1.
rationale: WCAG 1.4.3 Contrast
audit_check: Check the contrast for all large-sized text.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Check the contrast for all icons.
statement: Level AA compliance requires a contrast ratio of 3.0:1.
rationale: WCAG 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast
audit_check: Check the contrast for all icons.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Check the contrast of borders for input elements (text input, radio buttons, checkboxes, etc.).
statement: Level AA compliance requires a contrast ratio of 3.0:1.
rationale: WCAG 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast
audit_check: Check the contrast of borders for input elements (text input, radio buttons, checkboxes, etc.).
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Check text that overlaps images or video.
statement: Is text still legible?
rationale: WCAG 1.4.3 Contrast
audit_check: Check text that overlaps images or video.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Check custom ::selection colors.
statement: Is the color contrast you set in your ::selection CSS declaration sufficient? Otherwise someone may not be able read it if they highlight it.
rationale: WCAG 1.4.3 Contrast
audit_check: Check custom ::selection colors.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Check that the site can be rotated to any orientation.
statement: Does the site only allow portrait orientation?
rationale: WCAG 1.3.4 Orientation
audit_check: Check that the site can be rotated to any orientation.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Remove horizontal scrolling.
statement: Requiring someone to scroll horizontally can be difficult for some, irritating for all.
rationale: WCAG 1.4.10 Reflow
audit_check: Remove horizontal scrolling.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Ensure that button and link icons can be activated with ease.
statement: It's good to make sure things like hamburger menus, social icons, gallery viewers, and other touch controls are usable by a wide range of hand and stylus sizes.
rationale: WCAG 2.5.5 Target Size
audit_check: Ensure that button and link icons can be activated with ease.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: The A11Y Project contributors
title: Ensure sufficient space between interactive items in order to provide a scroll area.
statement: Some people who experience motor control issues such as hand tremors may have a very difficult time scrolling past interactive items which feature zero spacing.
rationale: WCAG 2.4.1 Bypass Blocks
audit_check: Ensure sufficient space between interactive items in order to provide a scroll area.
citation: The A11Y Project. Checklist.

author: David Dias
title: Provide accessible authentication methods
statement: Authentication flows avoid unnecessary cognitive tests and support assistive mechanisms such as password managers, paste, OTP autofill, and passkeys. TL;DR: Do not block paste or password managers in login and recovery flows / Prefer passkeys, magic links, device approval, or password-manager-friendly flows / Support OTP autofill and paste with appropriate semantics such as `autocomplete="one-time-code"` / Avoid CAPTCHA or secondary checks that require memorizing or transcribing information without an alternative
rationale: Authentication often becomes the first hard blocker for users with cognitive, motor, low-vision, or speech-input needs. If sign-in, MFA, or recovery relies on memorization or transcription with no assisted path, the user may be locked out before they can access the product at all.
audit_check: Review login, MFA, password reset, and account recovery for accessible authentication problems. Flag blocked paste, password-manager hostility, manual transcription requirements, inaccessible OTP handling, and CAPTCHA or knowledge checks without a compliant alternative.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Provide accessible authentication methods".

author: David Dias
title: Use semantic table markup for screen readers
statement: Data tables use proper semantic markup with headers, captions, and scope attributes for screen reader accessibility. TL;DR: Use <th> elements for headers with scope='col' or scope='row' / Add <caption> to describe the table's purpose / Never use tables for layout—use CSS Grid or Flexbox instead / Use id/headers for complex tables with merged cells / For simple tables with a clear adjacent section heading, missing `scope` is often a stronger finding than missing `<caption>` / Prefer one strong table-semantics finding over multiple weaker enhancements on the same simple table
rationale: Screen readers read table data cell-by-cell—without proper headers, users hear meaningless numbers without context. 'Row 3, Column 2: $99' vs just '$99'.
audit_check: Verify tables use proper th elements with scope, caption or aria-labelledby, and semantic table structure.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Use semantic table markup for screen readers".

author: David Dias
title: Ensure accesskey values are unique
statement: Checks that accesskey values are unique to avoid shortcut conflicts. TL;DR: Each `accesskey` attribute value must be unique on the page / Duplicate access keys can lead to unpredictable browser behavior / Helps keyboard users navigate reliably using defined shortcuts
rationale: Duplicate access keys cause conflicts where only one element (usually the first) is reachable via the shortcut, making other elements inaccessible to keyboard users.
audit_check: Check for duplicate `accesskey` attributes across the document to ensure each shortcut is unique.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Ensure accesskey values are unique".

author: David Dias
title: Provide instant anchor scroll option
statement: Smooth scroll animations to anchor links respect motion preferences or provide an instant alternative. TL;DR: Disable smooth scroll when prefers-reduced-motion is set / Use CSS scroll-behavior: smooth with media query check / Ensure focus moves to anchor target for keyboard users / Provide instant scroll as default or fallback
rationale: Smooth scroll animations can trigger vertigo, nausea, and disorientation for users with vestibular disorders—instant navigation is safer and often faster.
audit_check: Click anchor links (same-page navigation) and verify smooth scrolling is disabled when prefers-reduced-motion is set. Confirm anchor navigation works correctly with keyboard and screen readers.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Provide instant anchor scroll option".

author: David Dias
title: Use only allowed ARIA attributes for each role
statement: Checks that ARIA attributes are allowed on their elements to ensure valid accessibility trees. TL;DR: Each ARIA role only supports a specific set of ARIA attributes / Using unsupported attributes can confuse assistive technologies / Ensures the accessibility tree remains valid and meaningful
rationale: Invalid ARIA attributes are ignored by screen readers or may cause them to misinterpret the element's purpose, leading to a broken experience for users with disabilities.
audit_check: Verify that all ARIA attributes used on elements are valid for their assigned WAI-ARIA roles.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Use only allowed ARIA attributes for each role".

author: David Dias
title: Provide accessible names for ARIA command elements
statement: Checks that command elements like buttons and links have accessible names for screen reader support. TL;DR: Elements with command roles (button, link, menuitem) must have a label / Accessible names can be provided via text content, `aria-label`, or `aria-labelledby` / Ensures users know the purpose of the interactive element
rationale: Without an accessible name, screen reader users will only hear the role (e.g., 'button') without knowing what it does, making the interface impossible to navigate.
audit_check: Identify elements with command roles (like button or link) that lack a clear accessible name.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Provide accessible names for ARIA command elements".

author: David Dias
title: Avoid using deprecated ARIA roles
statement: Checks for deprecated or abstract ARIA roles to ensure long-term compatibility. TL;DR: Deprecated ARIA roles should be replaced with modern equivalents / Browsers may drop support for deprecated roles in future versions / Ensures long-term compatibility with assistive technologies
rationale: Using deprecated roles can lead to inconsistent behavior across different browsers and screen readers as they transition to newer standards.
audit_check: Search the codebase for deprecated ARIA roles like `directory` or abstract roles that shouldn't be used in HTML.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Avoid using deprecated ARIA roles".

author: David Dias
title: Ensure dialogs have an accessible name
statement: Checks that dialog elements have accessible names to orient screen reader users. TL;DR: All dialog and alertdialog elements must have a descriptive label / Use `aria-labelledby` to point to a title or `aria-label` for a direct string / Helps users understand the context and purpose of the modal
rationale: When a dialog opens, screen readers should announce its purpose immediately so users know why their focus has shifted and what information is required.
audit_check: Verify that every element with `role="dialog"` or `role="alertdialog"` has an accessible name.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Ensure dialogs have an accessible name".

author: David Dias
title: Do not use aria-hidden on the document body
statement: Ensures the document body is not set to aria-hidden, which would hide the entire page from screen readers. TL;DR: The `<body>` element should never have `aria-hidden="true"` / Hiding the body makes the entire page invisible to assistive technologies / Often happens accidentally when managing modal states
rationale: Setting `aria-hidden="true"` on the body effectively silences the entire application for screen reader users, rendering the site completely unusable.
audit_check: Check if the `<body>` element has `aria-hidden="true"` applied at any point in the lifecycle.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Do not use aria-hidden on the document body".

author: David Dias
title: Remove focusable elements from aria-hidden containers
statement: Ensures aria-hidden elements do not contain focusable content to avoid "ghost" focus. TL;DR: Elements with `aria-hidden="true"` must not contain focusable children / Focusing on a hidden element creates a 'ghost' focus for screen reader users / Use `tabindex="-1"` or `inert` to properly hide interactive elements
rationale: When a keyboard user tabs into an `aria-hidden` element, the screen reader remains silent, leaving the user with no idea where their focus is or what they can interact with.
audit_check: Scan `aria-hidden="true"` containers for focusable elements like links, buttons, or inputs.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Remove focusable elements from aria-hidden containers".

author: David Dias
title: Ensure all input fields have accessible names
statement: Checks that input fields have accessible names so screen reader users know what data each field expects. TL;DR: Every `<input>`, `<textarea>`, and `<select>` must have a programmatically associated accessible name / Preferred: associate a `<label>` via matching `for`/`id` attributes / Alternatives: `aria-label` (inline string) or `aria-labelledby` (references another element's `id`) / Placeholder text is not an accessible name — it disappears on input and is not reliably announced / Applies to WCAG 2.1 SC 1.3.1 (Info and Relationships) and SC 4.1.2 (Name, Role, Value)
rationale: Screen readers announce the accessible name of a focused input before the user types. Without a name, VoiceOver reads 'text field' and NVDA reads 'edit' with no context, making it impossible for blind users to fill out forms correctly. Voice control users (Dragon NaturallySpeaking) also need the visible label text to match the accessible name so they can say 'click Email Address' to move focus to the field.
audit_check: Find all `<input>` (excluding type='hidden'), `<textarea>`, and `<select>` elements. For each, check that one of these is true: (1) a `<label>` element with a `for` attribute matching the input's `id` exists, (2) the input has a non-empty `aria-label` attribute, or (3) the input has an `aria-labelledby` attribute pointing to a visible element. Flag any that use only `placeholder` as their label. Also check custom widgets using role=textbox, role=combobox, etc.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Ensure all input fields have accessible names".

author: David Dias
title: Provide accessible names for all interactive elements
statement: Checks that interactive elements have accessible names for clear navigation. TL;DR: Buttons, links, and other controls must have a discernable name / Names should be concise and describe the action or destination / Avoid generic names like 'Click Here' or 'More'
rationale: Interactive elements are the core of web navigation; without names, they become 'mystery meat' that users cannot confidently interact with.
audit_check: Audit all interactive elements (buttons, links, widgets) for missing or unhelpful accessible names.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Provide accessible names for all interactive elements".

author: David Dias
title: Announce dynamic content with ARIA live regions
statement: Dynamic content updates are announced to screen readers using appropriate ARIA live regions. TL;DR: Use aria-live='polite' for non-urgent updates (cart count, status messages) / Use aria-live='assertive' only for critical alerts (errors, session expiry) / Use role='alert' or role='status' for semantic live regions / The live region must exist in DOM before content changes
rationale: Without live regions, screen reader users miss dynamic updates entirely—they won't know their form submitted, their cart updated, or an error occurred.
audit_check: Verify that dynamic content changes (notifications, form errors, loading states) use aria-live regions appropriately.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Announce dynamic content with ARIA live regions".

author: David Dias
title: Provide accessible names for meter elements
statement: Checks that meter elements have accessible names to provide context for measurements. TL;DR: The `<meter>` element or `role="meter"` must have an accessible label / Use `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby` to provide context / Helps users understand what measurement is being displayed
rationale: A meter represents a scalar measurement; without a label, a user might hear a value (e.g., '50%') but have no idea if it refers to battery life, storage space, or a password strength.
audit_check: Check for `<meter>` elements or elements with `role="meter"` that lack an accessible name.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Provide accessible names for meter elements".

author: David Dias
title: Provide accessible names for progress bars
statement: Checks that progressbar elements have accessible names TL;DR: Use `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby` to name progress bars / Ensure the name describes what the progress indicates / Avoid redundant text like "progress" in the label / Provide `aria-valuenow`, `aria-valuemin`, and `aria-valuemax` when the value is known / Visual progress meters should use real progress semantics rather than decorative divs when they communicate status
rationale: Without an accessible name, screen reader users will only hear that a progress bar exists but won't know what task or process it represents.
audit_check: Check if all progress bar elements (role="progressbar") have an accessible name via aria-label or aria-labelledby.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Provide accessible names for progress bars".

author: David Dias
title: Include required ARIA attributes for roles
statement: Checks that elements have required ARIA attributes for their roles TL;DR: Identify roles that require specific state or property attributes / Ensure attributes like `aria-valuenow` for sliders are present / Validate that all required ARIA attributes are correctly implemented
rationale: Certain ARIA roles are incomplete without their required attributes, preventing assistive technologies from correctly communicating the element's state or value.
audit_check: Verify that all ARIA roles have their mandatory attributes as defined by the WAI-ARIA specification.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Include required ARIA attributes for roles".

author: David Dias
title: Ensure ARIA roles contain required child roles
statement: Elements with certain ARIA roles must contain the required child roles or the widget structure will be broken for assistive technologies. TL;DR: Container roles mandate specific owned child roles: `tablist` → `tab`, `list`/`listbox` → `listitem`/`option`, `menu`/`menubar` → `menuitem`, `tree` → `treeitem`, `grid`/`rowgroup` → `row` / Missing required children break the accessibility tree so screen readers cannot enumerate items or announce counts / Use `role='none'` or `role='presentation'` on purely structural wrapper elements inside the container to avoid invalid nesting / Applies to WAI-ARIA 1.2 required owned elements for composite widget roles
rationale: Screen readers like NVDA and VoiceOver navigate composite widgets (menus, tabs, trees) by moving between the required child roles. If a `tablist` contains `<div>` elements instead of `role='tab'`, the user hears no tabs at all. JAWS announces 'list of 5 items' only when `role='listitem'` children exist inside `role='list'`. Without correct nesting, the entire widget becomes opaque to keyboard-only and screen reader users.
audit_check: Identify all elements with ARIA container roles (tablist, list, listbox, menu, menubar, tree, treegrid, grid, rowgroup, radiogroup). For each, verify it contains the required owned child roles per the WAI-ARIA spec: tablist must own tab elements; list must own listitem; listbox must own option; menu/menubar must own menuitem, menuitemcheckbox, or menuitemradio; tree must own treeitem; grid must own row (which owns gridcell); radiogroup must own radio. Flag any container roles missing required children.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Ensure ARIA roles contain required child roles".

author: David Dias
title: Ensure ARIA roles are contained by required parent roles
statement: Checks that elements with certain roles have required parent roles TL;DR: Certain roles (like `listitem`) must be owned by specific parent roles (like `list`) / Ensure children elements are not orphaned from their semantic containers / Maintain valid ARIA hierarchies for menu items, tabs, and list items
rationale: If an ARIA child role (like a menu item) is not contained within its required parent role (like a menu), screen readers may fail to announce the item as part of a group, breaking navigation.
audit_check: Verify that elements with roles like listitem, tab, or menuitem are correctly nested within their required parent roles.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Ensure ARIA roles are contained by required parent roles".

author: David Dias
title: Use valid ARIA role values
statement: Checks for valid ARIA role values TL;DR: Use only standard ARIA roles defined in the W3C specification / Avoid typos or non-existent roles (e.g., use `checkbox`, not `check-box`) / Ensure roles are applied to appropriate HTML elements / Prefer native HTML controls over custom ARIA widgets whenever possible
rationale: Invalid or misspelled ARIA roles are ignored by browsers and assistive technologies, rendering the intended accessibility features useless and potentially confusing users.
audit_check: Search for any role attributes that use non-standard or misspelled ARIA role values.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Use valid ARIA role values".

author: David Dias
title: Avoid focusable descendants in role="text" elements
statement: Checks that elements with role='text' have no focusable descendants TL;DR: Elements with `role="text"` should not contain interactive children (links, buttons) / Ensure `role="text"` only contains static text content / Prevent accessibility "black holes" where interactive items are hidden from screen readers
rationale: Using `role="text"` on a container forces screen readers to treat everything inside as a single string of text, which effectively hides any interactive elements from users who rely on assistive technology.
audit_check: Identify elements with role="text" and verify they do not contain any focusable elements like buttons, links, or inputs.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Avoid focusable descendants in role="text" elements".

author: David Dias
title: Provide accessible names for toggle fields
statement: Checks that toggle fields (checkbox, radio, switch) have accessible names TL;DR: Use `aria-label`, `aria-labelledby`, or `<label>` for checkboxes and radios / Ensure the label clearly describes the state or action of the toggle / Avoid empty or non-descriptive labels for switches
rationale: Toggle fields like checkboxes and switches are unusable for screen reader users if they don't have a label, as the user won't know what they are turning on or off.
audit_check: Check all toggle fields (checkboxes, radio buttons, switches) for a valid accessible name.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Provide accessible names for toggle fields".

author: David Dias
title: Provide accessible names for tooltips
statement: Checks that tooltip elements have accessible names TL;DR: Tooltips must have an accessible name or be referenced by `aria-describedby` / Ensure the tooltip content is actually accessible to assistive technology / Verify that tooltips are correctly associated with their trigger elements
rationale: Tooltips often contain essential information; if they aren't properly named or associated with an element, that information remains hidden from screen reader users.
audit_check: Verify that all elements with role="tooltip" have an accessible name or are linked to a trigger element via aria-describedby.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Provide accessible names for tooltips".

author: David Dias
title: Provide accessible names for tree items
statement: All elements with role="treeitem" must have a descriptive accessible name so screen reader users can navigate hierarchical tree widgets. TL;DR: Every element with `role='treeitem'` must have a non-empty accessible name / Text content of the element is used as the name by default — ensure it is descriptive / Use `aria-label` to override or supplement the visible text (e.g., adding file type context) / Use `aria-labelledby` to compose a name from multiple visible elements within the item / A treeitem with `aria-expanded` must also convey its expanded/collapsed state — this is separate from its name
rationale: Tree widgets represent hierarchical data (file explorers, nested navigation, organization charts). Screen readers announce each focused treeitem's name, level, and position — e.g., 'src, collapsed, level 1, 1 of 3'. If the name is empty or generic ('folder', 'item'), blind users cannot distinguish between nodes and cannot navigate the hierarchy with confidence. VoiceOver on macOS uses the name to populate the rotor, and NVDA reads it as the user moves through the tree with arrow keys.
audit_check: Find all elements with `role='treeitem'`. For each, determine its accessible name via the accname computation: check `aria-labelledby` first, then `aria-label`, then visible text content. Flag any treeitem with an empty or whitespace-only accessible name. Also check whether treeitems with children have `aria-expanded` set to 'true' or 'false' (not just absent).
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Provide accessible names for tree items".

author: David Dias
title: Use valid values for ARIA attributes
statement: Checks for valid values in ARIA attributes TL;DR: Ensure ARIA attribute values (like `aria-expanded="true"`) are valid / Avoid using "yes/no" where "true/false" is required / Check that IDs referenced in `aria-labelledby` or `aria-owns` actually exist
rationale: Invalid attribute values cause ARIA properties to be ignored or misinterpreted by assistive technologies, leading to a broken or confusing user experience.
audit_check: Validate that all ARIA attribute values conform to the allowed types (boolean, integer, ID list, etc.).
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Use valid values for ARIA attributes".

author: David Dias
title: Ensure ARIA attributes are valid
statement: All ARIA attributes must be valid and exist in the WAI-ARIA specification. TL;DR: Use only valid, standard-defined ARIA attributes / Avoid misspelled or non-existent aria-* properties / Ensure screen readers correctly interpret element roles and states
rationale: Invalid ARIA attributes are ignored by browsers and screen readers, potentially leaving users with disabilities unable to navigate or understand the interface.
audit_check: Identify any invalid or misspelled ARIA attributes on HTML elements.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Ensure ARIA attributes are valid".

author: David Dias
title: Provide audio descriptions for video
statement: Videos with important visual content include audio descriptions that narrate visual information for blind users. TL;DR: Add audio descriptions for visual-only content (actions, expressions, text) / Use track element with kind='descriptions' for separate description track / Provide extended description version if gaps between dialogue are too short / Integrate visual descriptions into main narration when possible
rationale: Blind users miss critical plot points, product demos, and on-screen information that's only shown visually—audio descriptions provide equal access to the complete experience.
audit_check: Identify videos where visual content conveys information not available in the audio track (actions, expressions, scene changes, on-screen text). Verify audio descriptions are available or visual content is described in dialogue.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Provide audio descriptions for video".

author: David Dias
title: Avoid autofocus on form fields
statement: Form fields do not use the autofocus attribute which can disorient screen reader users and cause unexpected page behavior. TL;DR: Avoid autofocus on pages with content before the form / Autofocus disrupts screen reader users who lose page context / Use JavaScript focus after user interaction instead of page load / Login and search-only pages are exceptions where autofocus may be acceptable
rationale: Autofocus teleports screen reader users to mid-page without context—they miss everything before the form and have no idea where they landed.
audit_check: Search for autofocus attributes on form elements. Verify that page load does not unexpectedly move focus away from the page top, especially on pages with content before the form.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Avoid autofocus on form fields".

author: David Dias
title: Avoid autoplaying media
statement: Audio and video content does not autoplay, or provides immediate controls to pause or stop playback. TL;DR: Never autoplay audio—it interferes with screen readers / If video must autoplay, ensure it's muted by default / Provide immediately accessible pause/stop controls / Autoplay should stop after 5 seconds or provide stop mechanism
rationale: Autoplaying audio drowns out screen reader speech, startles users, and wastes bandwidth—providing user control is essential for accessibility and good UX.
audit_check: Verify no audio or video autoplays on page load. If autoplay is essential, confirm media is muted by default and pause controls are immediately accessible via keyboard within the first few tab stops.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Avoid autoplaying media".

author: David Dias
title: Provide accessible names for buttons
statement: All buttons must have a discernible, descriptive accessible name for screen readers. TL;DR: Ensure every <button> has a discernible, descriptive label / Use inner text, aria-label, or aria-labelledby for identification / Use buttons for actions and state changes, not page navigation / Avoid empty buttons or those containing only non-text icons
rationale: Buttons without accessible names are announced as 'button' by screen readers, leaving users unable to determine what action will be triggered.
audit_check: Scan for buttons that lack descriptive text or accessible labels.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Provide accessible names for buttons".

author: David Dias
title: Meet minimum color contrast ratios
statement: Text and background colors must have sufficient contrast to be readable by users with low vision or color blindness. TL;DR: Normal text (< 18pt or < 14pt bold): minimum contrast ratio of 4.5:1 — WCAG 2.1 SC 1.4.3 Level AA / Large text (≥ 18pt / 24px, or ≥ 14pt bold / ~18.67px bold): minimum 3:1 contrast ratio / Non-text UI components (icons, focus indicators, input borders): minimum 3:1 against adjacent color — WCAG 2.1 SC 1.4.11 Level AA / WCAG 2.1 SC 1.4.6 (Level AAA) requires 7:1 for normal text and 4.5:1 for large text / Decorative text and logotypes are exempt from contrast requirements
rationale: Approximately 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women have some form of color vision deficiency. Low contrast text is also difficult for users with low vision, aging eyesight, or those reading in bright sunlight. Insufficient contrast is one of the most common WCAG failures and directly prevents users from reading content they need.
audit_check: Evaluate the contrast ratio between text color and its background for all text on the page. Use the WCAG relative luminance formula: for normal text (< 18pt or < 14pt bold), the ratio must be ≥ 4.5:1; for large text (≥ 18pt or ≥ 14pt bold), the ratio must be ≥ 3:1. Also check non-text UI components (input borders, button outlines, icons) for ≥ 3:1 ratio against adjacent colors per WCAG 2.1 SC 1.4.11. Check all interactive states: default, hover, focus, active, and visited.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Meet minimum color contrast ratios".

author: David Dias
title: Keep repeated help mechanisms in a consistent location
statement: When help or support mechanisms appear on multiple pages in the same flow, they stay in the same relative order so users can find them predictably. TL;DR: Put repeated help in the same place across related pages / Keep the same relative order at the same breakpoint and zoom level / Review chat, phone, contact, FAQ, and help-center entry points together / Inconsistency across steps matters more than the exact visual style
rationale: Users who need help during a task should not have to hunt for it on every screen. Predictable placement reduces stress and makes support easier to find when a user is already struggling.
audit_check: Audit repeated help mechanisms across this set of pages. Check whether contact links, chat triggers, help-center links, or support phone numbers appear in the same relative order on each page.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Keep repeated help mechanisms in a consistent location".

author: David Dias
title: Ensure content remains usable without CSS
statement: Content structure, instructions, and primary tasks remain understandable and operable when author CSS is disabled or replaced by user styles. TL;DR: Use semantic HTML so headings, lists, and form relationships survive without CSS / Keep DOM order aligned with the reading and task-completion order / Do not put essential labels, instructions, or required markers in CSS generated content / Test key journeys with author styles disabled or overridden by user styles
rationale: Users can browse with custom styles, high contrast modes, reader tools, or failed stylesheets. If the page only makes sense visually, content order, instructions, and task flow break as soon as presentation changes.
audit_check: Find pages or components that rely on CSS for meaning. Verify the page still has a logical reading order, visible labels, instructions, error text, and operable primary actions when author styles are disabled or replaced by user styles.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Ensure content remains usable without CSS".

author: David Dias
title: Hide decorative elements from assistive technology
statement: Decorative images and visual elements are hidden from screen readers using aria-hidden or empty alt attributes. TL;DR: Use alt='' (empty) for decorative images—not alt='image' or missing alt / Add aria-hidden='true' to decorative SVGs and icons / Use CSS background-image for purely decorative visuals / Role='presentation' removes semantic meaning from elements / Do not automatically raise performance findings on decorative micro-assets unless the snippet shows real layout instability / Example safe pattern: `` is usually a decorative no-op, not a finding by itself
rationale: Screen readers announce every image and icon—decorative elements clutter the experience with meaningless 'image, decorative border, image, bullet' announcements.
audit_check: Verify decorative images have empty alt attributes (alt=''), decorative icons use aria-hidden='true', and background images used for decoration are not announced by screen readers. Do not report decorative images as accessibility or performance failures unless the code shows a concrete problem rather than a hypothetical optimization.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Hide decorative elements from assistive technology".

author: David Dias
title: Use correct definition list structure
statement: Definition lists (<dl>) must only contain valid <dt> and <dd> elements. TL;DR: Ensure <dl> contains only <dt>, <dd>, or <script>/<template> tags / Avoid wrapping list items in invalid container elements like <div> / Maintain semantic relationships between terms and descriptions
rationale: Broken list structures confuse assistive technologies, preventing users from understanding the relationship between terms and their definitions.
audit_check: Verify that all <dl> elements contain only valid child elements (dt, dd, or allowed wrappers).
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Use correct definition list structure".

author: David Dias
title: Wrap definition items in a definition list
statement: Description terms (<dt>) and details (<dd>) must be contained within a <dl> element. TL;DR: Place all <dt> (terms) and <dd> (descriptions) within a <dl> / Avoid using description list items as standalone elements / Ensure proper grouping of related metadata or glossary terms
rationale: Standalone <dt> or <dd> elements lose their semantic meaning and fail to provide the context needed for assistive technologies to link terms with definitions.
audit_check: Locate any <dt> or <dd> elements that are not children of a <dl> element.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Wrap definition items in a definition list".

author: David Dias
title: Use unique IDs for active elements
statement: All focusable or active elements must have a unique ID attribute. TL;DR: Ensure all focusable elements (links, buttons, inputs) have unique id values / Avoid duplicate IDs that can break keyboard navigation and focus management / Prevent screen reader confusion when navigating interactive controls
rationale: Duplicate IDs on active elements can cause browsers and assistive technologies to skip items, misdirect focus, or fail to trigger the correct action.
audit_check: Search for duplicate id attributes on focusable or active HTML elements.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Use unique IDs for active elements".

author: David Dias
title: Use unique IDs for ARIA references
statement: IDs referenced by ARIA attributes must be unique to ensure correct accessibility relationships. TL;DR: Ensure IDs referenced by ARIA attributes (e.g., aria-labelledby) are unique / Avoid duplicate IDs that lead to ambiguous accessibility relationships / Verify that ARIA controls correctly target their intended elements
rationale: When ARIA attributes point to duplicate IDs, assistive technologies may read the wrong label or description, providing misleading information to the user.
audit_check: Identify elements where an ARIA attribute references an id that appears multiple times in the DOM.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Use unique IDs for ARIA references".

author: David Dias
title: Ensure headings contain text
statement: All heading elements (h1-h6) must have visible, descriptive content. TL;DR: Add visible, descriptive text to all heading elements (h1-h6) / Avoid using headings solely for styling or as empty placeholders / Ensure document structure is meaningful for screen reader navigation
rationale: Empty headings create 'ghost' stops in the document outline, confusing users who rely on headings to navigate and understand the page structure.
audit_check: Find any heading tags (h1 through h6) that are empty or contain only non-perceivable whitespace.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Ensure headings contain text".

author: David Dias
title: Fix empty and broken links
statement: All links contain accessible text content and do not lead to broken destinations. TL;DR: Every link must have accessible text (visible or via aria-label) / Icon-only links need aria-label describing the destination / Empty anchor tags are completely inaccessible—always add content / Use visually-hidden text when visual labels aren't desired
rationale: Screen readers announce empty links as just 'link' with no context—users have no idea where they lead or what they do, making navigation impossible.
audit_check: Scan for links with no text content (empty anchor tags, icon-only links without labels). Verify all links have accessible names via text content, aria-label, or aria-labelledby. Check for broken link destinations.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Fix empty and broken links".

author: David Dias
title: Prevent seizure-triggering flashing content
statement: Content does not flash more than three times per second to prevent seizures in users with photosensitive epilepsy. TL;DR: Never flash content more than 3 times per second (WCAG Level A) / Flashing area must be smaller than 25% of viewport / Red flashing is especially dangerous—avoid entirely / Test GIFs, videos, and CSS animations for rapid flashing
rationale: Flashing content between 3-60 Hz can trigger seizures in people with photosensitive epilepsy—this is a critical safety requirement, not just an accessibility preference.
audit_check: Verify no content flashes more than 3 times per second, and that any flashing content occupies less than 25% of the viewport. Test animated GIFs, videos, and CSS animations for rapid flashing patterns.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Prevent seizure-triggering flashing content".

author: David Dias
title: Manage focus during dynamic interactions
statement: Focus is programmatically managed during dynamic interactions like modals, page transitions, and content updates. TL;DR: Move focus to modal when opened, return to trigger when closed / Focus new content after SPA navigation or dynamic updates / Use tabindex='-1' to make non-interactive elements focusable / Never lose focus to an unexpected location
rationale: Poor focus management leaves keyboard users stranded—they can't find new content, get trapped in closed modals, or lose their place entirely after interactions.
audit_check: Verify that focus is properly managed when opening/closing modals, navigating between views, or updating content dynamically.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Manage focus during dynamic interactions".

author: David Dias
title: Keep focused elements unobscured
statement: Sticky headers, footers, banners, and overlays must not fully hide the element that currently has keyboard focus. TL;DR: Sticky UI must not cover the focused control while keyboard users tab through the page / Use `scroll-padding` or equivalent spacing when fixed headers or footers are present / Test with cookie banners, chat widgets, and consent bars open / Re-test at zoomed and mobile layouts where overlap problems usually appear
rationale: A visible focus ring is not enough if the focused element sits behind a sticky header or footer. Keyboard users need to see the actual focused control and the focus indicator at the same time in order to continue the task.
audit_check: Audit keyboard focus with all sticky UI active. Check headers, footers, cookie banners, promo bars, and chat launchers for cases where the focused element scrolls underneath them.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Keep focused elements unobscured".

author: David Dias
title: Ensure logical focus order
statement: Tab focus order follows the visual layout and logical reading sequence of the page. TL;DR: Tab order should match visual reading order (left-to-right, top-to-bottom) / DOM order determines tab order—arrange HTML to match visual layout / Never use positive tabindex values (1, 2, 3)—they break natural flow / Use CSS for visual positioning, not DOM reordering
rationale: When focus jumps unexpectedly, keyboard users get disoriented and can't find content—mismatched visual and focus order makes navigation impossible.
audit_check: Tab through the page and verify focus moves in a logical sequence matching visual layout. Check that modals trap focus appropriately, and focus returns to triggering elements when dialogs close.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Ensure logical focus order".

author: David Dias
title: Use a single label for each form field
statement: Form fields should have exactly one associated <label> element for maximum clarity. TL;DR: Associate each form input with exactly one <label> element / Use aria-labelledby if multiple pieces of text must label a single field / Avoid duplicate labels that can confuse screen readers and voice control
rationale: Multiple labels for a single field can cause screen readers to announce redundant information or fail to correctly associate the input with its purpose.
audit_check: Search for form inputs that are associated with more than one <label> element.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Use a single label for each form field".

author: David Dias
title: Associate labels with form controls
statement: Form inputs must have programmatically associated labels. TL;DR: Use `<label>` elements for all form inputs / Connect labels using `for` and `id` attributes / Placeholder text is not a label and must not be the only field name / Use `<fieldset>` and `<legend>` when multiple controls share one question / Ensure every input has a clear, accessible name
rationale: Properly associated labels ensure that screen readers can identify the purpose of form inputs and increase the clickable area for users with motor impairments.
audit_check: Verify that all form controls (input, select, textarea) have programmatically associated labels using the 'for' and 'id' attributes. Flag placeholder-only labels and grouped controls that lack a fieldset legend.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Associate labels with form controls".

author: David Dias
title: Provide titles for iframes and frames
statement: iframes and frames must have a title attribute to describe their content. TL;DR: Add a descriptive `title` attribute to every `<iframe>` / Ensure titles clearly describe the frame's content / Helps screen reader users navigate between frames
rationale: Frame titles allow users of assistive technology to quickly understand the content of an iframe without having to navigate into it, which is crucial for navigation and orientation.
audit_check: Verify that all <iframe> and <frame> elements have a non-empty 'title' attribute.
citation: Dias, D. Front-End Checklist, rule "Provide titles for iframes and frames".

author: David Dias
title: Use logical heading hierarchy
statement: Headings follow a sequential structure (h1 to h6) that reflects the content hierarchy without skipping levels. TL;DR: Use exactly one h1 per page for the main title / Never skip heading levels (h1 → h2 → h3, not h1 → h3) / Heading text should describe the content that follows / Don't use headings for visual styling—use CSS instead
