statement: Good alt text: - tells people what information the image provides - describes the content and function of the image - is specific, meaningful and concise Use normal punctuation, like commas and full stops, so the text is easy to read and understand. Generally, aim for no more than 2 sentences of alt text. Do not write alt text that: - includes the name of the photographer or person who created the image - starts with ‘Image of’, ‘Graphic of’ or common information that would repeat across every image - repeats information from the page - includes extra information not in the image
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Images" (Alt text > Writing good alt text).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
title: Images: Research on images
statement: In March 2023, we updated this page to help teams make decisions on when to use images in their services. In particular, we added a section on how to use images and ensure they’re as accessible as possible – giving advice to teams on how to meet or surpass relevant WCAG AA guidelines, in line with the GOV.UK Design System accessibility strategy. To help us validate that this guidance is useful and practical for service teams across government, we want to hear from you. We’re looking for feedback about any of these areas: - how you use images to give information to users - examples of the types of images used in services - how you create and choose images to use in your service - how you implement images (for frontend performance) Give us your feedback and examples by posting a comment on the ‘Images’ discussion on GitHub.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Images" (Research on images).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
title: Layout: Screen size
statement: Design for small screens first, starting with a single-column layout. For most types of page, we recommend using either a 'two-thirds' or a 'two-thirds and one-third' layout. That stops lines of text getting so long that the page becomes difficult to read on desktop devices. This would usually mean no more than 75 characters per line. Never make assumptions about what devices people are using. Design for different screen sizes rather than specific devices. The default maximum page width is 1020px, but you can make it wider if your content requires it.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Layout" (Screen size).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
title: Layout: Setting up page wrappers
statement: If you want to build your layout from scratch, or understand what each of the parts are responsible for, here’s an explanation of how the page wrappers work.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Layout" (Setting up page wrappers).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Layout > Setting up page wrappers > Limiting width of content
title: Layout: Limiting width of content
statement: To set up your layout you will need to create 2 wrappers. The first should have the class govuk-width-container, which sets the maximum width of the content but does not add any vertical margin or padding. If your design requires them, you should place components such as the Breadcrumbs component, Back link component and Phase banner component inside this wrapper so that they sit directly underneath the header.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Layout" (Setting up page wrappers > Limiting width of content).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Layout > Setting up page wrappers > Add vertical space
title: Layout: Add vertical space
statement: Within govuk-width-container you should add the govuk-main-wrapper class to your element. This adds responsive padding to the top and bottom of the page and will be the container for your main content. If you’re not using the Breadcrumbs component or Back link component in your design, add the correct amount of vertical padding above the content by adding one of the following to your element: - the govuk-main-wrapper--auto-spacing class - the govuk-main-wrapper--l class - if govuk-main-wrapper--auto-spacing does not work for your service
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Layout" (Setting up page wrappers > Add vertical space).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
title: Layout: Using the grid system
statement: Use the grid system to lay out the content on your service’s pages. Most GOV.UK pages follow a 'two-thirds and one-third' layout, but the grid system allows for a number of additional combinations when necessary. Your main content should always be in a two-thirds column even if you’re not using a corresponding one-third column for secondary content.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Layout" (Using the grid system).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Layout > Using the grid system > Understanding the grid system
title: Layout: Understanding the grid system
statement: The grid is structured with a govuk-grid-row wrapper which acts as a row to contain your grid columns. You can add columns inside this wrapper to create your layout. To define your columns add the class beginning with govuk-grid-column- to a new container followed by the width, for example govuk-grid-column-one-third to apply your desired width. The available widths are:
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Layout" (Using the grid system > Understanding the grid system).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Layout > Using the grid system > Desktop specific grid classes
title: Layout: Desktop specific grid classes
statement: To specify a width at the desktop breakpoint you can use the desktop specific grid classes. For example govuk-grid-column-two-thirds-from-desktop will set your column width to be two-thirds width at the desktop breakpoint only. The desktop specific classes also allow you to set the width of the tablet breakpoint by using them in combination with the standard grid classes. For example using govuk-grid-column-one-half and govuk-grid-column-two-thirds-from-desktop together will mean the column will be one-half at the tablet breakpoint and two-thirds width at desktop.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Layout" (Using the grid system > Desktop specific grid classes).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
title: Layout: Width override classes
statement: If you need to constrain the width of an element independently of the grid system, you can use width override classes. The width override classes start with govuk-!-width-, followed by the width on larger screen sizes. For example, govuk-!-width-one-half will apply a width of 50% and govuk-!-width-two-thirdswill apply a width of 66.66%. These examples are for the generic width override classes - read specific guidance on setting text input width.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Layout" (Width override classes).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
title: Layout: Override how elements display
statement: You can use display override classes if you need to override how elements display on the page. Use: - govuk-!-display-block to display as a block - govuk-!-display-inline to display inline - govuk-!-display-inline-block to display as an inline block - govuk-!-display-none to remove the element from the page You can also remove elements from the printed version of the page using govuk-!-display-none-print.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Layout" (Override how elements display).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Layout > Hide elements and keep them accessible to screen readers
title: Layout: Hide elements and keep them accessible to screen readers
statement: You can stop elements from being displayed on the page and keep their contents available to screen readers using govuk-visually-hidden. You can use this to present content to screen reader users that sighted users do not need. If the element is focusable, such as a link, you can make it become visible when receiving keyboard focus using govuk-visually-hidden-focusable.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Layout" (Hide elements and keep them accessible to screen readers).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
title: Links
statement: Links are blue and underlined by default. If your link is at the end of a sentence or paragraph, make sure that the linked text does not include the full stop.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Links" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Links > Links without a visited state
title: Links: Links without a visited state
statement: Use the govuk-link--no-visited-state modifier class where it is not helpful to distinguish between visited and unvisited states, for example when linking to pages with frequently-changing content such as the dashboard for an admin interface.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Links" (Links without a visited state).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
title: Links: External links
statement: If it's an external link to a non-government website, make that clear in the link text. For example, 'read advice on writing link text from [name of organisation]'. There's no need to say explicitly that you're linking to an external site. Do not use an external link icon.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Links" (External links).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Links > Opening links in a new tab
title: Links: Opening links in a new tab
statement: Avoid opening links in a new tab or window. It can be disorienting - and can cause accessibility problems for people who cannot visually perceive that the new tab has opened. If you need a link to open in a new tab, include the words ‘opens in new tab’ as part of the link. A use case example is to stop the user losing information they’ve entered into a form. There's no need to tell the user the new tab opens in a new window as this is the default behaviour for most browsers. Include rel="noreferrer noopener" along with target="blank" to reduce the risk of reverse tabnabbing. The following example shows how to do this in HTML. If you're displaying lots of links together and want to save space and avoid repetition, consider doing both of the following: - adding a line of text before the links saying 'The following links open in a new tab' - including (opens in new tab) as part of the link text, so that part of the link text is visually hidden but still accessible to screen readers
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Links" (Opening links in a new tab).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
title: Links: Links on dark backgrounds
statement: Use the govuk-link--inverse modifier class to show white links on dark backgrounds. For example, in headers, custom components, and patterns with darker backgrounds. Make sure all users can see the links. The white links and background colour must have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 to meet WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.3 Contrast (minimum), level AA.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Links" (Links on dark backgrounds).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
title: Links: Links without underlines
statement: Use the govuk-link--no-underline modifier class to remove underlines from links. Only do this if the context tells the user that the text is a link, even without the underline. For example, links in a header or side navigation might not need underlines. Users will understand that they’re links because of where they are on the page.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Links" (Links without underlines).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
title: Lists
statement: Use lists to make blocks of text easier to read, and to break information into manageable chunks.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Lists" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
title: Lists: Bulleted lists
statement: Introduce bulleted lists with a lead-in line ending in a colon. Start each item with a lowercase letter, and do not use a full stop at the end.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Lists" (Bulleted lists).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
title: Lists: Numbered lists
statement: Use numbered lists instead of bulleted lists when the order of the items is relevant. You do not need to use a lead-in line for numbered lists. Items in a numbered list should end in a full stop because each should be a complete sentence.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Lists" (Numbered lists).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Lists > Adding extra spacing between list items
title: Lists: Adding extra spacing between list items
statement: If a list is hard to read because the items run across multiple lines you can add extra spacing.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Lists" (Adding extra spacing between list items).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
title: Page template
statement: Use this template to keep your pages consistent with the rest of GOV.UK. This page template combines the boilerplate markup and components needed for a basic GOV.UK page. It includes: - JavaScript that adds a .govuk-frontend-supported class, which is required by components with JavaScript behaviour - the Skip link component, Header component and Footer component - the favicon, and other related theme icons In the examples provided, we show both HTML and Nunjucks. You can use the HTML examples if you are not able to use Nunjucks. If you use HTML you’ll need to update it manually when new versions are released. If you're using Nunjucks you can get this page template by installing GOV.UK Frontend. You’ll get updates to the page template when we update GOV.UK Frontend.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Page template" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
title: Page template: Customised page template
statement: You can customise the page template, for example, by: - adding a service name and navigation - including a Back link component or Phase banner component
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Page template" (Customised page template).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
title: Page template: Changing template content
statement: If you’re using Nunjucks, you can change the template’s content using options. How you set an option depends on whether it's a 'variable' option or a 'block' option. To set a 'variable' option, use set to pass in a single value or string. For example, to add a class to the element using the bodyClasses option: By default, the template contains a Skip link component, Header component and Footer component, all of which require 'blocks' to change. To set a 'block' option, use block to pass in a multiline value or HTML markup. For example, to add a block of HTML before the closing element in the page template using the bodyEnd option: To change the components that are included in the page template by default, set their equivalent blocks. For example:
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Page template" (Changing template content).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
title: Paragraphs
statement: The default paragraph font size is 19px. You can also add classes to create a lead paragraph or smaller body copy to convey hierarchy in your page.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Paragraphs" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
title: Paragraphs: Lead paragraph
statement: A lead paragraph is an introductory paragraph that you can use at the top of a page to summarise the content. Lead paragraphs use 24px type on desktop and if it’s needed you should only use it once per page.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Paragraphs" (Lead paragraph).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
title: Paragraphs: Body small
statement: You can use the govuk-body-s class sparingly to make your paragraph font size 16px instead of 19px. The majority of your body copy should use the standard 19px paragraph size.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Paragraphs" (Body small).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
title: Section break
statement: You can use the govuk-section-break classes on an element to create a thematic break between sections of content. govuk-section-break has class-based modifiers for different size margins. By default govuk-section-break is only visible by its margin. You can add the govuk-section-break--visible class to make it visible with a separator line.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Section break" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
title: Spacing
statement: The Design System uses two different spacing scales – responsive and static.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Spacing" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
title: Spacing: Responsive spacing
statement: The responsive spacing scale adapts based on screen size. The spacing for 'large screens' is used when the screen is wider than the tablet breakpoint (640px). Spacing for the smallest units (0-3) stays the same for all screen sizes. The responsive spacing scale Spacing unit Small screens Large screens 0 0 0 1 5px 5px 2 10px 10px 3 15px 15px 4 15px 20px 5 15px 25px 6 20px 30px 7 25px 40px 8 30px 50px 9 40px 60px
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Spacing" (Responsive spacing).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
title: Spacing: Static spacing
statement: The static spacing scale stays the same for all screen sizes, and uses the same spacing as 'large screens' in the responsive spacing scale. The static spacing scale Spacing unit All screens 0 0 1 5px 2 10px 3 15px 4 20px 5 25px 6 30px 7 40px 8 50px 9 60px
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Spacing" (Static spacing).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Spacing > Applying spacing in your own CSS
title: Spacing: Applying spacing in your own CSS
statement: If you want to reference the spacing scale in your CSS, use the spacing helpers.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Spacing" (Applying spacing in your own CSS).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Spacing > Applying spacing in your own CSS > Using the responsive spacing helper
title: Spacing: Using the responsive spacing helper
statement: To use the responsive spacing scale, include either: - the govuk-responsive-margin mixin - the govuk-responsive-padding mixin For example, to apply spacing unit 6 for 30px padding on large screens and 20px on small screens, use: You can also add an argument to apply margin or padding in a single direction. For example, to apply spacing unit 6 for a 30px bottom margin on large screens and a 20px bottom margin on small screens, use:

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Spacing > Applying spacing in your own CSS > Using the static spacing helper
title: Spacing: Using the static spacing helper
statement: For the static spacing scale, use the govuk-spacing function. For example, to apply spacing unit 6 for 30px top padding on all screens, use: For negative spacing, use a negative spacing unit number. For example, to apply spacing unit -3 for a negative 15px top margin all screens, use:
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Spacing" (Applying spacing in your own CSS > Using the static spacing helper).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
title: Spacing: Overriding spacing
statement: Occasionally, you might need to make minor adjustments like adding or removing spacing to elements of your design. You can use the spacing override classes for this.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Spacing" (Overriding spacing).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Spacing > Overriding spacing > Responsive spacing override classes
title: Spacing: Responsive spacing override classes
statement: The responsive spacing override classes start with: govuk-!-, followed by either margin- or padding-, and then a spacing unit number. To apply spacing in a single direction, include left-, right-, top-, or bottom- just before the spacing unit. For example, use: - govuk-!-margin-9 to apply a 40px margin to all sides of the element on small screens, increasing to 60px on large screens - govuk-!-padding-right-5 to apply 15px of padding to the right side of the element on small screens, increasing to 25px on large screens - govuk-!-margin-0 to remove all margins at all screen sizes
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Spacing" (Overriding spacing > Responsive spacing override classes).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Spacing > Overriding spacing > Static spacing override classes
title: Spacing: Static spacing override classes
statement: The static spacing override classes start with govuk-!-static. Use them the same way as the responsive spacing override classes. For example, use: - govuk-!-static-margin-9 to apply a 60px margin to all sides of the element at all screen sizes - govuk-!-static-padding-right-5 to apply 25px of padding to the right side of the element at all screen sizes - govuk-!-static-margin-0 to remove all margins at all screen sizes, same as govuk-!-margin-0
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Spacing" (Overriding spacing > Static spacing override classes).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
title: Type scale
statement: The type scale is a collection of font sizes and line heights that underpin all of the typographic styles on GOV.UK. It has been tested and iterated for readability on different devices. When creating new components, always start by using the existing typography styles. If you need to create a new style, align it with one of the points on the type scale.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Type scale" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
title: Type scale: How it works
statement: Like the spacing scale, every point on the type scale uses a line height in a multiple of 5px. This creates a consistent vertical rhythm, which makes pages easier to scan and read. GOV.UK Frontend outputs CSS in relative units like em or rem. This helps the type resize better when zoomed or magnified. We've used pixels (px) here so it's easier to understand.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Type scale" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
title: Type scale: Responsive behaviour
statement: The type scale changes based on screen size. The scale for ‘large screens’ is used when the screen is wider than the tablet breakpoint (640px).
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Type scale" (Responsive behaviour).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Type scale > Using the type scale in your own CSS
title: Type scale: Using the type scale in your own CSS
statement: Include the govuk-font mixin to use GOV.UK typography in your CSS. For example, if you want a custom element to use type scale point 19, use: You can add additional arguments to control font weight, use tabular font spacing, or to override the line height:
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Type scale" (Using the type scale in your own CSS).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Type scale > Using the type scale in your own CSS > If you only want to set the font size
title: Type scale: If you only want to set the font size
statement: Do not use govuk-font if you only want to change the font size and line height as it includes additional typography-related CSS like the New Transport font family. Instead, you should use the govuk-font-size mixin:
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Type scale" (Using the type scale in your own CSS > If you only want to set the font size).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
title: Typeface
statement: If your service is on the service.gov.uk subdomain you must use the GDS Transport font.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Typeface" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Typeface > When not to use the GDS Transport font
title: Typeface: When not to use the GDS Transport font
statement: If your service is publicly available on a subdomain other than service.gov.uk, use an alternative typeface. Read our guidance on Using GOV.UK Frontend without GOV.UK branding for how to change your service’s font to a similar typeface. If you’re not sure whether you should use GDS Transport, do one of the following: - read the service manual section ‘If your service is not on GOV.UK’ section on ‘Making your service look like GOV.UK’ - contact the Design System team
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Typeface" (When not to use the GDS Transport font).

title: Content
statement: Use the NHS accessibility checklist for: a full list of WCAG 2.2 success criteria and guidance for levels A and AA some success criteria and best practice for level AAA
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Content".

author: NHS England
title: Design
statement: Use the NHS accessibility checklist for: a full list of WCAG 2.2 success criteria and guidance for levels A and AA some success criteria and best practice for level AAA
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Design".

author: NHS England
title: Development
statement: Use the NHS accessibility checklist for: a full list of WCAG 2.2 success criteria and guidance for levels A and AA some success criteria and best practice for level AAA
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Development".

author: NHS England
title: Download accessibility posters
statement: Download all 6 accessibility posters (PDF, 88KB) These posters contain some basic principles of accessibility on a coloured background. Display them in your workplace to encourage your team to think about accessibility and to find out more.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Download accessibility posters".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Download accessibility posters > What the posters say > Product and delivery
title: Download accessibility posters: Product and delivery
statement: Make sure everyone knows their responsibilities. If a team member does not have a basic understanding already, help them get started with accessibility. (On a blue background, with an icon showing 2 hands holding a phone.) Download poster for product and delivery (PDF, 44KB)
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Download accessibility posters".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Download accessibility posters > What the posters say > User research
title: Download accessibility posters: User research
statement: Involve people with access needs at every stage. Understand participants' needs beforehand and make your sessions accessible on the day. (On a yellow background, with an icon showing research notes.) Download poster for user research (PDF, 44KB)
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Download accessibility posters".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Download accessibility posters > What the posters say > Content
title: Download accessibility posters: Content
statement: Write content that's inclusive and easy to understand. Use alternative text for images in content – and use captions to complement alt-text. (On a pink background, with an icon showing a phone with text and a video on it.) Download poster for content (PDF, 44KB)
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Download accessibility posters".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Download accessibility posters > What the posters say > Development
title: Download accessibility posters: Development
statement: Check keyboard accessibility – start with the correct HTML for links, buttons and form controls. Use ARIA patterns to let people who use assistive tech know what's going on. (On a purple background, with an icon showing an HTML tag.) Download poster for development (PDF, 44KB)
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Download accessibility posters".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Download accessibility posters > What the posters say > Design
title: Download accessibility posters: Design
statement: Use headings correctly, define focus styles, and build with tested, accessible components. Check colour contrast meets at least level AA and aim for AAA where possible. (On an orange background, with an icon showing 2 hands framing a square.) Download poster for design (PDF, 44KB)
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Download accessibility posters".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Download accessibility posters > What the posters say > Testing
title: Download accessibility posters: Testing
statement: Learn about accessibility before you start. Do 3 kinds of tests: test with people with access needs, do automated tests, and manual testing with guidelines. (On a green background, with an icon showing a clipboard with a tick on it.) Download poster for testing (PDF, 44KB)
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Download accessibility posters".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Getting started with accessibility > Attend accessibility training sessions
title: Getting started with accessibility: Attend accessibility training sessions
statement: Find out if your organisation offers accessibility training or can bring in an accessibility agency to run a session. For example, NHS England runs introductory sessions and lunch and learn meetings on accessibility topics for its staff.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Getting started with accessibility".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Getting started with accessibility > Learn on your own
title: Getting started with accessibility: Learn on your own
statement: You can learn a lot through reading blogs and watching videos. There are some good resources online. Accessibility and me (GOV.UK blog) – a series of interviews with people with access needs Accessibility in government (GOV.UK blog) Dos and don'ts on designing for accessibility (GOV.UK blog) with GOV.UK posters about designing inclusive services Understanding disabilities and impairments: user profiles (GOV.UK) – a set of profiles highlighting common barriers users face when accessing digital services. Please share any accessibility user profiles for NHS services on our public Slack channel . Web accessibility perspectives (W3C) – a series of videos about how accessible design can help people with disabilities
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Getting started with accessibility".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Getting started with accessibility > Book a session in an accessibility lab
title: Getting started with accessibility: Book a session in an accessibility lab
statement: An accessibility lab will give you hands-on experience of some of the technologies that people use with online services. Some labs also have goggles that simulate visual impairments and headphones to simulate hearing loss. NHS England has its own accessibility lab. NHS England staff can find information on the intranet about how to book it.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Getting started with accessibility".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Getting started with accessibility > Try out assistive technologies
title: Getting started with accessibility: Try out assistive technologies
statement: Get some understanding of how different technologies work. Use a screenreader, for example, and check how your web pages or other websites perform. If you have a Mac, try out VoiceOver , or download NVDA for Windows . If you're not confident about doing this, book a session in an accessibility lab first.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Getting started with accessibility".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Getting started with accessibility > Talk to other people with an interest in accessibility
title: Getting started with accessibility: Talk to other people with an interest in accessibility
statement: Join the GOV.UK accessibility community or talk to NHS colleagues on our public Slack workspace to get advice and support, stay up to date and share examples.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Getting started with accessibility".

author: NHS England
subcategory: How to make digital services accessible > Consider accessibility at every stage
title: How to make digital services accessible: Consider accessibility at every stage
statement: Think about how you are going to address accessibility at the beginning and at every stage of your project. It's much harder to make a service accessible if you only address it later on. Making your service accessible: an introduction (GOV.UK service manual) explains what to do at different stages.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "How to make digital services accessible".

author: NHS England
subcategory: How to make digital services accessible > Make it the whole team's responsibility
title: How to make digital services accessible: Make it the whole team's responsibility
statement: Every member of the team should contribute to making your service inclusive. You should all: have a good understanding of accessibility observe research with people with access needs follow the guidance for your role
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "How to make digital services accessible".

author: NHS England
subcategory: How to make digital services accessible > Research with users with access needs
title: How to make digital services accessible: Research with users with access needs
statement: Involve people with access needs, including disabled people, in every round of user research. Consider cognitive and physical impairments, visual impairments, and temporary or permanent access needs. Follow our guidance on user research .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "How to make digital services accessible".

author: NHS England
subcategory: How to make digital services accessible > Use progressive enhancement
title: How to make digital services accessible: Use progressive enhancement
statement: Progressive enhancement is about making your page work with just HTML, before adding anything else like cascading style sheets (CSS) and Javascript. That helps people who live in areas with slow connections or whose devices or browsers fail to load or recognise something. The NHS.UK frontend library uses JavaScript for "enhancement" – as an extra. It works without it. See Building a resilient frontend using progressive enhancement (GOV.UK service manual) .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "How to make digital services accessible".

author: NHS England
subcategory: How to make digital services accessible > Follow NHS accessibility guidance
title: How to make digital services accessible: Follow NHS accessibility guidance
statement: Use this accessibility guidance to get started. For more detail, follow the NHS accessibility checklist . The checklist contains: a full list of WCAG 2.2 success criteria and guidance for levels A and AA that NHS websites and public mobile apps need to conform to some success criteria and best practice to improve accessibility for level AAA
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "How to make digital services accessible".

author: NHS England
subcategory: How to make digital services accessible > Test throughout and get an independent audit
title: How to make digital services accessible: Test throughout and get an independent audit
statement: An expert audit can help find accessibility problems with your service and make sure it meets accessibility requirements. If you run your own tests regularly, the audit should find very little that needs changing. Follow our guidance on testing and our guidance on monitoring and recording accessibility testing (for product and delivery managers). Find out about getting an accessibility audit (GOV.UK service manual) . Digital teams in NHS England can arrange an audit by getting in touch with the service manual team .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "How to make digital services accessible".

author: NHS England
title: Accessibility
statement: Your service must be accessible to everyone who needs it. If it is not, you may be breaking the law. Everyone who works on NHS digital services has a role to play in making them accessible and inclusive.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Accessibility".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Accessibility > Make sure your service meets Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2
title: Accessibility: Make sure your service meets Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2
statement: The service manual is up to date with WCAG 2.2. Find out more about the new criteria that WCAG 2.2 introduced . The Government Digital Service, Department of Health and Social Care and NHS England are now monitoring accessibility to WCAG 2.2.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Accessibility".

author: NHS England
title: New criteria in WCAG 2.2
statement: The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, known as WCAG, have been updated to version 2.2, which includes all the success criteria of WCAG 2.1 plus 9 new criteria. As a public sector organisation, by law you must meet the guidelines to level AA for all patient and staff facing services.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "New criteria in WCAG 2.2".

author: NHS England
subcategory: New criteria in WCAG 2.2 > What you need to do
title: New criteria in WCAG 2.2: What you need to do
statement: To get from WCAG 2.1 to WCAG 2.2, follow these steps. Read this page to understand the new criteria you must comply with. Assess your service to see what updates you need to make. Plan and implement your updates. The Government Digital Service, Department of Health and Social Care and NHS England are now monitoring accessibility to WCAG 2.2. Use the NHS accessibility checklist for: a full list of WCAG 2.2 success criteria and guidance for levels A and AA some success criteria and best practice for level AAA
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "New criteria in WCAG 2.2".

author: NHS England
subcategory: New criteria in WCAG 2.2 > The extra criteria
title: New criteria in WCAG 2.2: The extra criteria
statement: WCAG 2.2 includes the WCAG 2.1 criteria, plus 9 new criteria. The 9 new criteria are made up of: 6 at A and AA level, which means they're a requirement for NHS websites and mobile apps 3 at AAA These are the 6 new criteria you'll need to meet, as a minimum.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "New criteria in WCAG 2.2".

author: NHS England
subcategory: New criteria in WCAG 2.2 > The extra criteria > Focus not obscured (minimum)
title: New criteria in WCAG 2.2: Focus not obscured (minimum)
statement: Some websites have sticky or fixed headers or footers that remain at the top or bottom of the page when users scroll. This can make it difficult for users navigating with a keyboard to identify which components are focused. Learn more about focus not obscured (W3C website) .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "New criteria in WCAG 2.2".

author: NHS England
subcategory: New criteria in WCAG 2.2 > The extra criteria > Dragging movements
title: New criteria in WCAG 2.2: Dragging movements
statement: If there is interactive content that users can move by dragging, they must be able to do it with a "single pointer". For example, to reorder items in a list that can be dragged, an alternative can be to have up and down arrows to reorder them. Clicking and dragging is impossible for some users. Learn more about dragging movements (W3C website) .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "New criteria in WCAG 2.2".

author: NHS England
subcategory: New criteria in WCAG 2.2 > The extra criteria > Target size (minimum)
title: New criteria in WCAG 2.2: Target size (minimum)
statement: Interactive content must have a minimum size of 24 by 24 CSS pixels. This does not apply to interactive content that is a part of text such as links. Learn more about target size (W3C website) .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "New criteria in WCAG 2.2".

author: NHS England
subcategory: New criteria in WCAG 2.2 > The extra criteria > Redundant entry
title: New criteria in WCAG 2.2: Redundant entry
statement: A user should not have to enter the same information more than once on a single journey, unless it is required for security purposes, for example passwords. Learn more about redundant entry (W3C website) .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "New criteria in WCAG 2.2".

author: NHS England
subcategory: New criteria in WCAG 2.2 > The extra criteria > Accessible authentication (minimum)
title: New criteria in WCAG 2.2: Accessible authentication (minimum)
statement: A user should not have to perform a cognitive function test, such as solving a puzzle or "Enter the 3rd, 4th, and 6th character of your password". If you need the user to enter a password, they should be able to copy and paste it. Learn more about accessible authentication (W3C website) .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "New criteria in WCAG 2.2".

author: NHS England
subcategory: New criteria in WCAG 2.2 > The extra criteria > Consistent help
title: New criteria in WCAG 2.2: Consistent help
statement: If your service provides help options such as contact details or live chat, they should be presented consistently across pages, to make sure users can find and interact with them easily. Learn more about consistent help (W3C website) .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "New criteria in WCAG 2.2".

author: NHS England
title: Testing
statement: Use the NHS accessibility checklist for: a full list of WCAG 2.2 success criteria and guidance for levels A and AA some success criteria and best practice for level AAA
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Testing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: What all NHS services need to do about accessibility > Accessibility and the law
title: What all NHS services need to do about accessibility: Accessibility and the law
statement: If your service isn't accessible to everyone who needs it, you may be breaking the 2010 Equality Act . Public sector websites must meet the Public Sector Bodies Accessibility Regulations 2018 and publish an accessibility statement. Find out about the accessibility requirements for public sector bodies on GOV.UK .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "What all NHS services need to do about accessibility".

author: NHS England
subcategory: What all NHS services need to do about accessibility > Meeting the requirements
title: What all NHS services need to do about accessibility: Meeting the requirements
statement: Digital services in the NHS must: meet at least level AA of the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines ( WCAG 2.2 ) and aim for AAA where possible work on the most commonly used assistive technologies ( follow GOV.UK guidance on testing with assistive technologies ) include people with access needs in user research publish an accessibility statement that complies with GOV.UK requirements
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "What all NHS services need to do about accessibility".

author: NHS England
subcategory: What all NHS services need to do about accessibility > Meeting the requirements > Teams on short deadlines
title: What all NHS services need to do about accessibility: Teams on short deadlines
statement: If you're working to a tight deadline, you must: check the GOV.UK guidance on making services in an emergency consider exclusion as you design your service, for example, with GOV.UK's user profiles for understanding disabilities and impairments use the NHS production code and design system set up automated accessibility testing and fix issues you identify use the NHS accessibility checklist to carry out an initial WCAG evaluation test service journeys with a range of assistive technologies plan user research to identify and remove barriers
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "What all NHS services need to do about accessibility".

author: NHS England
subcategory: What all NHS services need to do about accessibility > Meeting the requirements > Internal services
title: What all NHS services need to do about accessibility: Internal services
statement: NHS staff and civil servants are users too and the NHS is committed to equality, diversity and inclusion. Internal services need to meet the same accessibility requirements.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "What all NHS services need to do about accessibility".

author: NHS England
subcategory: What all NHS services need to do about accessibility > Meeting the requirements > Suppliers and contractors
title: What all NHS services need to do about accessibility: Suppliers and contractors
statement: External suppliers contracted to the NHS must also make sure their work meets the same standard. The NHS may test the product or ask suppliers to arrange an independent accessibility test.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "What all NHS services need to do about accessibility".

author: NHS England
subcategory: What all NHS services need to do about accessibility > Why it's important
title: What all NHS services need to do about accessibility: Why it's important
statement: In the UK, almost 1 in 5 people have a disability of some kind. Many more have temporary or situational disabilities, like an illness or injury. When you're working on NHS services, think about how people with different needs might use what you're making. For example, can someone with dyslexia read your content easily? Or how would someone with a broken arm interact on a mobile device?
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "What all NHS services need to do about accessibility".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > A > A&E
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: A&E
statement: We use "A&E". You do not need to spell out "accident and emergency".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > A > abbreviations
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: abbreviations
statement: See the guidance on abbreviations and acronyms on the Formatting page .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > A > abdomen and abdominal
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: abdomen and abdominal
statement: It's OK to use "abdomen" where people are familiar with this term. For example, we know that pregnant women talk about "abdominal pain". If users may not be familiar with "abdomen" but are likely to hear their GP or another health professional use this word, we may add "abdomen" after "tummy". a dull ache in your tummy (abdomen)
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > A > acronyms
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: acronyms
statement: See the guidance on abbreviations and acronyms on the Formatting page .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > A > acute
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: acute
statement: We prefer "sudden", "starts suddenly", "in a short period of time" or, where appropriate, "short-term". We do use "acute" in the names of conditions like "acute lymphoblastic leukaemia". We also use it if our search analytics, user testing or survey feedback suggest that people will hear their doctor use the word "acute" or will search for it. If we use it, we explain what it means.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > A > addresses
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: addresses
statement: Display addresses vertically. For example: NHS England London 10 South Colonnade Poplar London E14 4PU Start each part of the address on a new line. Write the town and postcode on separate lines. Do not use punctuation at the end of each line. If you need to display addresses horizontally, for example to present multiple addresses on results pages, punctuate them. For example: NHS England, 7 and 8 Wellington Place, Leeds, West Yorkshire, LS1 4AP To ask users for their address, use the address pattern in the GOV.UK design system .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > A > affects
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: affects
statement: It's alright to use "affects" but in some contexts, for example with medicines, it can be better to say that "something changes the way something else works". Check a dictionary if you're not sure of the difference between "affect" and "effect".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > A > age
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: age
statement: Find out how we talk about age in the Inclusive content section .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > A > alternative
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: alternative
statement: We generally use "different" or "other". An exception is "complementary and alternative medicines".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > A > Alzheimer's disease
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: Alzheimer's disease
statement: We capitalise the names of conditions that start with a proper name, like Alzheimer's disease. Note the apostrophe.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > A > ampersand (&)
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: ampersand (&)
statement: Avoid using an ampersand, except in " A&E ". Use "and" instead.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > A > anonymised, anonymisation
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: anonymised, anonymisation
statement: We prefer not to use these words. Instead we might explain what anonymisation means and talk about information that has personal details removed. We might give examples, like "When we share your information with another organisation, we take out all personal details, such as your name and address." Depending on your audience and the context, for example in a cookie banner, you might not need this much detail. A short, simple explanation might do.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > A > antibody test
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: antibody test
statement: This is a blood test to check if it is likely that someone has: had an infection before, such as COVID-19 made antibodies to a virus after having a vaccine, such as the COVID-19 vaccine Use lower case "antibody test", not "Antibody Test". Do not use "virus test", "coronavirus test" or "COVID-19 test" when referring to an antibody test.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > A > anus
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: anus
statement: We prefer " bottom " (as in "bleeding from your bottom") to "anus" or " rectum ". You can add "anus" in brackets after "bottom". For example, in "enlarged blood vessels found inside or around the bottom (anus)". Or you can use "anus" on its own when you need to be more precise, for example when you're talking about anal cancer. User testing showed that people understand "bottom" better than "anus". They do search for "anus" in Google, however.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > A > app
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: app
statement: Lower case, unless referring to an official name, such as the NHS App .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > A > apply
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: apply
statement: If we are talking about a medicine, we prefer "use", "put on" or "rub in".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > B > baby
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: baby
statement: We use "baby" or "your baby" (not "unborn baby") in pregnancy content, from the early stages of pregnancy to birth and during the baby's first year. "Baby" is simpler than "embryo" or "foetus". For example, in our medicines content, we talk about how medicines can "affect you and your baby in pregnancy". The words we use depend on the context, however. In content about an unwanted pregnancy or abortion, for example, we use "pregnancy" and "ending the pregnancy". Test with users to make sure that the words you use are right for their circumstances.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > B > back passage
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: back passage
statement: We do not use "back passage". Instead we use " bottom ", " anus " or, rarely, " rectum ".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > B > bacteria
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: bacteria
statement: People often are not interested in the kind of bacteria that caused their problem. They want to know what to do about it. Only mention the name of the bacteria (full or short name) if your audience (users) need it. If you give the full Latin name of a bacterium, capitalise the first word, for example, "Staphylococcus aureus" but put the shortened "staphylococcus" in lower case. Do not use italics.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > B > BAME
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: BAME
statement: Use "ethnic minorities", not "BAME" or "BME". Find out how we talk about ethnicity, religion and nationality in the Inclusive content section .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > B > Black or black
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: Black or black
statement: Use a capital letter when you're writing about ethnicity or when you're asking users for their ethnic group. Use lower case when you're writing about skin colour. "Black, Asian, African, Black British or Caribbean" "On white skin the rash can appear red, but on brown and black skin the rash may be harder to see."
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > B > black skin
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: black skin
statement: We talk about skin colour clearly and use terms that are easy to understand, including "brown and black skin". We do not refer to brown or black skin as "dark" or "darker". See the guidance on skin symptoms in the Inclusive content section .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > B > BME
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: BME
statement: Use "ethnic minorities", not "BAME" or "BME". Find out how we talk about ethnicity, religion and nationality in the Inclusive content section .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > B > bold
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: bold
statement: See the guidance on how we use bold on the Formatting page .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > B > booster
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: booster
statement: A booster is a dose of a vaccine that increases or renews the effect of a vaccine you had earlier. Explain in more detail the 1st time you mention it, for example "a booster dose of the COVID-19 vaccine". Then you can refer to it as a "booster" or "booster dose".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > B > bottom
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: bottom
statement: We prefer the word "bottom" (in phrases like "bleeding from your bottom") to " anus " or " rectum ". User testing showed that people understand "bottom" better than "anus".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > B > brown skin
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: brown skin
statement: We talk about skin colour clearly and use terms that are easy to understand, including "brown and black skin". We do not refer to brown or black skin as "dark" or "darker". See the guidance on skin symptoms in the Inclusive content section .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > B > bullet points
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: bullet points
statement: Find out how we use bullet points in the guidance on lists on the Formatting page .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > B > bum
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: bum
statement: We prefer " bottom " (in phrases like "bleeding from your bottom").
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > C > calories (kcal)
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: calories (kcal)
statement: See calories on our Numbers, measurements, dates and time page .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > C > can't or cannot
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: can't or cannot
statement: We use "cannot" instead of "can't". Read why in the contractions section .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > C > carer
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: carer
statement: We use "carer" when we're talking about a family member or friend who cares for someone but is not paid for this. We use "paid carer" for a carer who works for social services or another agency. A paid carer can help with personal care, for example getting washed and dressed. We do not use "care worker" because we found that it is ambiguous. Compare "carer" and " home help ".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > C > cervical screening
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: cervical screening
statement: We prefer the term "cervical screening" to "smear test". But we add "smear test" in brackets the first time we mention cervical screening. "Smear test" is a dated term and the cervical screening programme no longer uses it. The invitation and results letters use "cervical screening" and our content reflects that. We've seen anecdotal evidence from Public Health England, cervical screening service providers and smear takers that some users find the word "smear" off-putting.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > C > chemist
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: chemist
statement: We use "pharmacy", not "chemist". Our users are more likely to look for the word "pharmacy".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > C > chronic
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: chronic
statement: We prefer "for a long time" or "does not go away". We have seen evidence that the word "chronic" confuses people. Some people think it means "bad" or "serious". We do use "chronic" in the names of conditions like "chronic fatigue syndrome". We also use it if our search analytics, user testing or survey feedback suggest that people will hear their doctor use the word "chronic" or will search for it. If we use it, we explain what "chronic" means.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > C > CJD
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: CJD
statement: We use "CJD" – or "variant CJD (vCJD)" as the human form of BSE. Use full name "Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease" when you first mention CJD. We do not use "mad cow disease" or "BSE".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > C > clinical commissioning groups (CCGs)
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: clinical commissioning groups (CCGs)
statement: CCGs were replaced by integrated care boards (ICBs) in July 2022.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > C > clinician
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: clinician
statement: Do not use the word "clinician". We've found many patients do not know what a clinician is. Instead you could use "a doctor , nurse or other healthcare professional", for example.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > C > condition
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: condition
statement: We use "condition", "problem" or "illness". We avoid words like "disease" and "disorder" as they can sound negative. But we do use these words in the names of specific diseases or disorders, like Alzheimer's disease or obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) or terms like "tropical diseases". Find out how we talk about disabilities and conditions in the Inclusive content section .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > C > continuing healthcare
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: continuing healthcare
statement: Lower case and "healthcare" is one word. We explain NHS continuing healthcare on the NHS website .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > C > contractions
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: contractions
statement: To find out how we use contractions, like "we're" and "don't", see the guidance on contractions on the Punctuation page .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > C > COVID-19
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: COVID-19
statement: Upper case. Do not use: "Covid-19" with only the first letter capitalised "covid-19" lower case "coronavirus" as "COVID-19" is the specific condition See also on this page: COVID-19 vaccination status long COVID
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > C > COVID-19 vaccination status
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: COVID-19 vaccination status
statement: In the context of COVID-19, vaccination status refers to which vaccine someone has had and how many doses. Use "vaccination status" lower case. Do not use "COVID-19 status".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > D > dashes
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: dashes
statement: See the guidance on hyphens and dashes on the Punctuation page .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > D > data
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: data
statement: Treat data as a singular noun: "Your data is stored on a secure server."​ For job titles, like data analyst, see the GOV.UK A to Z style guide on job titles .​
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > D > dates
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: dates
statement: See our guidance on dates on the Numbers, measurements, dates and time page .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > D > Deaf people
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: Deaf people
statement: If you're creating content for or about people who are Deaf and use British Sign Language to communicate, bear in mind that their needs will be different from those of people who have a hearing loss or tinnitus. We use a capital D when we're talking to or about people who are Deaf and use British Sign Language to communicate because many Deaf people prefer it. We recognise that this doesn't apply to everyone who comes to the NHS for information about deafness and so, as always, we check with the people we're creating content for how they want to be described.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > D > deafness
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: deafness
statement: We use "deafness" (with a lower case d) in our health content when we're writing about it, for example, as a symptom. But we prefer the term " hearing loss ".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > D > death
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: death
statement: Be direct wherever possible. Say "death" instead of: "fatality" "passing" We do not use "loss" and "bereavement" as euphemisms for death. We do use them when we are talking about feelings of loss or grieving in our mental health content. Say "died" instead of: "passed away" "deceased" We do not recommend this language in cases of miscarriage or abortion, however. We are working on guidance on this.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > D > degrees (temperature)
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: degrees (temperature)
statement: We use C for centigrade or Celsius – for example, 38C or −4C. Do not include the degree symbol (°). We are no longer including references to Fahrenheit . Also see fever and temperature .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > D > diabetic
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: diabetic
statement: We do not talk about people as "diabetic". We say they have diabetes. We do use "diabetic" in phrases like "diabetic eye screening". Find out how we talk about disabilities and conditions in the Inclusive content section .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > D > disabilities
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: disabilities
statement: We use positive language to talk about disabilities. Read more about how we talk about disabilities and conditions in our Inclusive content section .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > D > diuretics
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: diuretics
statement: We do not call them "water tablets". We explain that diuretics are "tablets that make you pee more".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > D > doctor
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: doctor
statement: We mostly use " GP ". We use "doctor" when someone might see a GP, a specialist or consultant in a surgery, hospital or clinic setting. We also use "doctor" when we're writing about healthcare abroad. We use "your doctor" when we're writing about follow-up or ongoing care with a health professional, for example, when a doctor is prescribing and monitoring medicine. We use phrases like: "talk with your doctor" "follow your doctor's instructions" Also see " specialist ".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > D > don't or do not
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: don't or do not
statement: We use "do not" instead of "don't". Read why in the contractions section . We use "Don't" in headings for Do and Don't lists . But we use "do not" for the commands in the list.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > D > dosage
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: dosage
statement: See dosage on our Numbers, measurements, dates and time page .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > D > drowsy
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: drowsy
statement: Generally, we prefer the word "sleepy" to "drowsy" as people are more likely to search for "sleepy". But "drowsy" may be better if you're writing about feeling unusually sleepy in the daytime, particularly in the context of medicines. In information about medicines, for example antihistamines, we prefer the terms: "drowsy (sedating)" to describe a medicine because these are the words people search for and see or hear in a GP or pharmacy setting "feeling sleepy (drowsy)" to describe a side effect
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > E > ear drop and words like eardrum and earlobe
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: ear drop and words like eardrum and earlobe
statement: We split "ear drop" into 2 words. Ear drops are medicines. Using 2 words makes them easier to read and is consistent with patient information leaflets. For similar words, like "eardrum" and "earlobe", follow common usage unless you have evidence that users find separate words easier to read and understand.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > E > eg
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: eg
statement: eg can sometimes be read aloud as "egg" by screen readers. We prefer "for example" or "such as" or "like" or "including" – whichever works best.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > E > epileptic
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: epileptic
statement: We do not talk about people as "epileptics". We say they have epilepsy. Find out how we talk about conditions in the Inclusive content section .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > E > etc
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: etc
statement: Avoid etc. Try using "for example" or "such as" or "like" or "including" instead.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > E > ethnicity
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: ethnicity
statement: Use "ethnicity", not "race". Find out how we talk about ethnicity, religion and nationality in the Inclusive content section .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > E > eye drop and words like eyelash and eyelid
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: eye drop and words like eyelash and eyelid
statement: We split "eye drop" into 2 words. Eye drops are medicines. Using 2 words makes them easier to read and is consistent with patient information leaflets. For similar words, like "eyelash" and "eyelid", follow common usage unless you have evidence that users find separate words easier to read and understand.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > F > A Day
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: A Day
statement: Note the number and capital letters. This is the campaign which encourages people to eat 5 portions of fruit and vegetables every day.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > F > Fahrenheit
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: Fahrenheit
statement: We are taking references to Fahrenheit out of our content and just using Celsius. This is because healthcare professionals in the UK use Celsius. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) also uses it and we refer to NICE for evidence-based guidance. Celsius has been the official temperature scale in the UK since 1965. Giving 2 different temperatures can confuse people who may be anxious or unwell. It's easier to have just one number to tell your GP.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > F > fart
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: fart
statement: We use "fart" and "farting" when we're talking about symptoms. People understand "fart" better than "passing wind" or " flatulence ". We use " wind " for "trapped wind" or bloating.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > F > fetus
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: fetus
statement: We spell "fetus" and "fetal" without an "o". We do not commonly use "fetus", except in the names of conditions like "fetal alcohol syndrome". We prefer "pregnancy".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > F > fever
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: fever
statement: We prefer the words "high temperature " to "fever", for example in a list of symptoms. Our user research shows that "fever" is not a well understood word. But we still use it when we're writing specifically about fever or different types of fever (such as scarlet fever).
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > F > fit note
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: fit note
statement: Use "fit note (sick note)" at first mention, then use "fit note". Or, if your users need more information, explain it in a sentence. If you are unwell and cannot work, you may need a fit note (sometimes called a sick note) for your employer.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > F > flatulence
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: flatulence
statement: We prefer " farting " to "flatulence". We only use "flatulence" when we need to for clinical content (for example, in a health information page about flatulence). We explain that flatulence is the same as wind or farting.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > F > flu jab or flu vaccine
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: flu jab or flu vaccine
statement: We sometimes use "flu jab" for adults, because people search for this. But we use "flu vaccine" for children. (The child vaccine is a spray.) People who are looking for information about flu vaccination in pregnancy search for "jab". For the annual flu vaccination programme, we use the term "flu vaccine" as that covers children and adults.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > F > formulations
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: formulations
statement: Rather than talking about different medicines formulations, we talk about "different types" (for example, of hydrocortisone) or "different ways" of using a medicine.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > F > foundation trust
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: foundation trust
statement: Lower case, unless you are giving the full name of a foundation trust. For example: Anytown NHS Foundation Trust.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > F > fractions
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: fractions
statement: See our guidance on fractions on the Numbers, measurements, dates and time page .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > G > gas
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: gas
statement: We do not use "gas". Instead we talk about " wind ", " burping " or " farting ".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > G > gender
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: gender
statement: Find out how we talk about gender in the Inclusive content section .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > G > GP
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: GP
