statement: We mostly use "GP". We use " doctor ", where someone may see either a GP or another health professional like a specialist or consultant in a surgery, hospital or clinic setting. We also use "doctor" when we're writing about healthcare abroad. We use "a GP" (rather than "your GP") when we're advising people to get medical advice, care or treatment, for example in a care card. (Find out more about helping users decide when and where to get care, with care cards .) This is particularly important when the user may need urgent care or to act out of hours. Not all users are registered with a GP or have a regular GP. We use "a GP" to emphasise that users should get help and that it doesn't matter which GP they see. Once we've used "a GP", we follow up with "the GP". Talk to a GP about your condition. The GP might suggest... We use "your GP" when the user is likely to be under a GP's ongoing care, for example, for a condition like diabetes or in the context of follow-up care. We also use "your GP" rather than "a GP" in a transactional journey, such as NHS 111 online, where we have information about the user and we are referring them to their GP during office hours.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > G > GP online services
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: GP online services
statement: We use "GP online services" as the collective term for online services like appointment booking, repeat prescription orders and medical record access. Or you can use "GP surgery's online services" if this is clearer for your users. See also GP system supplier names and patient-facing services .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > G > GP surgery
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: GP surgery
statement: When we're writing for the public, we use "GP surgery" or "surgery" rather than "practice", because our research shows us that this is the word patients are more likely to search for and use. When we're writing for healthcare staff, we may use the term "GP practice" or "practice" for short. For example, for "practice managers". Note that a GP practice can have more than 1 surgery.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > G > GP system supplier names and patient-facing services
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: GP system supplier names and patient-facing services
statement: Users often do not recognise the name of GP systems in isolation from their patient-facing services. Usability testing by the NHS App team showed that: users recognise "Patient Access" but often do not recognise the name of the supplier "EMIS" they recognise "SystmOnline" but often do not recognise the name of the supplier "TPP" For patients, when referring to the GP system we say: EMIS (Patient Access) TPP (SystmOnline) Vision (Patient Services) For patients, when referring to the patient-facing service of a GP system, it's OK not to include the supplier name. For example: Patient Access SystmOnline Patient Services For healthcare staff, it's OK to refer to the system name of the GP supplier if appropriate. For example: EMIS or EMIS Web TPP or TPP SystmOne Vision or Vision 3 See also GP online services .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > G > GUM clinic
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: GUM clinic
statement: GUM is short for genito-urinary medicine. We use sexual health clinic .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > H > haemorrhage
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: haemorrhage
statement: We often use the words "a very heavy bleed" instead of "haemorrhage". If you need to use the word "haemorrhage", for example, in the name of a condition like a subarachnoid haemorrhage, explain what it is.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > H > health record
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: health record
statement: We use "health record" rather than "medical record". "Health record" is more accurate as someone's record may cover social care as well as medical content. In our user research, we haven't seen anyone confused by "health record". People see it as the same as a "medical record". In some contexts, for example in forms, rather than asking about someone's "health record", we ask about "your health, and any health problems or treatments you've had in the past".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > H > hearing loss
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: hearing loss
statement: If you're creating content for people who have a hearing loss, bear in mind that their needs may be different from those of people who are Deaf and people who have tinnitus.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > H > home help
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: home help
statement: A home help helps with domestic tasks like cleaning and doing the laundry. Compare this with a " carer ".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > H > homeless
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: homeless
statement: We do not say "the homeless" or "homeless people". We prefer to talk about "people who are homeless".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > H > hyphens
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: hyphens
statement: See the guidance on hyphens and dashes on the Punctuation page .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > I > ID
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: ID
statement: Use ID without full stops. This is fine for most screen readers.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > I > ie
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: ie
statement: We try not to use "ie" (which means "that is" or "that means"). You can usually write your sentence in another way.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > I > immunisation
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: immunisation
statement: Only use "immunisation" in the names of organisations or programmes. For example, the Public Health England (PHE) immunisation programme or Joint Committee on Vaccination and Immunisation (JCVI). We use " vaccination " otherwise.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > I > imperial measurements
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: imperial measurements
statement: See the guidance on metric and imperial measurements on the Numbers, measurements, dates and time page .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > I > incontinence products
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: incontinence products
statement: It's OK to use "incontinence products". It may help to specify the products you mean. For example, pads, pants or sheaths.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > I > injection
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: injection
statement: You can use "injection" or "jab" for the injection of vaccine .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > I > integrated care boards (ICBs)
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: integrated care boards (ICBs)
statement: Lower case when spelt out in full, except when you are referring to a particular ICB. For example: Anytown Integrated Care Board. We treat integrated care systems (ICSs) and integrated care partnerships (ICPs) the same way.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > J > jab
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: jab
statement: We use " vaccine ", not "jab", for the dose people get in their vaccination. For example: 6‑in‑1 vaccine COVID-19 vaccine HPV vaccine It's OK to use "injection" if a substance or medicine is injected. Research shows that "jab" can make people who are scared of needles more anxious. If "jab" is a popular search term for your content (for example, "flu jab"), call it the "flu vaccine" but add "sometimes called the flu jab". Do this in the body content and the meta description.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > K > kidney
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: kidney
statement: We use "kidney" instead of "renal". We may mention "renal" as well as "kidney" if our search analytics, user testing or survey feedback suggest that people will hear their doctor use "renal" or will search for it.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > K > kilobytes and megabytes (KB and MB)
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: kilobytes and megabytes (KB and MB)
statement: Use MB for anything over 1MB: 4MB not 4096KB. Use KB for anything under 1MB: 569KB not 0.55MB. Find out how we use KB and MB for document size in our guidance on links .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > L > licensed for
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: licensed for
statement: For medicines, we say "can be used for" or is or isn't "officially approved for".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > L > log in and log out
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: log in and log out
statement: Use "log in" and "log out" (verb), not "sign in" and "sign out". Avoid "login" as a noun, except in NHS login . Tell the user what they need to enter, for example their email or NHS number.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > L > long COVID
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: long COVID
statement: Long COVID refers to symptoms that can last weeks or months after COVID-19 infection has gone. It is also referred to as post-COVID-19 syndrome. Find out about long COVID on the NHS website . Use "long COVID": "long" is lower case and "COVID" is upper case. Do not use: a capital L for "long" unless it is at the start of a sentence "Covid" with only the first letter capitalised or "covid" lower case the number "19" as you would when writing "COVID-19" "long coronavirus"
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > M > measurements
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: measurements
statement: See the section on measurements on the Numbers, measurements, dates and time page .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > M > mental health
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: mental health
statement: See the section on mental health on the disabilities and conditions page .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > M > metric measurements
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: metric measurements
statement: See the guidance on metric and imperial measurements on the Numbers, measurements, dates and time page .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > M > microgram
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: microgram
statement: Write "microgram" in full. We only shorten microgram to mcg or μg if people will find that helpful, for example, if they will see it on their medicines or vitamins packet. In cases like these, we add the following when we first mention micrograms: "The word microgram is sometimes written as mcg or with the symbol μ followed by the letter g (μg)." We explain that it's a symbol so that people who use screen readers understand it when they hear an unexpected sound. We do not use mcg or μg as an abbreviation in text that follows.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > M > milk
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: milk
statement: In "cows' milk" and "goats' milk", the apostrophe comes after the "s". In "sheep's milk", the apostrophe comes before the "s", because "sheep" is plural. We write "breast milk" as two words.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > M > money
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: money
statement: Do not use decimals unless pence are included. Write "£75" and "£75.50", but not "£75.00". Write out "pence" in full: "Calls will cost 4 pence a minute from a landline". See also our guidance on numbers, measurements, dates and time .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > M > morning after pill
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: morning after pill
statement: Lower case without hyphens. It can be "emergency contraception".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > M > mucus and mucous
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: mucus and mucous
statement: "Mucus" is a noun. "Mucous" is an adjective. If you have allergic rhinitis, the inside layer of your nose (the mucous membrane) may become swollen and you may produce a lot of mucus.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > N > nationality
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: nationality
statement: Find out how we talk about ethnicity, religion and nationality in the Inclusive content section .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > N > nausea
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: nausea
statement: We prefer "feeling sick". You may want to put "nausea" in brackets afterwards: feeling sick (nausea).
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > N > negative
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: negative
statement: If you use the word "negative" in the context of test results, be aware that some users may interpret it as bad news. In other words, they may think they have the disease. If you have to use "negative", because this is the word people will hear when they get their test results, explain what it means. Negative means the test did not find what it was looking for.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > N > NHS
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: NHS
statement: We do not usually spell out "National Health Service". It's fine to use the abbreviation. We refer to it as "the NHS", unless we're using NHS as an adjective, for example: "an NHS appointment" "NHS services"
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > N > NHS 111 online
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: NHS 111 online
statement: On the NHS website and in national digital services, say "Go to NHS 111 online or call 111" if it's a call to action. Include the word "NHS" and give "online" a small "o". Shorten it to "111 online" if you mention it more than once on a page. On non-NHS services, always use "NHS 111 online". 111 online is not for children under 5. Do not direct users to 111 online if the call to action is only about young children.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > N > NHS App
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: NHS App
statement: With an upper case A. It's the name of a specific app. To avoid repetition of "NHS App", you can use "the app" where needed, for example "You can also order repeat prescriptions in the app". When referring to something inside the NHS App, use "in" the app, not "on" or "with" the app. You can get health advice in the NHS App. When advising users about the browser version of the NHS App, we say: "You can also access NHS App services from the browser on your desktop or laptop computer". Find out more about the NHS App on NHS England's website See also " app ".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > N > NHS England (NHSE)
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: NHS England (NHSE)
statement: The full name of the organisation is NHS England. The abbreviation is NHSE.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > N > NHS login
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: NHS login
statement: We write "login" in lower case and as one word. The NHS login lets people see their personal health information online. See also " log in and log out ".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > N > NHS number
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: NHS number
statement: Write the NHS number as 3 groups of numbers, with a single space between them, like this: 999 123 4567. (This is an example or test number.) The format is 3 3 4: 2 groups of 3 digits followed by 4 digits. This number format makes it easier for people and assistive technologies to read. It also makes it less likely that people will make mistakes. Ask your frontend or coding colleagues how to stop the NHS number breaking over 2 lines. Make sure that you: use this format whenever you include an NHS number only use a space as a separator – do not use dashes or dots do not use a real NHS number as an example – use 999 123 4567 or another number that starts with 9 as these are test numbers and not given to real patients See our design pattern for asking users for their NHS number .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > N > NHS website
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: NHS website
statement: Lower case "website". The NHS website is the website at nhs.uk .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > N > nhs.uk and NHS.UK
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: nhs.uk and NHS.UK
statement: When we're referring to the website at nhs.uk , we call it "the NHS website". We give the url in lower case. If we're talking about NHS.UK as a programme in NHS England, we use capital letters.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > N > NHSX
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: NHSX
statement: We no longer use NHSX. It is now part of the Transformation Directorate at NHS England.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > N > normally
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: normally
statement: We use "usually". "Normally" in a health context can make people feel they are not "normal".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > N > numbered lists
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: numbered lists
statement: Find out how we use numbered lists in the guidance on lists on the Formatting page .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > O > occur
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: occur
statement: Avoid "occur". Try other words, like "happen", or reword your sentence. For example: instead of "Symptoms only occur in children under the age of 2", we say: "Only children under the age of 2 get symptoms".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > O > OK
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: OK
statement: It's OK to use OK. We've tested it on screen readers and it reads out OK.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > O > online consultation
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: online consultation
statement: Do not use the term "online consultation" or any variation of it, like "eConsultation". If you're writing about using an online form to contact a GP surgery, be clear about the task and the outcome. The best way to describe this may depend on the context and the service that's available. For example, you could use phrases like: "Contact your GP using an online form" "Request an appointment (online)" where this is relevant, for example on a GP website alongside offline booking options Our research showed people are not familiar with "online consultation". When the term is used for an online form it's misleading. Many people think it means they'll have a consultation with a doctor online, rather than complete a form to request an appointment. If you are talking about a phone, video or face to face consultation with a doctor or other health professional, be clear about the format.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > O > opticians, optometrists, ophthalmologists and orthoptists
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: opticians, optometrists, ophthalmologists and orthoptists
statement: We say "go to an opticians" (plural in this context) when we're telling people to take action. We only mention specific job roles where there's a user need for this. An optician (sometimes called a dispensing optician) checks prescriptions, fits and repairs glasses and lenses and helps with choosing frames and lenses. We use "opticians" for the place where you get your eyes tested. Note: an optician does not carry out eye tests. An optometrist carries out eye tests and checks for vision problems or health issues such as high blood pressure. They prescribe lenses and refer patients for treatment. An ophthalmic medical practitioner is a doctor who specialises in eye care. Like an optometrist, they examine eyes, test vision and prescribe lenses. An ophthalmologist is a medical doctor who can perform eye surgery. They also diagnose and treat eye conditions, and prescribe medicine, glasses or contact lenses. An orthoptist is a specialist in squints and eye movement problems.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > O > oral
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: oral
statement: We use the word "mouth". For example, we say "mouth cancer" rather than "oral cancer". If we're talking about taking medicines, we say "by mouth" or "that you swallow".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > O > organisations
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: organisations
statement: We use a singular verb for an organisation. For example: "The NHS in England deals with over 1 million patients every 36 hours." Or "The World Health Organization says …". We use the pronoun "it" for the NHS. Organisations do not do things. The people in organisations do. So we say: "Tell hospital staff in advance if you can't attend your appointment and they will try to arrange a new one", rather than "… the hospital will arrange a new one".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > O > over the counter or OTC
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: over the counter or OTC
statement: We say "medicine you buy (from a pharmacy or shop)". We put pharmacies first, ahead of supermarkets and shops.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > P > page titles
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: page titles
statement: See the guidance on headings, including page titles, on the Formatting page .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > P > passing wind
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: passing wind
statement: We do not use "passing wind". People understand " fart " better.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > P > PCR test
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: PCR test
statement: PCR (polymerase chain reaction) tests are sent to a lab to get the results. Use "PCR test". For example "PCR home test kit" or "PCR test site". Do not use: "virus test" "antigen test" "swab test" "lab test" "symptomatic test" "home test" or "home kit" "drive-through test" or "walk-in test" on their own
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > P > pee
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: pee
statement: We use the nouns "pee" and "urine". We know that everyone can understand "pee", including people who find reading difficult. Most people also understand and search for "urine", for example in phrases like "blood in urine". We do not use "wee" because it can confuse people who use voice technologies or screen readers. We use "pee" for the verb, not "urinate" or "pass urine". We know that the people who use NHS digital services talk about and search for "peeing more often" and "peeing at night".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > P > people or patients
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: people or patients
statement: Generally, we address people as "you". If we're writing in the third person, we mostly use "people" but this varies depending on the context. "People" is a broad term which covers patients, carers, their family and friends. We prefer "people" for content aimed at the general public but we sometimes use "patients" if the word "people" might be confusing, for example, where we need to distinguish patients from the general public. "Patients" may also be more suitable in content for health professionals.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > P > percentages
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: percentages
statement: See our guidance on fractions and percentages on the Numbers, measurements, dates and time page .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > P > perinatal
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: perinatal
statement: Do not use "perinatal". In our user research, most people did not use the term "perinatal". Instead, they refer to "pregnancy" and the stage of their pregnancy. If you need to use "perinatal" because users will come across the word, explain what it means, depending on the content. In most cases, it means the time you are pregnant and up to 12 months after giving birth. Perinatal mental health teams also offer support to people with mental health problems when they are planning to get pregnant.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > P > period products
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: period products
statement: Do not use "sanitary products" or "hygiene products". You could use "period products" or specify the products you mean.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > P > personal child health record (red book)
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: personal child health record (red book)
statement: All lower case. We include the phrase "red book" in brackets the first time we mention "personal child health record". Then we usually call it the "red book" after the first mention. Also see health record .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > P > personal protective equipment (PPE)
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: personal protective equipment (PPE)
statement: Use "personal protective equipment (PPE)" the first time you mention it, then you can use "PPE" after that. Use "personal protective equipment (PPE)" in the page title (H1), not "PPE". Do not use "Personal Protective Equipment" with capital letters. Do not use "personal protective equipment (PPE)" when referring to "face coverings".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > P > pharmacy
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: pharmacy
statement: We use "pharmacy", not "chemist". Our users are more likely to look for the word "pharmacy".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > P > phone and phone numbers
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: phone and phone numbers
statement: We use "phone" rather than "telephone" for mobile and landline phones. Use phone: 011 111 111 or mobile:. Do not use mob:. Use spaces between city and local exchange. Here are the different formats to use: 01273 800 900 020 7450 4000 0800 890 567 07700 900 866 +44 (0)20 7450 4000 +39 1 33 45 70 90 When an organisation has chosen a memorable number, for example for a campaign, group the numbers into easily remembered units. An example is the number for the Samaritans: 116 123. We prefer to use "call" or "phone", not "ring" or "dial". Survey responses show that users are more likely to use "call" or "phone".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > P > PMS (premenstrual syndrome)
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: PMS (premenstrual syndrome)
statement: We prefer "PMS" instead of "premenstrual syndrome". PMS is a commonly understood term and it is used more often than "premenstrual syndrome". But we should write it as "PMS (premenstrual syndrome)" at the first mention to make it clear what PMS stands for. We do not say "premenstrual tension" or "PMT" as these terms are more dated and users do not search for these as much as PMS.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > P > poo
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: poo
statement: We mostly use "poo", rather than "stool". We know that everyone can understand "poo", including people who find reading difficult. We do not use "opening your bowels" or "bowel movements". We sometimes use the words "stool" or "bowel" when people will hear their GP use them. But we will explain the term or phrase. For example: "a sample of poo (stool sample)" "Bowel incontinence can affect people in different ways. You may have a problem if you have sudden urges to poo that you can't control."
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > P > positive
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: positive
statement: If you use the word "positive" in the context of test results, be aware that some users may interpret it as positive news. In other words, they may think they do not have the disease. If you have to use "positive", because this is the word people will hear when they get their test results, explain what it means. Positive means the test found what it was looking for. A positive result means it's likely you had COVID-19 when the test was done.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > P > practice
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: practice
statement: "Practice" is the noun, as in "GP practice". "Practise" is a verb. For example: "Practise pelvic floor exercises". When we're writing for the public, we use "surgery" rather than "practice", because our research shows us that this is the word patients are more likely to search for and use. When we're writing for healthcare staff, we may use the word "practice". For example, for "practice managers". Note that a GP practice can have more than 1 surgery.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > P > preconception care
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: preconception care
statement: We prefer "planning your pregnancy" or "thinking about your health before you get pregnant" or just "getting pregnant". This is the kind of language our users use. Clinicians sometimes use "preconception care" when they're talking about women who need special care before they get pregnant, for example changes to their medicine. We do not use "preconception care" as a topic. Instead we give specific advice where people need it, for example: "Talk to your doctor if you want to get pregnant. It's best to stop taking [name of medicine] at least 3 months before you start trying for a baby."
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > Q > quotation marks
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: quotation marks
statement: See the guidance on quotation marks on the Punctuation page .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > R > race
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: race
statement: Use "ethnicity", not "race". Find out how we talk about ethnicity, religion and nationality in the Inclusive content section .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > R > rectum
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: rectum
statement: We prefer " bottom " or " anus ". Only use "rectum" when the other alternatives are not clear enough, for example when talking about surgery to remove part of the rectum. We found that people do not search for "rectum" in Google as much as other terms.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > R > redness
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: redness
statement: Redness is often mentioned as a symptom of health problems such as skin conditions, infections, and allergies. But this may be based on how the symptom appears on white skin. When you mention redness in content, always consider whether the description is accurate for all skin tones. A symptom that looks red when it appears on white skin may not look red on skin that's brown or black. See the guidance on skin symptoms in the Inclusive content section .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > R > religion
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: religion
statement: Find out how we talk about ethnicity, religion and nationality in the Inclusive content section .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > R > renal
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: renal
statement: We prefer "kidney". We may mention "renal" as well as "kidney" if our search analytics, user testing or survey feedback suggest that people will hear their doctor use "renal" or will search for it.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > R > risk and risk factors
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: risk and risk factors
statement: We prefer "chance" to "risk" when we're writing for the public. We try not to talk about "risk factors" and instead explain them some other way. We do use "risk" and "risk factors" when we are writing for a more specialist audience.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > S > safe and safer
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: safe and safer
statement: Beware of saying "safe drinking" or "safe sex". It's hard to know what is really "safe" so we talk about "safer sex" or "safer drinking". That suggests that people can lower but not necessarily get rid of the risk altogether.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > S > secure message
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: secure message
statement: We've found that people do not understand "secure message". Also, the word "secure" makes some users question security. Instead, make it clear how people will get a message. Use the words "text" or "email" or, for example, "messages through the NHS App".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > S > seizure (fit)
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: seizure (fit)
statement: Use: "seizure (fit)" in most contexts, for example medicines side effects or as a symptom, with "fit" only included at 1st mention "seizure (sometimes called fit)" in content about epilepsy or brain tumours aimed at a general audience "seizure" without any mention of "fit" in content aimed specifically at people with epilepsy (in other words, information not targeted at the general public) We only mention "convulsions" where there's good evidence that users are searching for the term.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > S > service user
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: service user
statement: We prefer " people" or "patients " – or in social services "people who use services".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > S > setting
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: setting
statement: We avoid the term "hospital setting". We just say "in hospital". Instead of "community setting", we mention the place, for example, "in school", "in a clinic" or "at home".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > S > sex and sexuality
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: sex and sexuality
statement: Find out how we talk about sex, gender and sexuality in the Inclusive content section .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > S > sex assigned or registered at birth
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: sex assigned or registered at birth
statement: We use the phrase "sex assigned at birth" when we're talking about trans health and gender dysphoria, as this is the language our audience uses. In other cases, we use "the sex someone was registered with at birth" because user research shows that most people understand this better as it refers to an actual event.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > S > sexual health clinic
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: sexual health clinic
statement: We use "sexual health clinic", not "STI clinic". Sexual health clinics can offer different services. So, when we mention them for the first time and are talking about STIs, we sometimes add that they may also be called "GUM clinics". When we are talking about contraception, we sometimes add that they may also be called "family planning or contraception clinics". Also see " STI ".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > S > sick
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: sick
statement: We use "feeling sick" instead of "nausea", but you may want to put "nausea" in brackets afterwards: feeling sick (nausea). We use "being sick" instead of "vomiting". Again, you may want to put "vomiting" in brackets afterwards: being sick (vomiting). We use "vomiting" in phrases like "vomiting blood". We use "vomit" as the noun. For example, "blood in your vomit".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > S > side effects
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: side effects
statement: Two words. We say that people may "get" or "have" side effects, not "develop" or "experience" them. Check a dictionary if you're not sure of the difference between "affect" and "effect".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > S > site map
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: site map
statement: We write "site map" as 2 words so that screen readers pronounce it clearly.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > S > sleepy
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: sleepy
statement: Generally, we prefer the word "sleepy" to "drowsy" as people are more likely to search for "sleepy". But " drowsy " may be better if you're writing about feeling unusually sleepy in the daytime, particularly in the context of medicines.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > S > skin colour changes
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: skin colour changes
statement: When you mention a change in skin colour, such as a red rash, redness with swelling, or skin turning yellow or blue, always consider whether the change will look the same on all skin tones. See the guidance on skin symptoms in the Inclusive content section .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > S > specialist
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: specialist
statement: We generally use the word "specialist" for consultants and other specialist medical professions. For example, we use "a heart specialist" instead of "a cardiologist". Also see " doctor ".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > S > specialty
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: specialty
statement: Although we can use "specialty" in a medical context (doctors and hospitals have "specialties"), we generally avoid using it. We're more likely to use the word " specialist " or to talk about a health professional who "specialises in" something.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > S > statistics
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: statistics
statement: See our guidance on statistics on the Numbers, measurements, dates and time page .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > S > STI
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: STI
statement: You might want to spell out "sexually transmitted infection" the first time you mention it. Otherwise it's fine to use the abbreviation STI. We talk about "a" sexually transmitted infection but "an" STI. We do not use the terms "sexually transmitted disease" or "STD". Also see " sexual health clinic ".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > S > stomach
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: stomach
statement: We use "stomach" for the internal organ and in some common phrases like "stomach ache" and "stomach bug". We sometimes use " tummy " for short, for example in "tummy bug". Also see " abdomen ".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > S > suffering from
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: suffering from
statement: We do not use "suffering from". We talk about people having or living with a disability or condition. Read more about how we talk about disabilities and conditions in the Inclusive content section .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > S > summary care record
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: summary care record
statement: Lower case. For a professional audience (people who will know the abbreviation already), it's OK to use SCR after the first mention of a summary care record. (It's "an", not "a", SCR.) For the public, we avoid the abbreviation. Instead it may be better to say: "your health record " or "a summary of your health record".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > S > surgery
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: surgery
statement: When we're writing for the public, we use "GP surgery" or "surgery" rather than "practice", because our research shows us that this is the word patients are more likely to search for and use. When we're writing for healthcare staff, we may use the word "practice". For example, for "practice managers". Note that a practice can have more than 1 surgery.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > S > symptoms
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: symptoms
statement: We say that people may "get" or "have" symptoms, not "develop" or "experience" them.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > T > temperature
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: temperature
statement: We avoid giving a specific temperature in most cases. This is because it's normal for people's temperature to rise when they are ill or have an infection. How much their temperature changes varies from person to person. So we do not focus on a particular temperature. In a list of symptoms, we say "a high temperature" or "if your child is feeling hotter than usual if you touch their neck, back or tummy". When we're telling people to do something about a high temperature in an adult or a child over 6 months old (for example, in the pattern to help users decide when and where to get care, with care cards ), we say: "if your temperature is very high, or you feel hot, cold or shivery" "if your child's temperature is very high, or they feel hot, cold or shivery" The exception is when talking about the temperature of a child under 6 months old. In these cases we state a specific temperature and say: "if your child is under 3 months old and has a temperature of 38C or higher, or you think they have a high temperature" "if your child is 3 to 6 months old and has a temperature of 39C or higher, or you think they have a high temperature" Also see " degrees (temperature) " and " fever ".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > T > terminal
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: terminal
statement: We use "terminal" when a condition or illness is likely to lead to death. We find that people with cancer, for example, often use this word.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > T > third party
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: third party
statement: Avoid the term "third party". Only use it if your user research shows that users hear the term and need to understand it.​
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > T > time
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: time
statement: See our guidance on time on the Numbers, measurements, dates and time page .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > T > tranquillise and tranquilliser
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: tranquillise and tranquilliser
statement: Note the double "ll". We use the British spelling with "s", not "z".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > T > triage
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: triage
statement: Do not use the word "triage" in a GP setting. People do not understand what it means and if they do, they associate it with A&E. In a GP setting you could say, for example: "We will look at the information you give us and decide the most suitable person for you to see and when they are available". If you have to use "triage" in the context of A&E or urgent treatment centres, explain what it means. For example: "A doctor or nurse will work out what order to see patients in, so they see the most serious cases first. People who arrive after you may be seen before you."
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > T > trimesters
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: trimesters
statement: We mostly use "weeks" when writing about time in pregnancy. We've found that most users think about their pregnancy in "weeks" or "months", but using "weeks" means we can be more precise. Trimesters are less clear. If you do use the word "trimester", explain what you mean, for example: "the 1st trimester (up to about 13 weeks)". We use numerals for numbers , for example "13 weeks", instead of "thirteen weeks".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > T > tummy
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: tummy
statement: Some users feel that "tummy" is childish but it can work well in content about children. It can also be a good alternative to abdomen when you're talking about the outside of the body (a broader area than the stomach). Also see " abdomen " and " stomach ".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > U > United Kingdom
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: United Kingdom
statement: Use "United Kingdom" or "UK" rather than "Britain" or "Great Britain". United Kingdom includes England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Great Britain refers only to England, Scotland and Wales. Our work is focused on the NHS in England. Take care not to refer to the UK when you mean England.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > U > unplanned
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: unplanned
statement: Use "unplanned' rather than "unwanted" when talking about pregnancy.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > U > urinary tract infections
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: urinary tract infections
statement: We use "urinary tract infections (UTIs)", not "water infections".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > V > vaccination
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: vaccination
statement: We use "vaccination" for the process or national programme. (We do not say "immunisation programme".) NHS vaccination schedule flu vaccination programme COVID-19 vaccination programme Most people search for "vaccination", not "immunisation". "Vaccination" includes injections and oral or nasal spray.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > V > vaccine
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: vaccine
statement: We use "vaccine" for the dose people get as part of a vaccination programme. the 6‑in‑1 vaccine the HPV vaccine you will have the vaccine as an injection in (part of the body) Use "COVID-19 vaccine". Use "COVID-19 vaccination" for the vaccination process or programme. Example: someone will get the COVID-19 vaccine as part of the COVID-19 vaccination programme. For the annual flu vaccination programme, use the term "flu vaccine". The child vaccine is a spray, so "flu vaccine" covers children and adults. See also the entries for booster and jab .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > V > vial
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: vial
statement: We prefer plain English terms like "plastic tube" or "glass container". If people need to know the word "vial", we might add it in brackets, for example: "plastic tube (vial)".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > V > vomiting
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: vomiting
statement: We use "being sick" instead of "vomiting". You may want to put "vomiting" in brackets afterwards: being sick (vomiting). We use "vomiting" in phrases like "vomiting blood". We use "vomit" as the noun. For example, "blood in your vomit".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > W > walk-in centre
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: walk-in centre
statement: Not walk in centre or Walk-In Centre (unless it's the name of a particular centre).
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > W > water tablets
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: water tablets
statement: We do not use "water tablets". We explain that diuretics are "tablets that make you pee more".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > W > White or white
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: White or white
statement: Use a capital letter when you're writing about ethnicity or when you're asking users for their ethnic group, for example: "people from a White British background". Use lower case when you're writing about skin colour.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > W > white skin
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: white skin
statement: We talk about skin colour clearly and use terms that are easy to understand, including "white skin". We do not describe white skin as "fair" or "light". See the guidance on skin symptoms in the Inclusive content section .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > W > Wi-Fi
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: Wi-Fi
statement: With capital letters and a hyphen. Find out more about NHS Wi-Fi on NHS England's website .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > W > wind
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: wind
statement: We use "wind" when we're talking about babies. For example, "bringing up wind". We also use it when we're talking about "trapped wind" or bloating. We use "burping" too. Also see " fart ".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > Y > you and your
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: you and your
statement: We address users as "you". See the section on voice and tone . We use "your" for parts of the body, where appropriate. For example: "the cells in your liver".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: A to Z of NHS health writing > Z > zimmer frame
title: A to Z of NHS health writing: zimmer frame
statement: Two words, lower case. When we talk about "walking frames", we also mention "zimmer frames". We have found that older people are more likely to know them as "zimmer frames".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "A to Z of NHS health writing".

author: NHS England
subcategory: British Sign Language (BSL) quality assurance standard > BSL and accessibility
title: British Sign Language (BSL) quality assurance standard: BSL and accessibility
statement: Providing BSL translations of pre-recorded audio and video content is a WCAG 2.2 AAA criterion. The NHS is legally required to meet, at a minimum, Level AA. AAA is best practice.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "British Sign Language (BSL) quality assurance standard".

author: NHS England
subcategory: British Sign Language (BSL) quality assurance standard > Make sure your original video is high quality health content
title: British Sign Language (BSL) quality assurance standard: Make sure your original video is high quality health content
statement: Before you create a BSL translation, your original video must meet the requirements in the Standard for creating health content . This includes, for example: getting clinicians or other subject matter experts to review your content meeting relevant laws, such as data protection regulations focusing on user needs and, where possible, testing your content
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "British Sign Language (BSL) quality assurance standard".

author: NHS England
subcategory: British Sign Language (BSL) quality assurance standard > Quality assuring the BSL translation
title: British Sign Language (BSL) quality assurance standard: Quality assuring the BSL translation
statement: You must get BSL videos independently assured by a Deaf-led BSL supplier.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "British Sign Language (BSL) quality assurance standard".

author: NHS England
subcategory: British Sign Language (BSL) quality assurance standard > Quality assuring the BSL translation > 1. Choose a supplier with appropriately qualified staff
title: British Sign Language (BSL) quality assurance standard: 1. Choose a supplier with appropriately qualified staff
statement: Your supplier must have sign language translators or interpreters who are registered with the National Registers of Communications Professionals Working with Deaf and Deafblind People (NRCPD) . The supplier should use 2 NRCPD registered translators to assure the video: 1 to translate it and the other to check their work. If this is not possible, they can use 1 registered translator and 1 registered interpreter or 2 NRCPD registered interpreters. The translators or interpreters should be trained in medical translation and have experience in the healthcare field.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "British Sign Language (BSL) quality assurance standard".

author: NHS England
subcategory: British Sign Language (BSL) quality assurance standard > Quality assuring the BSL translation > 2. Get the video translated and checked
title: British Sign Language (BSL) quality assurance standard: 2. Get the video translated and checked
statement: 1 translator must present the BSL translation on video. The other translator must check that the translation is accurate and clear.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "British Sign Language (BSL) quality assurance standard".

author: NHS England
subcategory: British Sign Language (BSL) quality assurance standard > Quality assuring the BSL translation > 3. Document what you have done
title: British Sign Language (BSL) quality assurance standard: 3. Document what you have done
statement: Record the details of both NRCPD registered sign language translators or interpreters including: their names their registration numbers evidence of current registration which translator or interpreter translated the content and which checked it We are also looking into creating BSL-only videos. We'll share guidance when we've researched and tested BSL-only content.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "British Sign Language (BSL) quality assurance standard".

author: NHS England
subcategory: British Sign Language (BSL) quality assurance standard > Production guidance for BSL translations of pre-recorded videos
title: British Sign Language (BSL) quality assurance standard: Production guidance for BSL translations of pre-recorded videos
statement: Use a diverse and representative selection of presenters. There are regional variations of BSL but try to cater for a nationwide Deaf audience. Talk with the supplier to understand if there is anything in the script that would benefit from a graphic ("transliteration") on screen to help users understand it. Do not hide any key content. Make sure BSL users can see the presenter at the same time as any graphics, text or other visual elements. Place the translator or interpreter in the bottom right-hand corner of the video. The BSL presenter size should be at least 1/6th of the screen. Make sure the video is culturally appropriate by working with the BSL community, testing it, or getting feedback.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "British Sign Language (BSL) quality assurance standard".

author: NHS England
subcategory: British Sign Language (BSL) quality assurance standard > Production guidance for BSL translations of pre-recorded videos > Find out more
title: British Sign Language (BSL) quality assurance standard: Find out more
statement: Follow NHS accessibility guidance on making videos and other multimedia content accessible See examples of NHS BSL videos on YouTube Use the BSL icon to help users find BSL content
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "British Sign Language (BSL) quality assurance standard".

author: NHS England
subcategory: British Sign Language (BSL) quality assurance standard > Developing this standard
title: British Sign Language (BSL) quality assurance standard: Developing this standard
statement: This standard was created by the NHS website team in collaboration with: the British Deaf Association NHS 24 (Scotland) the RNID (Royal National Institute for Deaf People) SignHealth It follows the process used for approving videos for the NHS website and NHS YouTube channel. It also aligns with the Accessible Information Standard implementation guidance (NHS England) . The standard is new and we're still testing it. Please feed back.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "British Sign Language (BSL) quality assurance standard".

citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Formatting".

author: NHS England
title: Formatting: Abbreviations and acronyms
statement: We explain an abbreviation or acronym in full on its first use unless it's well known, like UK, NHS, GP. Then we refer to it by initials. Example: A body mass index (BMI) above the healthy weight range can increase your risk of serious health problems.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Formatting".

author: NHS England
title: Formatting: Aligning text
statement: Left-align text in English. Some people with cognitive differences have difficulty with blocks of text that are justified (aligned to left and right margins). Also people who use screen magnifiers may miss text that is not left-aligned. For translations into languages that run right to left (like Arabic), right-align instead. Find out more about text alignment in the design system .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Formatting".

author: NHS England
title: Formatting: Bold, italics and underlining
statement: Use bold sparingly. Do not use italics or underlining (except for links, which are underlined by default). Use bold in technical instructions to tell users which element (for example, a text input or button) to select. For example: Select More , then select Messages . Do not use bold to emphasise text. To emphasise words or phrases, you can: front-load sentences use headings use bullets use words like "important" in your content Large areas of bold, italics or underlining can be difficult for some people to read. Too much bold makes it difficult for them to know which parts of your content to pay most attention to. People may mistake stand-alone bold text for a heading and underlined text for a link. By default, screen readers do not announce text in these HTML tags differently: <b> or <strong> for bold <i> for italics <em> for emphasis Users may miss anything you wanted to express by using them.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Formatting".

author: NHS England
title: Formatting: Headings
statement: Headings help users understand what the page covers and find the information they need. Use them to break up and structure text.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Formatting".

author: NHS England
title: Formatting: Write good headings
statement: Make sure your headings: are written in sentence case (see capitalisation on the Punctuation page ) are clear and concise describe the content that follows start with keywords, if possible are action-oriented, if possible (for example, "View your GP health record") are not written as questions (except on question pages when you need to ask users questions in your service)
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Formatting".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Formatting > Headings > Main heading or h1
title: Formatting: Main heading or h1
statement: Give your content a unique and informative main heading, which will be heading level 1, or h1. You should only have one h1 per page. Keep your h1 concise, ideally 65 characters or less, including spaces. The page title in the HTML metadata (the <title> tag) usually includes the h1 together with the website name, separated by an en dash (–). A simple example is "Flu – NHS", which is the page title for the flu page on the NHS website . It shows in the browser tab. If you use a content management system (CMS), it may create the title from your h1 automatically. Find more information about setting up page titles in the Page template , including examples of different text in the h1 and page title.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Formatting".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Formatting > Headings > Structure content with headings
title: Formatting: Structure content with headings
statement: Use heading levels (subheadings, starting with h2 and going down to h4) to break up your content and give it a sensible structure. With each heading, ask yourself if it's a sub-section of the previous heading, the same level or higher. Make sure that headings follow the correct "nesting" order, without skipping a level. h1 h2 h3 h4 Avoid using h5 headings. If you need 5 heading levels, your content is probably too complex.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Formatting".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Formatting > Headings > More information in the service manual
title: Formatting: More information in the service manual
statement: Find out about: setting up page titles in HTML, in the page template section of the design system using headings correctly, in the accessibility guidance styling headings, in the typography section of the design system using legends, labels and captions with page headings, in the question pages pattern
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Formatting".

author: NHS England
title: Formatting: Links
statement: Make links active, specific and concise. Links should describe where they're taking the user. Where you can, use the same words as the title of the page you're linking to. That way, the user will know what to expect. We do not use link text such as "click here" or anything that does not make sense when read out of context. Screen readers can move between links without reading the surrounding content. It's OK to use "see", "read" or "view" in link text. There's no reason to avoid these words from the point of view of inclusion or accessibility. If your link is at the end of a sentence, do not include the full stop in the linked text.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Formatting".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Formatting > Links > Avoid opening new tabs or windows
title: Formatting: Avoid opening new tabs or windows
statement: Avoid using links or buttons that open new tabs or windows. There are 2 exceptions to this: for instructions or other help with filling in a form (for example, a date picker) if a user has logged into a secure site and the link would take them away from it Read more about opening new tabs or windows only when necessary (on W3C, WCAG2.2) . If links do go to a new tab, warn the user by saying: "Link name (opens in new tab)". Include all of this in the link text.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Formatting".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Formatting > Links > Avoid linking to PDFs
title: Formatting: Avoid linking to PDFs
statement: Wherever possible, we avoid publishing PDFs or linking to them. Read our guidance on PDFs and other non-HTML documents . We prefer to link to an HTML page containing the PDF. That way, if the PDF is changed or updated, users can still find the latest information. If we need to link to a PDF, we: open it in the same tab add "PDF only, [file size in MB or KB]" in brackets to the end of the link text, for example: "weight loss progress chart (PDF only, 545KB)" Round up values over 1MB to 2 decimal places to keep it as accurate as possible. Round up values under 1MB to the nearest KB. For example, round up 835.74KB to 836KB.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Formatting".

author: NHS England
title: Formatting: Lists
statement: Use lists to make text easier to read.​ Bulleted lists should be short and snappy. If possible, limit your list to no more than 6 items.​ Each item in the list should be roughly the same length. We use bullet points in: the pattern to help users decide when and where to get care (care cards) Do and Don't lists
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Formatting".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Formatting > Lists > Lists with a lead-in line
title: Formatting: Lists with a lead-in line
statement: This is our preferred list style. Use a lead-in line with a colon. The bullets should make sense running on from the lead-in line. In effect, the list is 1 continuous sentence. A pharmacist can recommend: creams to ease pain and irritation antiviral creams to speed up healing time cold sore patches to protect the skin while it heals Each bullet point starts lower case and has no punctuation at the end, including after the last point. Do not include more than 1 sentence at each bullet point. Do not use a heading for a lead-in line. Avoid ending a bullet point with "and" and "or". Use the lead-in to let people know the options.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Formatting".

author: NHS England
title: Formatting: Full sentence lists
statement: If your user research shows that it helps your users, you can use full sentence bullet points. For example, our medicines information uses full sentence bullet points for key facts.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Formatting".

author: NHS England
title: Formatting: Key facts
statement: Paracetamol takes up to an hour to work. The usual dose of paracetamol is one or two 500mg tablets at a time. Do not take paracetamol with other medicines containing paracetamol. Paracetamol is safe to take in pregnancy and while breastfeeding, at recommended doses. Brand names include Disprol, Hedex, Medinol and Panadol. Each bullet point should be distinct information, start with a capital letter and end with a full stop. There should be no lead in line.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Formatting".

author: NHS England
title: Formatting: Numbered lists
statement: We use numbered lists instead of bulleted ones to guide people through a process. Each point starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop, without a lead-in line.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Formatting".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Formatting > Lists > How to gargle with salt water
title: Formatting: How to gargle with salt water
statement: Dissolve half a teaspoon of salt in a glass of warm water. Gargle with the solution then spit it out – do not swallow it. Repeat as often as you like.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Formatting".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Health literacy > What is health literacy?
title: Health literacy: What is health literacy?
statement: Health literacy is about a person's ability to understand and use information to make decisions about their health. A user with low health literacy will generally struggle to: read and understand health information know how to act on this information know which health services to use and when to use them Research shows that: more than 4 in 10 adults struggle with health content for the public more than 6 in 10 adults struggle with health content that includes numbers and statistics This is because a lot of health content is written, often unintentionally, for people with higher health literacy skills.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Health literacy".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Health literacy > Why health literacy is important
title: Health literacy: Why health literacy is important
statement: Low health literacy has been linked to a range of important problems. These include: unhealthy lifestyles and poor general health low use of preventative services, like vaccinations and screening difficulty taking medicines correctly increased A&E attendances and hospital admissions reduced life expectancy It's estimated that health literacy-related problems like these account for up to 5% of national health spending. Health literacy is also a health inequality issue. There is a close link between socio-economic deprivation and low health literacy.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Health literacy".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Health literacy > How you can create better content
title: Health literacy: How you can create better content
statement: You can help reduce the problems caused by low health literacy by making sure your content is written at a level most users can understand. You can do this by: following the NHS design principles when you create content following our advice how to write for NHS digital services doing user research with users who have low health literacy We've found that doing these things benefits all users, not just those with low health literacy.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Health literacy".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Health literacy > How you can create better content > Readability tools
title: Health literacy: Readability tools
statement: We do not recommend readability tools, except to help you prioritise your content. Tools cannot tell you how usable your content is. It's best to test it with your users. If you want a tool to help you write clearer, more usable content, you could try the Hemingway Editor . It will show you where you have long sentences, complicated words, adverbs or the passive voice.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Health literacy".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Health literacy > How you can create better content > Read more about this
title: Health literacy: Read more about this
statement: NHS Knowledge and Library Services: health information (includes health literacy toolkit) US Office for Disease Prevention and Health Promotion: Health literacy online
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Health literacy".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Consider the sensitivities around your questions > Understand the topics that are especially sensitive
title: Consider the sensitivities around your questions: Understand the topics that are especially sensitive
