What Carbon provides Design recommendations Development considerations
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Loading" ().

author: IBM
title: Loading: What Carbon provides
statement: The loading component has no keyboard accessibility considerations since it is intentionally not operable or navigable. However, Carbon incorporates other accessibility considerations, some of which are described below.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Loading" (What Carbon provides).

author: IBM
subcategory: Loading > What Carbon provides > Status updates
title: Loading: Status updates
statement: The primary accessibility consideration for the loading component is to convey its meaning to assistive technologies so users are aware of changes in status. Carbon achieves this by exposing the title value (normally “loading”) of the spinning wheel SVG image. Screen readers hear “loading” when a spinning icon appears on the screen.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Loading" (What Carbon provides > Status updates).

author: IBM
subcategory: Loading > Design recommendations > Convey when loading has completed
title: Loading: Convey when loading has completed
statement: When the loading indicator disappears, it conveys a second meaning, which is ‘not loading’ or ‘finished’. However, especially where loads may take more than a few seconds, a user who cannot see the icon disappear needs to be made aware the system is no longer “loading” and is thus available for usage. There are several ways to do this. If new content takes focus when the loading is completed (for instance after a full page load), then users will understand the system is now available. Annotating what component takes focus will ensure this is properly implemented. Annotate if a control takes focus after a loading completes. Where a change of focus is not appropriate when the loading icon disappears, the information can be surfaced to users through a non-displayed status message, such as "finished" or "loading complete," that can be conveyed to users through assistive technology. Annotate the information that developers need to convey programmatically to assistive technology.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Loading" (Design recommendations > Convey when loading has completed).

author: IBM
title: Loading: Development considerations
statement: Keep these considerations in mind if you are modifying Carbon or creating a custom component. - Carbon uses aria-live set to “assertive” to immediately surface a loading status to assistive technologies. - Carbon provides an SVG title value for the loading icon, which is exposed through the aria-live section. - The completion of the loading state should be conveyed to assistive technologies. A non-visible status message such as "loading complete" could be put in the aria-live section or exposed through a role="status". Alternatively, focus could be set to an appropriate element. - See the Equal Access Toolkit information on status messages.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Loading" (Development considerations).

author: IBM
title: Loading
statement: Loading indicators are used when retrieving data or performing slow computations and help notify users that a process is underway. Live demo Overview Formatting Content Behaviors Related Feedback
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Loading" ().

author: IBM
title: Loading: Overview
statement: The loading component provides visual feedback indicating a process or action is in progress. It helps set users' expectations during wait times by signaling that the system is working behind the scenes. Depending on the context, it can be used as a full-page overlay or placed within a specific section or UI element. Use a loading indicator if the expected wait time exceeds three seconds. Example of the loading component in a UI
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Loading" (Overview).

author: IBM
title: Loading: When to use
statement: - Use when retrieving data or performing slow computations to indicate that a request is being processed. - Use when the entire page or a key section is processing, such as after a user submits or saves data.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Loading" (Overview > When to use).

author: IBM
subcategory: Loading > Overview > When not to use
title: Loading: When not to use
statement: - Avoid using loading indicators for progressively displaying content; use skeleton states for a better experience. - Do not use loading indicators if user interaction is required to proceed; use alternatives like tooltips, progress indicators, or notifications instead. - For full-screen loads, skeleton states are preferred over indicators to create a smoother experience. - Refrain from using multiple loading indicators simultaneously, as it may overwhelm users.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Loading" (Overview > When not to use).

author: IBM
title: Loading: Anatomy
statement: 1. Loading indicator: A circular animated icon indicating that a process is underway. It serves as the primary visual cue for the loading state.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Loading" (Formatting > Anatomy).

author: IBM
title: Loading: Sizing
statement: The loading component is available in two sizes: large and small. The large loading indicator size is the default size. Large and small sizes of loading component
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Loading" (Formatting > Sizing).

author: IBM
title: Loading: Large size
statement: The large loading indicator is most commonly used to display loading in full-screen takeover situations. It can also appear on sections within a page, in modals, and on individual tiles. A background overlay is typically placed behind the large loading indicator so the user cannot interact with the elements currently in the loading state. Example of the large loading component in a UI
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Loading" (Formatting > Large size).

author: IBM
title: Loading: Small size
statement: The small loading indicator is best suited for contextual or localized loading experiences within a specific UI element, particularly in inline loading scenarios. It works well for quick-loading tasks and can be placed within or near the triggering element—such as a button—to indicate that a process is underway. Common examples include saving after clicking on a button, uploading a file, or placing the indicator beside label text to communicate the loading status. For detailed guidance, refer to the inline loading component Usage tab. Example of the small loading component in a UI
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Loading" (Formatting > Small size).

author: IBM
title: Loading: Large loading placement
statement: The large loading indicator is commonly used for full-screen and component-level loading scenarios. For full-screen loading, place the indicator at the center of the viewport and apply a semi-transparent overlay to signal that the entire interface is inactive. Example of the large loading indicator placement for full-screen loading with an overlay When used within a component, such as a modal, tile, or side panel, center the indicator in that space and use an overlay to prevent interaction with the content while it is loading. Example of the large loading indicator placement for component-level loading with an overlay
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Loading" (Formatting > Large loading placement).

author: IBM
title: Loading: Small loading placement
statement: The small loading indicator is ideal for inline or localized loading within elements like buttons or compact content areas. It should appear inline with or adjacent to the related action without using overlays. During the loading state, any related action buttons—such as “Cancel”—should be temporarily disabled. For more information about inline loading, refer to the inline loading component Usage tab. Example of the small loading indicator placement for inline loading
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Loading" (Formatting > Small loading placement).

author: IBM
title: Loading: Main elements
statement: The loading indicator can be paired with an optional label to provide additional context during a loading state. For large loading indicators, adding a brief status message below the indicator, such as “Loading data…” can help set users’ expectations. The label text is not included by default in the component but can be customized to include it if needed. Example of the large loading indicator with label text For small loading indicators, especially in inline use, content should be concise and placed near the related action. For more detailed guidance, refer to the inline loading component’s Content section.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Loading" (Content > Main elements).

author: IBM
title: Loading: Further guidance
statement: For further content guidance, see Carbon's content guidelines.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Loading" (Content > Further guidance).

author: IBM
title: Loading: States
statement: The loading component has two states: inactive and active. For detailed visual information about the various states for this component, see the Style tab. ; State ; When to use ; ; Inactive; The inactive loading state is when no data is being loaded and has no visual indicator.; Active ; The active loading state indicates that the action is still in progress. ;
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Loading" (Behaviors > States).

author: IBM
title: Loading: Interactions
statement: For large loading indicators, a semi-transparent overlay is applied over the page or component, blocking all interaction. During this state, users should not be able to interact with any elements, as the overlay indicates the interface is temporarily unavailable. For small loading indicators in inline loading scenarios, interactive elements like buttons should be temporarily disabled while loading is in progress. This prevents repeated actions and ensures a smooth user experience. For more guidance, see the inline loading component Interactions section.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Loading" (Behaviors > Interactions).

author: IBM
title: Loading: Feedback
statement: Help us improve this component by providing feedback, asking questions, and leaving any other comments on GitHub.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Loading" (Feedback).

author: IBM
title: Menu buttons
statement: Design annotations are needed for specific instances shown below, but for the standard menu button, combo button, and overflow menu, Carbon already incorporates accessibility. What Carbon provides Design recommendations Development considerations
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu buttons" ().

author: IBM
title: Menu buttons: What Carbon provides
statement: Carbon bakes keyboard operation into its components, improving the experience of blind users and others who operate via keyboard. Carbon incorporates other accessibility considerations, some of which are described below.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu buttons" (What Carbon provides).

author: IBM
subcategory: Menu buttons > What Carbon provides > Menu button
title: Menu buttons: Menu button
statement: The menu button is set in the tab order and is activated by Space or Enter. When the menu is open, the first item takes focus. Focus is moved between menu items with the Up and Down arrow keys. Space or Enter activates the item with focus, which causes focus to go somewhere else and the menu to close. Esc collapses the menu and puts focus back onto the menu button. Menu button is reached by Tab. Space and Enter keys open the menu as well as activating menu items with focus. When opened, the first item in the menu takes focus. Arrow keys move focus and Esc closes the menu.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu buttons" (What Carbon provides > Menu button).

author: IBM
subcategory: Menu buttons > What Carbon provides > Combo button
title: Menu buttons: Combo button
statement: The combo button is set in the tab order where the first tab brings focus on the primary button and the second tab brings focus on the icon button that contains the menu. The respective buttons are activated by Space or Enter. When the menu is open, the first item takes focus. Focus is moved between menu items with the Up and Down arrow keys. Space or Enter activates the item with focus, which causes focus to go somewhere else and the menu to close. Esc collapses the menu and puts focus back onto the icon button. Combo button items are reached by two Tab stops. Space and Enter keys open the menu as well as activating menu items with focus. When opened, the first item in the menu takes focus. Arrow keys move focus and Esc closes the menu.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu buttons" (What Carbon provides > Combo button).

author: IBM
subcategory: Menu buttons > What Carbon provides > Overflow menu
title: Menu buttons: Overflow menu
statement: Each overflow menu is in the tab order and is activated by Space or Enter. When the menu is open, the first item takes focus. Focus is moved between menu items with the Up and Down arrow keys. Space or Enter activates the item with focus, which causes focus to go somewhere else and the menu to close. Esc collapses the menu and puts focus onto the menu button. Overflow menus are reached by Tab. Space and Enter keys open the menu as well as activating menu items with focus. When opened, the first item in the menu takes focus. Arrow keys move focus and Esc closes the menu.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu buttons" (What Carbon provides > Overflow menu).

author: IBM
subcategory: Menu buttons > Design recommendations > Combo button
title: Menu buttons: Combo button
statement: Combo button has a prop that can be used to change the tooltip label and is only intended to be changed to translate "Additional actions" into other languages. If translation is required, the translation must be annotated with a label that is exposed on hover or focus. Annotate the label for combo button so the proper tooltip appears, which should only be used for translation purposes.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu buttons" (Design recommendations > Combo button).

author: IBM
subcategory: Menu buttons > Design recommendations > Overflow menu
title: Menu buttons: Overflow menu
statement: Overflow menu’s custom icon variant has a prop that can be used to change the tooltip label. If the tooltip label is changed, they must be annotated with a label that will be exposed on hover or focus. Annotate the label for overflow menu’s custom icon variant so the proper tooltip appears.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu buttons" (Design recommendations > Overflow menu).

author: IBM
title: Menu buttons: Development considerations
statement: Keep these considerations in mind if you are modifying Carbon or creating a custom component. - Menu button, combo button, and the overflow menu are buttons with aria-haspopup set to "true". - The menu button, combo button, and the overflow menu is named with aria-label. - Each menu item across menu button, combo button, and overflow menu is an li in a ul. - Each list item across menu button, combo button, and overflow menu contains a button with role="menuitem" and tabindex="-1". See the ARIA authoring practices on menubutton for more considerations. - Combo button and overflow menu has an iconDescription prop that can be used to change the tooltip label. See the design recommendations for more guidelines on tooltip labels. - For combo button, the menu is given an id. When the menu is open, the icon button is given aria-controls with a value of the menu id. aria-expanded is also set based on the open state. - When the combo button menu is open, the element (div) wrapping the entire combo button is given aria-owns with a value of the menu id.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu buttons" (Development considerations).

author: IBM
title: Menu buttons
statement: Feature flag Menu buttons, including menu buttons, combo buttons, and overflow menus, open a menu with a list of interactive options. Live demo Overview Formatting Content Universal behaviors Menu button Combo button Overflow menu Related References Feedback
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu buttons" ().

author: IBM
title: Menu buttons: Overview
statement: There are three variants of menu buttons (or menu triggers): menu button, combo button, and overflow menu button. Menu buttons are comprised of a button and a menu, which can be clicked to trigger an action or selected to initiate an action from a menu.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu buttons" (Overview).

author: IBM
subcategory: Menu buttons > Overview > Hiding extra actions in limited screen space
title: Menu buttons: Hiding extra actions in limited screen space
statement: Menu button, combo button, and overflow menu are useful when you need to show numerous options but have limited screen space available to display them. By hiding less frequently used or advanced options until the user needs them, it avoids cluttering the main interface with too many options.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu buttons" (Overview > Hiding extra actions in limited screen space).

author: IBM
title: Menu buttons: Variants
statement: ; Variant ; Purpose ; ; Menu button ; Use a menu button when all actions in the menu list share the same level of importance. They are usually used in the page header. ; Combo button ; Use a combo button when screen real estate is limited and one of the actions has particular importance. They are usually used in the page header.; Overflow menu; Use an overflow menu when additional options are available to the user and there is a space constraint. They are usually used in rows or cards. ;
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu buttons" (Overview > Variants).

author: IBM
title: Menu buttons: Feature flags
statement: A feature flag has been added to the overflow menu variant of menu buttons to improve accessibility and changes parts of its functionality, not its visual appearance. For code-specific feature flag information, refer to the Code tab. The current overflow menu is not being deprecated, but teams are encouraged to use the feature flag overflow menu for their products moving forward. Once the next major release (v12) is released in the future, this feature flag will become the default version of the component.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu buttons" (Overview > Feature flags).

author: IBM
title: Menu buttons: Height
statement: Menu buttons come in four sizes: extra small, small, medium, and large. When using menu buttons, the height of each item in the menu reflects the same size of the trigger button being used. See more about size specifications on the Style tab. ; Size ; Height (px / rem); ; Extra small; 24 / 1.5 ; Small ; 32 / 2 ; Medium ; 40 / 2.5 ; Large ; 48 / 3 ;
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu buttons" (Formatting > Height).

author: IBM
title: Menu buttons: Width
statement: By default, the menu button and combo button follow the button structure style, and the menu maintains a minimum width of 160px to prevent a narrow appearance. Menu default width when both button label and menu option labels are short If the menu item labels become longer, the menu button and combo button remain the same size while the menu component can expand up to a maximum of 288px. Conversely, if the button labels become longer, the menu component should not appear narrower but should extend to match the width of the menu buttons. If you opt for fluid-width default buttons, both the menu button (or the combo button) and the menu should have the same width. Ghost buttons only adhere to the button style. This is because enlarging the ghost button's width to match the menu's width would result in the caret appearing disconnected from its associated button, especially when the menu button is in its closed state.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu buttons" (Formatting > Width).

author: IBM
title: Menu buttons: Default
statement: By default, combo button, menu button, or overflow button remains positioned at the top, to the left or right side of the menu when it is open, depending on the available space and layout.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu buttons" (Formatting > Default).

author: IBM
title: Menu buttons: Alternatives
statement: Alternatively, open menus can be positioned at the bottom, to the left or right of its associated menu button trigger, depending on the available space and layout.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu buttons" (Formatting > Alternatives).

author: IBM
subcategory: Menu buttons > Formatting > Menu and combo buttons
title: Menu buttons: Menu and combo buttons
statement: These buttons are ideal for page headers, where multiple, distinct actions may impact the page content, and where real-estate is limited. In the page header component, multiple buttons will become a single action button at smaller screen sizes. These buttons should only be used when the actions affect a full page or a large object on a page (examples include a canvas UI, diagram, or whole data table).
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu buttons" (Formatting > Menu and combo buttons).

author: IBM
title: Menu buttons: Overflow menu
statement: When actions affect a smaller proportion of a page, such as table rows or cards, use an overflow menu.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu buttons" (Formatting > Overflow menu).

author: IBM
title: Menu buttons: Label
statement: The text label of the button is important to communicate the action that is triggered when the user interacts with it. The text label must accurately describe the button action or indicate that interacting with it displays a list of possible actions.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu buttons" (Content > Label).

author: IBM
title: Menu buttons: Further guidance
statement: For further content guidance, see Carbon's content guidelines.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu buttons" (Content > Further guidance).

author: IBM
title: Menu buttons: States
statement: The default and interactive states of menu buttons should follow the button style guidelines. - Combo buttons are available only as primary buttons. - Menu buttons come in three different button types: primary, tertiary, and ghost. - The icon button of overflow menu is treated as the ghost button, displaying only an icon and following its designated color and style.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu buttons" (Universal behaviors > States).

author: IBM
subcategory: Menu buttons > Universal behaviors > Menu button
title: Menu buttons: Menu button
statement: Users can reveal the menu by: - Clicking anywhere on the container of a menu button - Or tabbing into the menu button and pressing Return or Enter Mouse and keyboard interactions for menu button
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu buttons" (Universal behaviors > Menu button).

author: IBM
subcategory: Menu buttons > Universal behaviors > Combo button
title: Menu buttons: Combo button
statement: Users can reveal the menu by: - Clicking anywhere on the container of the primary button or the icon button. If clicking on the primary button, this will apply to certain elements, depending on user interaction. - Or tabbing into the combo button which will focus on the primary button first then the icon button. Then, pressing the Return or Enter to trigger the action of the primary button or menu under the icon button. Mouse interactions for combo button Keyboard interactions for combo button
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu buttons" (Universal behaviors > Combo button).

author: IBM
subcategory: Menu buttons > Universal behaviors > Overflow menu
title: Menu buttons: Overflow menu
statement: Users can reveal the overflow menu by: - Clicking anywhere on the container of the icon button - Or tabbing into the icon button and pressing Return or Enter Keyboard interactions for overflow menu
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu buttons" (Universal behaviors > Overflow menu).

author: IBM
title: Menu buttons: Menu button
statement: Menu buttons group actions that share the same level of importance. The icon used within the menu button should always be a caret in order to visually convey to the user that there are options to select from. There are three main use cases where using a menu button is recommended: - Grouping objects with the same common action - Actions related to a common label - Distinct actions applied to the same object or page Menu button comes in three different button types: primary, tertiary, and ghost. For detailed visuals, visit the Style tab.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu buttons" (Menu button).

author: IBM
subcategory: Menu buttons > Menu button > Grouping objects with the same common action
title: Menu buttons: Grouping objects with the same common action
statement: Menu buttons are effective when a single action affects multiple distinct objects. This is particularly applicable when users need to Create or Add various objects, and all these objects are equally relevant options. The shared action should not be repeated in the menu list. This adds unnecessary clutter and makes each option less distinct at a glance.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu buttons" (Menu button > Grouping objects with the same common action).

author: IBM
subcategory: Menu buttons > Menu button > Actions associated with a shared label
title: Menu buttons: Actions associated with a shared label
statement: Another common use of a menu button is grouping actions related to a common label. An example of this is when users have multiple approaches to execute an action, all of which are presented as choices within the menu button.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu buttons" (Menu button > Actions associated with a shared label).

author: IBM
subcategory: Menu buttons > Menu button > Distinct actions applied to the same object or page
title: Menu buttons: Distinct actions applied to the same object or page
statement: In many cases, actions on a page may not use the same verb or have a shared label for the menu button. When grouped actions remain distinct, consider labeling the menu button as 'Actions' to encompass all available choices. Example shows the menu button with possible actions that could influence the data within tab contents
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu buttons" (Menu button > Distinct actions applied to the same object or page).

author: IBM
title: Menu buttons: Combo button
statement: A combo button is composed of two buttons: the left is the default option (the most commonly used selection), and the right (chevron icon) shows the rest of the available options. A combo button provides quick access to a default action while also offering a list of related actions or options. The combo button is expected to have less use than the menu button, as the additional actions are more hidden than they would be in menu button. However, this button does have particular use where screen real estate is limited and one of the actions has particular importance. Combo button has only one button type: primary.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu buttons" (Combo button).

author: IBM
subcategory: Menu buttons > Combo button > Choose a default action
title: Menu buttons: Choose a default action
statement: Remember to choose the default, primary action that will be displayed in the primary button so it is not hidden within the menu of additional actions. The primary default action is typically the most commonly used action there is to take. Example shows that users mostly choose to save records, while less common options are hidden as extra actions.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu buttons" (Combo button > Choose a default action).

author: IBM
subcategory: Menu buttons > Combo button > Reduce visual complexity on a page
title: Menu buttons: Reduce visual complexity on a page
statement: Combo buttons reduce visual complexity by grouping similar commands together. For example, how navigation menus group together related options to enable conceptual understanding of the site information structure. Example shows that many actions (ghost buttons) applying to the same data can be replaced by the combo button.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu buttons" (Combo button > Reduce visual complexity on a page).

author: IBM
title: Menu buttons: Overflow menu
statement: Overflow menu is also another option that is available to the user when there is a space constraint, usually used in data table rows or in cards. Overflow menu has the ghost button style only.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu buttons" (Overflow menu).

author: IBM
subcategory: Menu buttons > Overflow menu > Overflow menu in cards
title: Menu buttons: Overflow menu in cards
statement: When there are more than three interactive icons, consider moving less important ones into the overflow menu. The overflow menu then takes the place of a third action.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu buttons" (Overflow menu > Overflow menu in cards).

author: IBM
subcategory: Menu buttons > Overflow menu > Overflow menu icon
title: Menu buttons: Overflow menu icon
statement: The overflow icon can be customized to align with the product's requirements. However, it's advisable to make minimal changes to the overflow menu's icon to maintain consistency across the product and ensure a consistent user experience.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu buttons" (Overflow menu > Overflow menu icon).

author: IBM
subcategory: Menu buttons > Overflow menu > Overflow versus tab tip (popover)
title: Menu buttons: Overflow versus tab tip (popover)
statement: Overflow menu displays extra options with simple text, typically utilized within data table rows or cards. The tab tip popover allows the user to include more complex inputs such as a checkbox group or a radio button group, usually connected to a data table toolbar. Use overflow menus in data table row Use a popover in the data table toolbar
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu buttons" (Overflow menu > Overflow versus tab tip (popover)).

author: IBM
title: Menu buttons: Feedback
statement: Help us improve this component by providing feedback, asking questions, and leaving any other comments on GitHub.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu buttons" (Feedback).

author: IBM
title: Menu
statement: No accessibility annotations are needed for menus, but keep these considerations in mind if you are modifying Carbon or creating a custom component. What Carbon provides Development considerations
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu" ().

author: IBM
title: Menu: What Carbon provides
statement: Carbon bakes keyboard operation into its components, improving the experience of blind users and others who operate via keyboard. Carbon incorporates many other accessibility considerations, some of which are described below.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu" (What Carbon provides).

author: IBM
subcategory: Menu > What Carbon provides > Keyboard interaction
title: Menu: Keyboard interaction
statement: The menu is reached by Tab. When the menu is open, the first item takes focus. Use the Up and Down arrow keys to navigate between menu items. Menu is reached by Tab and when opened, the first menu item takes focus. Arrow keys move focus. Pressing Space or Enter on a focused menu item activates it and collapses the menu. Pressing Space or Enter on a submenu opens it. A submenu can also be opened and closed using the right and left arrow keys respectively. When the menu or submenu is open, the first item takes focus. An activated menu item can have different results depending on its functionality. If the item is a link, it launches the selection. If the item is selectable, it selects or deselects the item. The menu item retains its selected or unselected state when the menu is opened again. Space and Enter keys activates, selects, or deselects the menu item with focus. A submenu is opened and closed with the right and left arrow keys respectively.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu" (What Carbon provides > Keyboard interaction).

author: IBM
title: Menu: Development considerations
statement: Keep these considerations in mind if you are modifying Carbon or creating a custom component. - Each menu, including nested menus, are ul elements with role="menu". - Menu items are li elements with role="menuitem". - If a Menu item contains a sub-menu, it is given aria-haspopup="true" and aria-expanded of true or false depending on if the sub-menu is open/visible. - Selectable menu items are given role="menuitemcheckbox". - Menu item groups are li elements with role="group". - Menu item radio groups get role="menuitemradio". - Menu items with really long labels can get truncated depending on the screen size. This label will be exposed by a browser rendered tooltip on hover or focus. - Menu implements the menu design pattern defined in the ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG).
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu" (Development considerations).

author: IBM
title: Menu
statement: A menu is a list of interactive options that appears when users interact with an element or perform a specific action. Live demo Overview Formatting Content Behaviors Modifiers Related References Feedback
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu" ().

author: IBM
title: Menu: Overview
statement: A menu is a disclosure component that appears with a set of actions relevant to a specific control, interface area, data element, or application view. Typically, this context is determined by the user's current selection prior to invoking the menu. Menus can be opened from components such as menu buttons or through right-clicking. This guidance will help you understand how to format, structure, and use the menu component effectively.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu" (Overview).

author: IBM
title: Menu: Declutter interface
statement: In general, use menus to hide less frequently used or advanced options until users specifically need them. This keeps the interface clean and focused on essential elements.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu" (Overview > Declutter interface).

author: IBM
title: Menu: Context menu
statement: Context menus are triggered by a right-click interaction. A context menu is a defined list of options in a menu that appears above all other content on a page and is related to the selected content or element it was triggered from.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu" (Overview > Context menu).

author: IBM
title: Menu: Customizable actions
statement: Menus can speed up interactions for advanced users who are already familiar with the application. These users often rely on shortcuts and context-specific actions to work more efficiently.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu" (Overview > Customizable actions).

author: IBM
title: Menu: Form submission
statement: When submitting a form with a static list of options for users to choose from, or when filtering, use a dropdown instead of a menu.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu" (Overview > Form submission).

author: IBM
title: Menu: Complex inputs
statement: When many or complex inputs are used collectively, use a popover instead of a menu.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu" (Overview > Complex inputs).

author: IBM
title: Menu: Anatomy
statement: 1. Trigger: Elements that are triggered to display a list of available actions. These menu triggers can include a menu button, a combo button, and an overflow menu within menu buttons. Menus can also be opened when right-clicking on a page or specific element, like a column, or a row. 2. Action item: A menu item that can be activated to apply its action on certain elements. This item can be accompanied by a submenu indicator or keyboard shortcuts. 3. Divider: A rule that indicates different sections within the menu. 4. Submenu indicator: A caret icon that indicates a submenu. 5. Keyboard shortcut: Certain action items may also have keyboard shortcuts. 6. Menu: A container displays the open state and contains a list of actions that can be selected. 7. Selected item: An item that can be selected. The selection can be single or multi-selected. 8. Submenu: A nested level off of the primary level.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu" (Formatting > Anatomy).

author: IBM
title: Menu: Height
statement: Menu items come in four sizes: extra small, small, medium, and large. See more about size specifications on the style tab. When using a menu button trigger, the height of the menu item (singular) reflects the size of the button being used. Note Currently, Carbon does not support the extra-small size for buttons, only for rows or menu items. Therefore, this menu size cannot be utilized with menu button triggers. However, the extra-small menu size remains available for implementation in other contexts if needed. ; Size ; Height (px / rem); ; Extra small; 24 / 1.5 ; Small ; 32 / 2 ; Medium ; 40 / 2.5 ; Large ; 48 / 3 ;
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu" (Formatting > Height).

author: IBM
title: Menu: Width
statement: By default, the menu button and combo button follow the button structure style, and the menu maintains a minimum width of 160px to prevent a narrow appearance. Menu default width when both button label and menu option labels are short If the menu item labels become longer, the menu button and combo button remain the same size, while the menu component can expand up to a maximum of 288px. Conversely, if the button labels become longer, the menu component should not appear narrower but should extend to match the width of the menu buttons. If you opt for fluid-width default buttons, both the menu button (or the combo button) and the menu should have the same width. Ghost buttons only adhere to the button style. This is because enlarging the ghost button's width to match the menu's width would result in the caret appearing disconnected from its associated button, especially when the menu button is in its closed state.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu" (Formatting > Width).

author: IBM
title: Menu: Default
statement: By default, combo button, menu button, or overflow button remains positioned at the top, to the left or right side of the menu when it is open, depending on the available space and layout. Menu default width when both button label and menu item labels are short{' '}
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu" (Formatting > Default).

author: IBM
title: Menu: Alternatives
statement: Alternatively, open menus can be positioned at the bottom, to the left or right of its associated menu button trigger, depending on the available space and layout.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu" (Formatting > Alternatives).

author: IBM
title: Menu: Action items
statement: Ensuring consistent alignment when combining single or multi-select items with non-select items will improve the menu's readability.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu" (Formatting > Action items).

author: IBM
title: Menu: Right to left (RTL)
statement: For RTL (right-to-left) languages, the entire menu is mirrored horizontally, including the direction of the caret and keyboard shortcuts.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu" (Formatting > Right to left (RTL)).

author: IBM
title: Menu: Overflow
statement: Consider using short and precise labels for menu items. However, when deciding to truncate long menu items, a browser rendered title tooltip will reveal the full text on hover. Tooltip helps clarify the truncated text
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu" (Content > Overflow).

author: IBM
title: Menu: Ordering and grouping
statement: To aid discoverability, arrange menu items in a meaningful sequence that aligns with the order of operations. To help users focus on the most relevant options, place the ones used most often at the top. When there is a significant amount of menu items, it's advisable to group them into sections, separated by divider lines. Example shows how menu items are grouped into meaningful sections
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu" (Content > Ordering and grouping).

author: IBM
subcategory: Menu > Content > Number of items within a menu
title: Menu: Number of items within a menu
statement: Expansive lists of options in menus can overwhelm users. With context menu and overflow menu, keep the list length manageable by including no more than 12 items to help users scan through items easily without having to scroll. With menu buttons, keep the menu list smaller with under 5 items. Do consider including as few items as possible Do not overload choices
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu" (Content > Number of items within a menu).

author: IBM
title: Menu: Submenus
statement: A submenu is a menu item with the caret icon on the right, offering additional related commands. While submenus can help tidy up a context menu and make its options clearer, introducing multiple levels of submenus can make the user experience more complex and harder to navigate. Avoid multiple levels of nesting when it comes to submenus.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu" (Content > Submenus).

author: IBM
subcategory: Menu > Content > Actions associated with a shared label
title: Menu: Actions associated with a shared label
statement: When a term appears in more than two menu items in the same group, consider eliminating the recurring term in the submenu label to help people predict its content and scan easily.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu" (Content > Actions associated with a shared label).

author: IBM
title: Menu: Further guidance
statement: For further content guidance, see Carbon's content guidelines.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu" (Content > Further guidance).

author: IBM
title: Menu: States
statement: Menu items have seven states: enabled, hover, focus, focus and hover, danger hover, danger hover and focus, and disabled. Learn more about states on the style tab. ; State ; When to use ; ; Enabled ; When an action in the list is live but a user is not directly interacting with it. This is commonly referred to as the default or normal state of the component. ; Hover ; When a user’s mouse cursor is hovering over the menu item in menus or submenus. ; Focus ; When a user tabs to or clicks on a menu trigger. This will open up the menu list. The first item in the menu list has the focus state as default. ; Focus and hover ; When an item is in the focus state but the user’s mouse cursor is hovering over the item row. ; Danger hover ; When an action could have destructive effects on the user’s data (for example, delete or remove). ; Danger hover and focus; When a user tabs to a destructive menu item that has the danger hover state. ; Disabled ; When an action is not able to be performed at a certain time, but will be possible to be performed by that user, at another point in time. Actions that are permissions-based should be hidden if it is never possible for a user to perform that action.;
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu" (Behaviors > States).

author: IBM
title: Menu: Mouse
statement: Once the menu opens by clicking on a menu button trigger or right-clicking on an area, users can: - Select or deselect an item by clicking on it - Hover over the item with the caret icon to reveal additional options or actions from that item - Click outside of the menu area to close it Mouse interactions on menu
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu" (Behaviors > Mouse).

author: IBM
title: Menu: Keyboard
statement: Once the menu opens by pressing Return or Enter on the menu trigger, users can: - Press Up and Down arrows to navigate between menu options - Press Return or Enter or Right arrow on the item with the caret icon to reveal additional options - Press Return or Enter on an item to select or deselect it - Press Escape to close it
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu" (Behaviors > Keyboard).

author: IBM
title: Menu: Responsive behaviors
statement: Once the menu opens, the first option is highlighted. Users can then move through the list of options to activate or select one item at a time. Once users activate or select a menu item, the menu closes. Activating a menu item can trigger the following: - Open a dialog box - Set a value (which can perform an action or serve as a selected/deselected option in the menu) - Open a new page (typically in a new window or tab) - Initiate a new user task (potentially involving multiple steps) - Save or close something - Expand a submenu (though this can also occur without activation) - Undo or redo a user action - Perform various actions (e.g., editing actions like cut, paste, copy, format; application actions such as checking for updates) - Open a sidebar or toolbar - Access an existing page - Adjust the current window(s) (e.g., minimize, split, arrange, swap) - No action other than closing the menu
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu" (Behaviors > Responsive behaviors).

author: IBM
title: Menu: Dividers
statement: Divider lines serve the purpose of categorizing related actions into appropriate sections, while also distinguishing actions that might have a significant impact on the user's data, such as deleting an app or service.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu" (Modifiers > Dividers).

author: IBM
title: Menu: Keyboard shortcuts
statement: A menu item can display related values, like a caret indicator for accessing a submenu or a keyboard shortcut linked to the action.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu" (Modifiers > Keyboard shortcuts).

author: IBM
title: Menu: Single-select and multi-select
statement: Single-select or multi-select has the same visual with the checkmark in front of the menu item.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu" (Modifiers > Single-select and multi-select).

author: IBM
title: Menu: Danger state
statement: A danger hover state can be applied to actions that could cause significant changes, such as delete.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu" (Modifiers > Danger state).

author: IBM
title: Menu: Feedback
statement: Help us improve this component by providing feedback, asking questions, and leaving any other comments on GitHub.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Menu" (Feedback).

author: IBM
title: Modal
statement: StructuredListWrapper, StructuredListHead, StructuredListBody, StructuredListRow, StructuredListInput, StructuredListCell, OrderedList, ListItem, } from '@carbon/react'; Design annotations are needed for specific instances shown below, but for the standard modal dialog component, Carbon already incorporates accessibility. What Carbon provides Design recommendations Development considerations
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" ().

author: IBM
title: Modal: What Carbon provides
statement: Carbon bakes keyboard operation into its components, improving the experience of blind users and others who operate via the keyboard. Carbon incorporates many other accessibility considerations, some of which are described below.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (What Carbon provides).

author: IBM
subcategory: Modal > What Carbon provides > Keyboard interactions
title: Modal: Keyboard interactions
statement: Modal dialogs take focus on appearance, and the tab order is constrained to the modal’s controls until the modal is closed by choosing one of the buttons with Enter or Space, or is dismissed by pressing Esc. Keyboard navigation is constrained to the dialog. Tab cycles through the components that take focus. The dialog is resolved by the user pressing Esc or activating a button.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (What Carbon provides > Keyboard interactions).

author: IBM
subcategory: Modal > What Carbon provides > Focus handling
title: Modal: Focus handling
statement: When the dialog appears, the first item that gets focus depends on the type of dialog. Passive dialogs only contain a close button (X), so that takes focus. For dialogs which prompt for confirmation or user decision, the primary button takes focus (regardless of number of buttons). For destructive interactions, the “cancel” button takes focus, not the red danger/delete button. The tab order should proceed left and down from whichever item has focus then wrap back to the close button (X). The first item with focus varies depending on dialog type.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (What Carbon provides > Focus handling).

author: IBM
subcategory: Modal > Design recommendations > Designate the input that takes focus in a transactional
title: Modal: Designate the input that takes focus in a transactional
statement: The only time the starting focus would not be on a button is where a dialog contains input fields. For such transactional dialogs, designers should annotate that the first input field should receive focus. Note that text links are not considered a user input in this context.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Design recommendations > Designate the input that takes focus in a transactional).

author: IBM
title: Modal: Development considerations
statement: Keep these considerations in mind if you are modifying Carbon or creating a custom component. - Carbon assigns the container a role of "dialog" and sets aria-modal to "true". - The dialog is labelled via aria-label, using the same string used for the modal’s title; aria-labelledby could also be used to assign the title’s string. - See the modal pattern in the ARIA authoring practices for more considerations.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Development considerations).

author: IBM
title: Modal
statement: Feature flag Modals focus the user’s attention exclusively on one task or piece of information by using a window that is displayed on top of the page content. Modal with AI label is now stable. This addition changes the visual appearance of the component and introduces an AI explainability feature when AI is present in the component. See the AI presence section for more details. Live demo Overview Formatting Content Universal behaviors Modal variants AI presence Related Feedback
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" ().

author: IBM
title: Modal: Overview
statement: Modals are a type of dialog because it is a conversation between the user and the system. Use a modal to present critical information or request user input that's needed to complete a user’s workflow. Modals interrupt a user’s workflow for short and non-frequent tasks, such as editing or management tasks. When the modal is open, the user is blocked from the on-page content and can't return to their previous workflow until the modal task is completed or the user dismisses the modal. While effective when used correctly, modals should be used sparingly to limit disrupting the user. Therefore, if a user needs to repeatably perform a task, consider making the task completable on the main page.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Overview).

author: IBM
subcategory: Modal > Overview > Require an immediate response from the user
title: Modal: Require an immediate response from the user
statement: Use a dialog to request information that is preventing the system from continuing a user-initiated process.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Overview > Require an immediate response from the user).

author: IBM
subcategory: Modal > Overview > Notify the user of urgent information
title: Modal: Notify the user of urgent information
statement: Use a modal to notify the user of urgent information concerning their current work. Modals are commonly used to report system errors or convey a consequence of a user’s action.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Overview > Notify the user of urgent information).

author: IBM
subcategory: Modal > Overview > Confirm a user decision
title: Modal: Confirm a user decision
statement: Use a modal to confirm user decisions. Clearly describe the action being confirmed and explain any potential consequences that it may cause. Both the title and the button should reflect the action that will occur. If the action is destructive or irreversible, then use a transactional danger modal.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Overview > Confirm a user decision).

author: IBM
title: Modal: Variants
statement: ; Variant ; Usage ; ; Passive ; Presents information the user needs to be aware of concerning their current workflow. Contains no actions for the user to take. ; Transactional ; Requires an action to be taken for the modal to be completed and closed. Contains a cancel and primary action buttons. ; Danger ; A specific variant of transactional modal used for destructive or irreversible actions. ; Acknowledgment; System requires an acknowledgement of the information from the user. Contains only a single button, commonly OK. ; Progress ; Requires several steps to be completed before it can be closed. Contains a cancel, previous, and next or completion buttons, such as Complete or Done.;
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Overview > Variants).

author: IBM
title: Modal: Feature flags
statement: A feature flag was added to the modal component to improve accessibility and changes parts of its functionality, not its visual appearance. For code-specific feature flag information, refer to the Code tab. The current modal is not being deprecated, but teams are encouraged to use the feature flag modal for their products moving forward. Once the next major release (v12) is released in the future, this feature flag will become the default version of the component.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Overview > Feature flags).

author: IBM
title: Modal: Anatomy
statement: The modal has three distinct zones: A header, the body, and a footer. Components, for example a data table, form or, progress indicator, can occupy the full width of the modal. 1. Header: Includes a title, optional label, and the close icon. 2. Body: Contains the information and controls, or both that are needed to complete the modal's task. It can include message text and components. 3. Footer: Contains the main actions needed to complete or cancel the modal task. Button groupings change based on the modal variant. 4. x: The close x icon will close the modal without submitting any data. 5. Overlay: Screen overlay that obscures the on-page content.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Formatting > Anatomy).

author: IBM
title: Modal: Sizing
statement: There are four responsive modal sizes: extra small, small, medium, and large. Choose a size that works best for the amount of modal content you have. Modals with brief text should be extra small or small to avoid long single lines; for complex components, like a data table, the default or large modal is more suitable.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Formatting > Sizing).

author: IBM
title: Modal: Max heights
statement: To maintain a proper window ratio, each modal size has a maximum height. If your modal has too much scrolling because of a maximum height limitation, consider using the next modal size up. If the large modal height is still not enough space then a full page might be needed instead.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Formatting > Max heights).

author: IBM
title: Modal: Alignment
statement: In a modal that has larger breakpoints, body copy, including titles, use a 20% margin-right. However, form inputs and other components expand the entire width of a modal.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Formatting > Alignment).

author: IBM
title: Modal: Full-width content
statement: Certain components, such as a structure list or table, can expand into the margins of the modal and align flush to the container edges. These components typically have border dividers or containers that extend beyond the text or icon. Labels or text of any kind should never be in the modal margins.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Formatting > Full-width content).

author: IBM
title: Modal: Title
statement: - Use a brief verb phrase that describes the modal’s task or purpose. - If the modal is accessed by clicking a button, use the button label for the modal title: - For example, if the user clicks the Create access group button to open the modal, Create access group is the modal title. Modals might also be accessed by clicking a menu item or an icon. - Be aware of situations where there’s a tendency to mix and match button or icon labels and modal titles. For example, if the icon name is New user, use New user as the modal title, not Create user. - If your product has a more conversational tone, use articles (a, an, the) in the modal title even though the button label doesn't include the article, for example Create an access group. - Sometimes, you might need to provide contextual information for the modal, such as when the actions performed using the modal apply to a specific item and you want to make it clear which item the actions apply to. - In this case, you can use the optional label that is displayed above the title. - For example, if the user needs to know the path to the object that they are editing, you might put the path in the optional label.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Content > Title).

author: IBM
title: Modal: Modal description
statement: If the purpose or goal of the modal is not readily apparent, provide a sentence or two of embedded assistance to help the user understand the modal or to provide examples to explain how to use the modal. If the title and the purpose are clear, such as Edit object for the title when the purpose of the modal is to edit an object, a description is not needed.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Content > Modal description).

author: IBM
title: Modal: Body content
statement: - Include only fields, components, and embedded assistance that are relevant to completing the current task. - Ensure that the text is 80% of the modal’s width. The components can span 100% of the width. - To add a link to IBM Documentation, include it as a link in the body of the modal. - Use a clear label, such as Learn more about topic or IBM Docs. - Ensure that the URL is easy to update
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Content > Body content).

author: IBM
title: Modal: Buttons
statement: - For action button labels, use active words that describe the purpose of the modal, such as Add, Delete, and Save. For a list of approved action labels, see the Carbon content guidelines. - Avoid vague or passive words, such as Done or OK.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Content > Buttons).

author: IBM
title: Modal: Overflow content
statement: When the modal content is longer than the modal height then the body section should scroll vertically with the header and footer remaining fixed in place. The content should visibly fade at the end of the modal body area to indicate there is additional content out of view. Modal content should never scroll horizontally; instead, use a larger size modal.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Content > Overflow content).

author: IBM
title: Modal: Title as message
statement: For short, direct messages the title can include the whole message to add visual clarity to an otherwise repetitive title and body message. When using this style, no other body copy may be included.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Content > Title as message).

author: IBM
title: Modal: Further guidance
statement: For further content guidance, see Carbon's content guidelines.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Content > Further guidance).

author: IBM
title: Modal: Trigger
statement: Modals are triggered as a result of a user’s action and are not system generated. Common components that can trigger a modal include, button, link, or icon. On a keyboard, selecting Enter or Space should launch the modal.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Universal behaviors > Trigger).

author: IBM
title: Modal: Focus
statement: Once the modal is open, set the initial focus to the first location that accepts user input. For example, if the modal contains a form then the focus should automatically be set to the first field when opened. If it is a transactional modal without form inputs in the body section then the first focus should be on the primary button. Focus should then remain trapped in the dialog until it is closed. When navigating by keyboard, Tab and Shift-Tab do not move the focus outside of the modal.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Universal behaviors > Focus).

author: IBM
title: Modal: Loading
statement: The task completion action should take place immediately. If a longer loading period is needed, a loading spinner and overlay should appear on top of the modal body area with content disabled. The primary action button should be disabled while loading is in progress. If a quick loading period is needed, use an inline loading behavior on the primary button to indicate the data is being processed.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Universal behaviors > Loading).

author: IBM
title: Modal: Validation
statement: Validate a user’s entries before the modal is closed. If any entry is invalid then the modal should remain open with the entry marked in an error state and include an inline error message. The message should inform the user what has happened and provide guidance on next steps or possible resolutions. Effective and immediate error messaging can help the user to understand the problem and how to fix it. When possible, validate the user’s data before submission. This kind of inline validation (aka client-side validation) should happen as soon as the field loses focus. This will help easily identify the elements that need to be corrected. In-field error messages should disappear when the form criteria is met. If the data was not able to be submitted due to server-side issues, an inline notification should appear.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Universal behaviors > Validation).

author: IBM
title: Modal: Passive modal
statement: Passive modals presents information the user needs to be aware of concerning their current workflow. It contains no actions for the user to take and should not include any data that needs to be submitted. They serve as a type of notification alerting the user to urgent information such as reporting system errors or conveying a consequence of a user's action.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Modal variants > Passive modal).

author: IBM
subcategory: Modal > Modal variants > Dismissing a passive modal
title: Modal: x
statement: x : Clicking the close x icon in the upper right will close the modal
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Modal variants > Dismissing a passive modal).

author: IBM
subcategory: Modal > Modal variants > Dismissing a passive modal
title: Modal: Click elsewhere
statement: Click elsewhere : Clicking outside the passive modal area will
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Modal variants > Dismissing a passive modal).

author: IBM
subcategory: Modal > Modal variants > Dismissing a passive modal
title: Modal: Esc
statement: Esc : Pressing ESC on the keyboard
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Modal variants > Dismissing a passive modal).

author: IBM
title: Modal: Transactional modal
statement: Transactional modals are used to validate user decisions or to gain secondary confirmation from the user. Transactional modals require an action to be taken in order for the modal to be completed and closed. It contains a cancel and primary action buttons.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Modal variants > Transactional modal).

author: IBM
subcategory: Modal > Modal variants > Dismissing a transactional modal
title: Modal: Task completion
statement: Task completion : Clicking the primary action will complete the task and
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Modal variants > Dismissing a transactional modal).

author: IBM
subcategory: Modal > Modal variants > Dismissing a transactional modal
title: Modal: Cancel button
statement: Cancel button : Clicking the cancel button will close the modal and return
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Modal variants > Dismissing a transactional modal).

author: IBM
subcategory: Modal > Modal variants > Dismissing a transactional modal
title: Modal: Esc
statement: Esc : Press ESC on the keyboard.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Modal variants > Dismissing a transactional modal).

author: IBM
title: Modal: Two buttons
statement: When using two buttons, the secondary button is on the left and the primary button is placed on the right. Each button spans 50% of the modal and are full bleed to the edge.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Modal variants > Two buttons).

author: IBM
title: Modal: Three buttons
statement: In the rare case where three buttons are needed, each is 25% of the modal width and aligned to the right side of the modal. Only the outmost right button is allowed to be a primary button with the other two being secondary buttons. If all three actions have the same weight, all three should be secondary buttons.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Modal variants > Three buttons).

author: IBM
title: Modal: Danger modal
statement: Danger modal is a specific kind of transactional modal used for destructive or irreversible actions. In danger modal, the primary button is replaced by a danger button. They are commonly used in high impact moments as a confirmation for an action that would result in a significant data loss if done accidentally.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Modal variants > Danger modal).

author: IBM
title: Modal: Single button
statement: Single buttons are placed on the right side, span 50% of the modal, and bleed to the edge. In most scenarios, a primary button is used when one button is needed.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Modal variants > Single button).

author: IBM
title: Modal: Progress modal
statement: For longer tasks, use a progress modal to give the user a sense of completion and orientation within the focused flow. For complex flows with complex choices, consider using a full page instead of a modal. A progress modal is not a solution for excess modal content. It should only be used to present information in more consumable and focused chunks.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Modal variants > Progress modal).

author: IBM
subcategory: Modal > Modal variants > Dismissing a progress modal
title: Modal: Cancel button
statement: Cancel button : Clicking the Cancel button will close the modal and
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Modal variants > Dismissing a progress modal).

author: IBM
title: Modal: Button group
statement: There are three buttons in the progress modal footer: Cancel, Previous, Next. Each button’s width is 25% of the modal window and are full bleed. Previous and Next are grouped together and placed on the right half of the dialog, with Previous as a secondary button and Next as a primary button. In the last step of the sequence, the Next button label should change to reflect the final action. The Cancel button is aligned to left side of the modal and uses a ghost button.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Modal variants > Button group).

author: IBM
title: Modal: AI presence
statement: The modal component has a modification that takes on the AI visual styling when AI is present in the entire container. The AI variants of a modal function the same as the other modal variants except for the addition of the AI label, which is both a visual indicator and the trigger for the explainability popover. AI in modal can appear in two ways: broadly, over the whole modal, or focused, just in certain parts of the modal. When the entire modal is styled for AI, it indicates to the user that AI is present in all aspects of the modal. If only a limited amount of the modal content is generated by AI, then only those components should receive the AI presence styling, not the entire modal. For more information on designing for AI, see the Carbon for AI guidelines.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (AI presence).

author: IBM
title: Modal: Feedback
statement: Help us improve this component by providing feedback, asking questions, and leaving any other comments on GitHub.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Modal" (Feedback).
