author: Shopify
title: Index table: {frontmatter.title}
statement: An index table displays a collection of objects of the same type, like orders or products. The main job of an index table is to help merchants get an at-a-glance of the objects to perform actions or navigate to a full-page representation of it. Index tables can also: - Support customized index rows and columns - Include bulk actions so merchants can act on multiple objects at once - Support sorting and filtering of long lists - Be paired with pagination to make long lists digestible ---
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Index table" ({frontmatter.title}).

author: Shopify
title: Index table: Purpose
statement: Shopify is organized around objects that represent merchants' businesses, like customers, products, and orders. Each individual order, for example, is given a dedicated page that can be linked to. In Shopify, we call these types of objects resources, and we call the object’s dedicated page its details page.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Index table" (Purpose).

author: Shopify
title: Index table: Problem
statement: Take orders as an example. Merchants may have a lot of them. They need a way to scan their orders, view the different attributes on each order, and find out which ones need action first. In other words, they need a way find an individual order, call up more information about it, and take action on it.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Index table" (Purpose > Problem).

author: Shopify
title: Index table: Solution
statement: Index tables function as: - A content format, presenting a set of individual resources with multiple columns of information for each - A system for taking action on one or more individual resources - A way to navigate to an individual resource’s details page Because a details page displays all the content and actions for an individual resource, you can think of a resource list as a summary of these details pages. In this way resource lists bridge a middle level in Shopify’s navigation hierarchy. ---
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Index table" (Purpose > Solution).

author: Shopify
title: Index table: Best practices
statement: Index tables should: - Have items that perform an action when clicked. The action should navigate to the resource’s details page or otherwise provide more detail about the item. - Customize the content and layout of their items rows to surface information to support merchants’ needs. - Support sorting if the list can be long, and especially if different merchant tasks benefit from different sort orders. - Support filtering if the list can be long. - Paginate when the current list contains more than 50 items. - Use the skeleton page component on initial page load for the rest of the page if the loading prop is true and items are processing. - Numeric cells and titles should be right aligned with the Text component - Numeric cells should use the numeric style with the Text component Index tables can optionally: - Provide bulk actions for tasks that are often applied to many list items at once. For example, merchants may want to add the same tag to a large number of products. - Hide bulk actions on small screens using the condensed prop. We only recommend hiding bulk actions on screens smaller than 490px using our breakpoints-sm value: condensed={useBreakpoints().smDown}. - Hiding bulk actions means a merchant can’t select multiple items at once, so it should only be used when the bulk actions are not essential to the merchant’s workflow. ---
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Index table" (Best practices).

author: Shopify
title: Index table: Content guidelines
statement: Index tables should: - Identify the type of resource, usually with a heading
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Index table" (Content guidelines).

author: Shopify
title: Index table: Don’t
statement: - No heading - Indicate when not all members of a resource are being shown. For a card summarizing and linking to recently purchased products:
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Index table" (Content guidelines > Don’t).

author: Shopify
title: Index table: Don’t
statement: - Products - Follow the verb + noun formula for bulk actions - Follow the content guidelines for filter options and applied filters ---
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Index table" (Content guidelines > Don’t).

author: Shopify
title: Index table: IndexTable.Row
statement: An IndexTable.Row is used to render a row representing an item within an IndexTable
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Index table" (IndexTable.Row).

author: Shopify
title: Index table: IndexTable.Row properties
statement: ; Prop ; Type ; Description ; ; children ; ReactNode ; Table header or data cells ; id ; string ; A unique identifier for the row ; selected? ; boolean &124; "indeterminate" ; A boolean property indicating whether the row or it's related rows are selected ; position ; number ; The zero-indexed position of the row. Used for Shift key multi-selection as well as selection of a range of rows when a selectionRange is set. ; tone? ; "subdued" &124; "success" &124; "warning" &124; "critical"; Whether the row should visually indicate its status with a background color ; disabled? ; boolean ; Whether the row should be disabled ; selectionRange? ; [number, number] ; A tuple array with the first and last index of the range of other rows that the row describes. All non-disabled rows in the range are selected when the row with a selection range set is selected.; rowType? ; "data" &124; "subheader" &124; "child" ; Indicates the relationship or role of the row's contents. A rowType of "subheader" looks and behaves the same as the table header. Rows of type "child" are indented. Defaults to "data". ; accessibilityLabel?; string ; Label set on the row's checkbox. Defaults to "Select \{resourceName\}" ; onClick? ; () = void ; Callback fired when the row is clicked. Overrides the default click behaviour. ; onNavigation? ; (id: string) = void ; Callback fired when the row is clicked and contains an anchor element with the data-primary-link property set ;
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Index table" (IndexTable.Row > IndexTable.Row properties).

author: Shopify
title: Index table: IndexTable.Cell
statement: An IndexTable.Cell is used to render a single cell within an IndexTable.Row
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Index table" (IndexTable.Cell).

author: Shopify
title: Index table: IndexTable.Cell properties
statement: ; Prop ; Type ; Description ; ; as? ; 'th' &124; 'td' ; The table cell element to render. Render the cell as a th if it serves as a subheading. Defaults to td. ; id? ; string ; The unique ID to set on the cell element ; children? ; ReactNode ; The cell contents ; className?; string ; Adds a class to the cell. Use to set a custom cell width. ; flush? ; boolean ; Whether the cell padding should be removed. Defaults to false. ; colSpan? ; [HTMLTableCellElement['colSpan']](https://www.w3schools.com/tags/attcolspan.asp); For subheader cells -- The number of the columns that the cell element should extend to within the row. ; scope? ; [HTMLTableCellElement['scope']](https://www.w3schools.com/tags/attscope.asp) ; For subheader cells -- Indicates the cells that the th element relates to ; headers? ; [HTMLTableCellElement['headers']](https://www.w3schools.com/tags/attheaders.asp); A space-separated list of the th cell IDs that describe or apply to it. Use for cells within a row that relate to a subheader cell in addition to their column header.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Index table" (IndexTable.Cell > IndexTable.Cell properties).

author: Shopify
title: Index table: Structure
statement: The IndexTable is an actionable, filterable, and sortable table widget that supports row selection with subheaders. To ensure that the power of this table is accessible to all merchants when implementing IndexTable.Row subheaders, set the following props on IndexTable.Cell that are appropriate for the enhancement you are implementing. Merchants can select a group of rows at once by clicking or Space keypressing a subheader row's checkbox. To indicate that an IndexTable.Row serves as a subheader for 1 or more rows below it, set the: - Zero-indexed table position of the first and last IndexTable.Row described by the subheader IndexTable.Row as a tuple array on its selectionRange prop - Unique id on the IndexTable.Cell that contains the subheader content - Element tag to "th" on the as prop of the subheader IndexTable.Cell - Subheader IndexTable.Cell scope prop to "colgroup" To associate the subheader IndexTable.Row with each IndexTable.Cell that it describes, set the: - Unique id provided to the subheader IndexTable.Cell on the headers prop of each related IndexTable.Cell (contained by an IndexTable.Row that's position is within the selectionRange) as well as the unique id of its corresponding column heading that you provided to the IndexTable headings prop
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Index table" (Accessibility > Structure).

author: Shopify
title: Index table: Keyboard support
statement: IndexTable also supports multi-selection of a range of rows by keypressing the Shift key. To select a range, press and hold the Shift key while you click or keypress the Space key on a row checkbox and then do the same on another row's checkbox. All selectable rows between the selected checkboxes will also be selected.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Index table" (Accessibility > Keyboard support).

author: Shopify
title: Tables: {frontmatter.title}
statement: Display, organize, and sort data for merchants to analyze and take action on.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Tables" ({frontmatter.title}).

author: Shopify
title: Typography: {frontmatter.title}
statement: Establish hierarchy and communicate importance through text presentation.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Typography" ({frontmatter.title}).

author: Shopify
title: Text: {frontmatter.title}
statement: Typography helps establish hierarchy and communicate important content by creating clear visual patterns.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Text" ({frontmatter.title}).

author: Shopify
subcategory: Text > Mapping from previous type components
title: Text: Mapping from previous type components
statement: These are suggested replacements for existing text style components, but ultimately the best replacement should be evaluated based on the context of the usage. The Text component also requires setting the semantically appropriate html element through the as prop.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Text" (Mapping from previous type components).

author: Shopify
title: Text: Headings
statement: Headings use all the variants with heading in the name, such as headingMd. Headings should: - Clearly describe the section of interface they refer to - Highlight the most important concept or piece of information merchants need to know - Sit at the top of the section of interface they’re referring to
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Text" (Best practices > Headings).

author: Shopify
title: Text: Captions
statement: Captions use the bodySm Text variant. - Use for secondary labels in graphs and charts - May be used for timestamps in lists of content - Don’t use this variant for other cases - Don’t use this variant for text longer than a few words - Don’t use this variant for aesthetic effect or to break from the standard text size
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Text" (Best practices > Captions).

author: Shopify
title: Text: Text styles
statement: Text styles should be: - Used when enhancing the text to help merchants understand its meaning - Subdued if the text is less important than its surrounding text - Warning if the text denotes something that needs attention, or that merchants need to take action on. - Semibold for input fields, or for a row total in a price table - Paired with symbols, like an arrow or dollar sign, when using success or critical styles
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Text" (Best practices > Text styles).

author: Shopify
title: Text: Visually hidden
statement: Visually hidden text should: - Not be used if semantic markup can make content understandable to people using assistive technology - Be used to provide extra context when semantic markup isn’t enough - Be used on any content that is normally present but is being omitted - Make sense in context when used with a screen reader ---
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Text" (Best practices > Visually hidden).

author: Shopify
title: App provider: {frontmatter.title}
statement: App provider is a required component that enables sharing global settings throughout the hierarchy of your application.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "App provider" ({frontmatter.title}).

author: Shopify
title: App provider: Best practices
statement: The app provider component is required to use Polaris. Without it, the components in your application will not function correctly. You must wrap the root (the top) of your application in the app provider component. ---
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "App provider" (Best practices).

author: Shopify
title: App provider: Using translations
statement: Translations are provided in the locales folder. When using Polaris, you are able to import translations from all languages supported by the core Shopify product and consume them through the i18n prop. If a project has only one locale, then you can pass the JSON content from the locale file into AppProvider. If a project supports multiple locales, then load them dynamically using @shopify/react-i18n. This ensures that you load only the translations you need. ---
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "App provider" (Using translations).

author: Shopify
title: App provider: Using linkComponent
statement: By default Polaris renders elements (and action objects) as tags. That works well for simple one-page demos. However for more complex multi-page applications that use a router such as react-router you will want links to use the components provided by your router. If you don't then every link will be an tag and thus trigger a whole page refresh instead of navigating client-side. The linkComponent prop allows you to customise how links behave within Polaris by allowing you to inject your router's own Link component. The following example demonstrates using react-router's Link component. ---
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "App provider" (Using linkComponent).

author: Shopify
title: App provider: Testing components
statement: You must include Polaris context in your tests when you use Polaris components. To make this easier for you, we’ve provided: - a PolarisTestProvider component to provide the Polaris contexts for you
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "App provider" (Testing components).

author: Shopify
title: Collapsible: {frontmatter.title}
statement: The collapsible component is used to put long sections of information under a block that merchants can expand or collapse.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Collapsible" ({frontmatter.title}).

author: Shopify
title: Collapsible: Best practices
statement: The collapsible component should: - Be used for information that is lower priority or that merchants don’t need to see all the time - Not be used to hide error messages or other critical information that requires an immediate action ---
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Collapsible" (Best practices).

author: Shopify
title: Collapsible: Content guidelines
statement: Collapsible containers are cards with expandable and collapsible functionality, and should follow the content guidelines for cards. ---
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Collapsible" (Content guidelines).

author: Shopify
title: Collapsible: Accessibility
statement: Use the collapsible component in conjunction with a button. Place the collapsible content immediately after the button that controls it, so merchants with vision or attention issues can easily discover what content is being affected. - Use the required id prop of the collapsible component to give the content a unique id value - Use the ariaExpanded prop on the button component to add an aria-expanded attribute, which conveys the expanded or collapsed state to screen reader users - Use the ariaControls prop on the button component, and set its value to the id value of the collapsible component
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Collapsible" (Accessibility).

author: Shopify
title: Utilities: {frontmatter.title}
statement: Utilities are core tools for managing the structure of the admin and global settings.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Utilities" ({frontmatter.title}).

author: Shopify
title: Scrollable: {frontmatter.title}
statement: The scrollable component is a container for long form content, such as terms of service, that allows for scrolling so merchants can expose more text as they read.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Scrollable" ({frontmatter.title}).

author: Shopify
title: Scrollable: Best practices
statement: Scrollable containers should: - Be used when it’s helpful to provide an extra visual cue to let merchants know that content exists below or above the fold - Only be used for length text such as terms of service or other legal disclaimers and never for instructional or action-oriented text ---
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Scrollable" (Best practices).

author: Shopify
title: Scrollable: Content guidelines
statement: Scrollable containers are cards with scrolling functionality, and should follow the content guidelines for cards. ---
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Scrollable" (Content guidelines).

author: Shopify
title: Alternative text: {frontmatter.title}
statement: {frontmatter.description} Alt text is a text replacement for an image. Generally, it is represented by the alt HTML element attribute alt="alt text". Often used by people who are blind or have low vision, screen readers announce alt text to explain images. Alt text will also display when images fail to download (for example, there’s an unstable or low-bandwidth network connection). Alt text should: - Help visitors navigate the site - Provide an inclusive experience - Be as short and specific as possible - Be contextual to the intended message ---
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Alternative text" ({frontmatter.title}).

author: Shopify
subcategory: Alternative text > Alt text for images
title: Alternative text: Alt text for images
statement: Use alt text when the image conveys valuable information, such as the ability to play a demo video. Even if an image isn’t conveying meaningful information, don’t leave an tag without an alt text element. The screen reader may try to read the filename and create a negative experience. Instead, let the screen reader know to ignore the image by setting the alt to an empty string. All tags need an alt text attribute, even if it’s empty. For example, set an empty alt text attribute using .
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Alternative text" (Alt text for images).

author: Shopify
title: Alternative text: Writing alt text
statement: Always write alt text in plain text. The average rate of listening to a screen reader is 3x slower than that of an average visual reader. Many screen reader users listen at fast speeds to make up time. When writing alt text, be as brief as possible. - Be concise. Think about how to write for a small amount of space or a character limit. - Use simple words. If you’re stuck on how to replace a complicated word, check this A-Z list of alternative words or these plain language tips. Another good resource is the Hemingway editor. - Avoid needless words. If a phrase is still understandable without a specific word, remove it. - Remove articles like "a, an, one of," etc. whenever possible. Alt text has different grammatical rules. "Filler words" that assist understanding in speech can get in the way in alt text. - Avoid using "image of" or "photograph" unless the type of image is relevant to the context. Screenreaders already announce images with use of the attribute. - Avoid punctuation like !! and emoji like 🥰. Screen readers will announce these as "exclamation point, exclamation point" and "smiling face with three hearts." Use other punctuation marks as you regularly would, such as commas, or periods at the ends of the sentences. The screen-reader will react with a brief pause. - Only use acronyms you are confident your audience will understand. If using an acronym, write it with spaces in-between, like "Y M C A." Otherwise, most screen readers will try to read the acronym as a word. - Write in the active voice when possible. ---
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Alternative text" (Writing alt text).

author: Shopify
subcategory: Alternative text > Alt text in context
title: Alternative text: Alt text in context
statement: It can be tricky to decide whether an image needs alt text or should be ignored by screen readers. Ask yourself: - Is it interactive? - Does this image convey information that isn’t given elsewhere? - Does the context of the image communicate anything? The same image may have different alt text depending on what it conveys. For example, if you’re using a photo of sneakers purely decoratively as the hero image for a blog, tell screen readers to skip it. If you’re using the photo as an example of a certain type of sneaker mentioned in the blog, then convey relevant information about the image. For example, "High-top sneaker with gum soles." But if you’re using this image in a product listing, ensure shoppers know the important details of what they are buying, such as "Converse Chuck Taylor All Star Classic Black."
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Alternative text" (Alt text in context).

author: Shopify
subcategory: Alternative text > Alt text in context > Icons
title: Alternative text: Icons
statement: Icons that could be misinterpreted need an explanation, so use the Polaris accessibilityLabel prop or the aria-label HTML attribute. For interactive icons, don’t describe the image ("magnifying glass"). Instead, describe the action ("search").
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Alternative text" (Alt text in context > Icons).

author: Shopify
subcategory: Alternative text > Alt text in context > Actions
title: Alternative text: Actions
statement: Write clear and predictable link text. If space constraints require you to write calls to action that are unclear where they take you (like "Learn more" and "Apply now"), give further indication of where merchants will be sent after they select.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Alternative text" (Alt text in context > Actions).

author: Shopify
subcategory: Alternative text > Alt text in context > Complex images
title: Alternative text: Complex images
statement: Images with more complexity need some consideration. For example, groups of image elements can be described by a single text, rather than announcing each individual element. For more guidance, visit the W3C page on complex images.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Alternative text" (Alt text in context > Complex images).

author: Shopify
subcategory: Alternative text > Alt text in context > Situations that don’t need alt text
title: Alternative text: Situations that don’t need alt text
statement: Websites can sometimes be noisy for a screen reader user. While alt text is vital for an equal experience, the briefer you are, the happier your screen reader users will be. Avoid repetition and unnecessary announcements by setting alt="" in the scenarios that don’t need it.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Alternative text" (Alt text in context > Situations that don’t need alt text).

author: Shopify
subcategory: Alternative text > Alt text in context > Progress bars
title: Alternative text: Progress bars
statement: Progress bars often present visual information that can also be found in the text, such as "Loading 53%." Continuously announcing that change is generally considered annoying.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Alternative text" (Alt text in context > Progress bars).

author: Shopify
subcategory: Alternative text > Alt text in context > Decorative elements
title: Alternative text: Decorative elements
statement: This is a broad category covering elements that are purely for aesthetic reasons, such as empty state illustrations, dividers, or hero images. If you’re unsure whether valuable information is lost, consider testing with people who regularly use a screen reader.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Alternative text" (Alt text in context > Decorative elements).

author: Shopify
subcategory: Alternative text > Alt text in context > Images with adequate captions
title: Alternative text: Images with adequate captions
statement: Avoid adding repetitive alt text if an image has a caption that accurately reflects the information in the image, for example a photo of George Washington that is captioned "George Washington." If the image is presenting information that isn’t in the caption, consider adding it to the caption text. Only if this isn’t possible or appropriate should you add that information as alt text. If the image has a longer description in the caption or following paragraph text, you can associate this description with the aria-describedby attribute.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Alternative text" (Alt text in context > Images with adequate captions).

author: Shopify
subcategory: Alternative text > Alt text in context > Tracking images
title: Alternative text: Tracking images
statement: Images that would not be visible to a sighted user should not be announced to screen-readers. ---
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Alternative text" (Alt text in context > Tracking images).

author: Shopify
title: Alternative text: Pronunciation and translation
statement: Not only do we strive to make interactions with our products pleasant, but we want the listening experience for merchants to be positive, too. Always state the language of the page content with the HTML lang attribute. This will ensure pronunciation and translation tools will know what rules to use. If certain phrases are in a different language than the main content, you can also use the lang attribute in a tag or similar. Here’s a standard list of language attributes that you can use in your document.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Alternative text" (Pronunciation and translation).

author: Shopify
title: Alternative text: SEO
statement: Besides screen readers, search engines also read alt text. Alt text helps increase image ranking results and site searchability outside of Shopify’s admin. When accounting for SEO in your alt text: - Use logical keywords (the words that people search for). - Include relevant listing details, like if it is a limited edition or unique colorway. - Describe the image, not what you want your audience to think. - Don’t repeat your site name or brand name. Search engines will already associate your site with your images. - Avoid reducing the relevance or clarity of the alt text just to insert a keyword. - Never include unassociated lists of key words in the alt text. Instead, place those in your meta description.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Alternative text" (SEO).

author: Shopify
title: Error messages: {frontmatter.title}
statement: {frontmatter.description} Error messages should: - Explain what’s wrong and what the merchant needs to do - Be specific (exact numbers and dates, or even the merchant’s own data) - Don’t overapologize or bring “us”/”we” into the conversation unless Shopify caused the problem - Avoid error jargon like “invalid” - Use detailed instructions for the next step - Help merchants avoid mistakes in the first place, using clear content to manage expectations and highlight potential risks - Only explain what happened behind the scenes when it’s helpful to merchants or you can’t offer a solution As always, follow our content fundamentals of keeping it short, using plain language, and getting rid of repetition.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Error messages" ({frontmatter.title}).

author: Shopify
title: Error messages: Design for clarity
statement: - Use iconography and color to communicate the severity of the problem and draw the merchant’s attention to what’s wrong - Place the error close to what needs fixed - Use red for critical messages that merchants need to deal with immediately to avoid harm to their business form validation errors - Use yellow for errors that are part of a daily workflow or warnings that could lead to critical errors if not addressed
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Error messages" (Design for clarity).

author: Shopify
subcategory: Error messages > Anatomy of an error message > Heading (optional)
title: Error messages: Heading (optional)
statement: - Clearly state the effect of the error on the merchant - Command immediate attention
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Error messages" (Anatomy of an error message > Heading (optional)).

author: Shopify
subcategory: Error messages > Anatomy of an error message > Body
title: Error messages: Body
statement: - If you don’t have a header, clearly state the effect of the error on the merchant - Explain how to fix it - Link to help documentation
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Error messages" (Anatomy of an error message > Body).

author: Shopify
subcategory: Error messages > Anatomy of an error message > CTA (optional)
title: Error messages: CTA (optional)
statement: - Provide a one-step solution - Take merchants to another location expressly for fixing the issue
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Error messages" (Anatomy of an error message > CTA (optional)).

author: Shopify
title: Fundamentals: {frontmatter.title}
statement: {frontmatter.description} These fundamentals apply to every piece of content you create. For specific questions, dig into our detailed content guidelines for everything from grammar to components. Think of tools you use every day, such as your phone, car, or blender. They all have a learning curve, but the very best of them feel easy from the very first use. Buttons are where you expect them. Labeling is intuitive. Everything unnecessary has been removed, and what’s left is the perfect balance of words and visuals. That’s what we’re building here at Shopify.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Fundamentals" ({frontmatter.title}).

author: Shopify
title: Fundamentals: Content 🤝 design
statement: Words are an essential part of the design. Very few interfaces make sense without content. But each word and every period adds noise to the experience. So weigh every word. - Only add content that’s necessary for clarity - Let visuals and icons do the talking wherever you can (“+” not “+ Add”) - Remember design doesn’t always dictate content (not every situation calls for subcopy, even if the component has been designed to include it) Tip: Ask yourself, could this word be an icon? Could this header, subcopy, and button just be a button?
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Fundamentals" (Content 🤝 design).

author: Shopify
title: Fundamentals: Keep it lean
statement: Too much content makes a tool feel cheap and that it’s hard to use. Not enough leads to confusion and frustration. Great design means finding that sweet spot. - Find the shortest, clearest way to give merchants only the info they need to take action - Skip the punctuation (exceptions: questions or text with 2+ sentences) - Get rid of any repetition Tip: Approach content like Jenga. What’s the most you can take away before things fall apart?
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Fundamentals" (Keep it lean).

author: Shopify
title: Fundamentals: Write like merchants talk
statement: Don’t worry too much about voice and tone, just focus on sounding human - Use plain language - Use contractions (“don’t” not “do not”) - Some jargon is okay, as long as it’s what actual merchants say - Aim for a 7th grade reading level—it’s easiest for merchants to digest Tip: Read it out loud. Does it sound like something a human would say? Ship it.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Fundamentals" (Write like merchants talk).

author: Shopify
title: Fundamentals: Inspire action
statement: Don’t overwhelm people with too many choices or too much info upfront - Focus on the one thing merchants need to know or do next - Start sentences with verbs so they feel like actionable instructions - Be direct (“add apps” not “you can add apps”) - Use design (font size, location on the screen) to communicate importance - Break multi-part tasks down into digestible steps (aka “progressive disclosure”) Tip: What’s the most important thing for merchants to do here? If it’s not clear, start over.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Fundamentals" (Inspire action).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Address
statement: Lay out address forms in the following format: Please note, “optional” in Apartment, suite, etc. (optional) means that the field is optional for customers to complete, but we should always include it in the form.

statement: - Use locale-specific alternatives for province and postal code, for example, the US uses State and ZIP code

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Don’t
statement: Your store must be located in the US. When using a country as an adjective (such as when referring to currency), use the abbreviated form without punctuation.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Addresses > Don’t).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Don’t
statement: U.S. currency Things to watch for: - Don’t use colloquial forms of a nation or state name, for example, America instead of the United States - Search online to see whether nations commonly use “the” before their name, for example, the Philippines or the Falkland Islands
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Addresses > Don’t).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Bold
statement: When in doubt, don’t bold. Use bold sparingly and only where strong emphasis is required. Don’t use bold to create a heading or emphasize: - Proper nouns - Merchant input - Checkbox titles
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Formatting > Bold).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Do
statement: After your first sale, PayPal will email you at merchant&64;email.com with instructions.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Formatting > Do).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Headings
statement: Headings and subheadings are titles and subtitles that refer to sections of the interface.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Headings).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Basic structure
statement: Headings and subheadings should be: Informative and descriptive: - Highlight the most important concept or piece of information for merchants - Help merchants understand what they’ll find in the section below Concise and scannable: - Use simple, clear language - Keep headings to a single sentence - Avoid using punctuation such as periods, commas, or semicolons - Write in sentence case (capitalize the first word and proper nouns only) - Whether or not to use articles (“the,” “a,” “an”) in headings and subheadings depends on the type of message.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Headings > Basic structure).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Do
statement: - Online store dashboard - Custom reports - Sell your products in person
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Headings > Do).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Don’t
statement: - This is your online store dashboard - Custom Reports - Sell your products in person!
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Headings > Don’t).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Conversational headings
statement: For more conversational areas of the product, like Home cards, sell pages, and empty states, use articles. It makes the language more approachable and helps people to understand new, complex concepts.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Headings > Conversational headings).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Links
statement: Avoid links if possible: - Links add clutter and make things feel less like software, more like an old-fashioned webpage - Merchants are already in the habit of visiting the help center or using sidekick if they have Qs, so building links into the interface is rarely necessary If you have to point merchants to added info: - Never use “click here” or “here” for link text - For added info that it’s essential for most merchants to know, use the info icon (for short, stand-alone info), an embedded link (within the flow of an existing sentence), or a “learn more” link (for longer, multi-faceted info) - If you have to include “learn more” links, avoid having more than one per screen - Keep punctuation outside the link unless the link is a stand-alone sentence (exception: question marks)
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Links).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Do
statement: - Set up your store with a step-by-step guide - Show up where shoppers scroll, search, and shop with multichannel integration. - Track customer behavior on your online store to improve your marketing. Learn more - Log in - Forgot password?
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Links > Do).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Don’t
statement: - Want to learn more about how to set up your online store? Click here. - Show up where shoppers scroll, search, and shop with multichannel integration. Learn more. - Facebook Pixel tracks customer behavior on your online store. This data improves your marketing abilities, including retargeting ads. Learn more about Facebook Pixel - Log in. - Forgot password? ---
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Links > Don’t).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Bulleted
statement: Use a bulleted list when items are related but sequence or priority doesn’t matter. Introduce the list with a full sentence and a colon. Capitalize the first word of the bullet.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Lists > Bulleted).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Do
statement: Using Shopify Payments in your store provides the following benefits: - Avoids the hassle of setting up a third-party payment gateway - Tracks your payout schedule from the Shopify admin - Minimizes lost sales from chargebacks
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Lists > Do).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Don’t
statement: Use Shopify payments to - avoid the hassle of setting up a gateway, - track pending payout schedule, - minimize lost sales from chargebacks. And eliminate PCI fees If at least one of the bullet points requires a period due to having two sentences, then include punctuation on all the bullets. Avoid lists that have both single words and sentences as bullet points.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Lists > Don’t).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Do
statement: You can add a custom domain to your store in the following ways: - Buying the domain directly though your Shopify store. - Buying the domain through a third-party provider and then pointing it to your Shopify store. - Transferring the domain from another Shopify store to your Shopify store. You must be the account owner of the other Shopify store. - Transferring the domain from a third-party domain provider to your Shopify store.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Lists > Do).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Don’t
statement: You can add a custom domain to your store in the following ways: - Buying the domain from Shopify - Transferring. This can take up to 48 hours. - Buying the domain from a third party, and then pointing the domain to your Shopify store
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Lists > Don’t).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Numbered
statement: Use a numbered list when item sequence or priority does matter. Introduce the list with a full sentence and a colon. If at least one of the numbered bullet points requires a period due to having two sentences, then include punctuation on all the bullets. Avoid lists that have both single words and sentences as bullet points. Capitalize the first word of the bullet.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Lists > Numbered).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Do
statement: When checking out from your online store, the customer goes through the following steps: 1. Adds the products that they want to purchase to their cart 2. Goes to the cart page and proceeds to the checkout 3. Enters their shipping details 4. Enters their payment details 5. Confirms and places the order
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Lists > Do).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Don’t
statement: When checking out from your online store, the customer: 1. adds the products that they want to purchase to their cart. This could be one or many products. 2. goes to the cart page and proceeds to the checkout 3. enters their shipping details 4. enters their payment details 5. confirms and places the order
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Lists > Don’t).

author: Shopify
subcategory: Grammar > Lists > Actions in a menu
title: Grammar: Actions in a menu
statement: Menu lists give users a horizontal set of actions when space is limited. The order of actions is often based on logic, such as most popular actions. Actions in a menu follow a \{verb\}+\{noun\} pattern. If there’s enough context, only a verb might be required.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Lists > Actions in a menu).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Don’t
statement: - HTML - editing options - File name changes - Duplicate this order so that you can make edits, updates, or changes
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Lists > Don’t).

author: Shopify
subcategory: Grammar > Lists > Nouns in a menu
title: Grammar: Nouns in a menu
statement: Menu lists give users a horizontal set of nouns when space is limited. The order of nouns is often based on logic, such as most recent orders. Nouns in a menu should be concise, but still give the user enough information so that they can easily find and accurately select the item that they want.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Lists > Nouns in a menu).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Don’t
statement: - Filter visibility - Filter product type - Filter product vendor - Filter tagged with
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Lists > Don’t).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Punctuation in lists
statement: - Introduce bulleted lists with a colon or a heading. - Don’t use commas at the end of list items (for bulleted or numbered lists). - If any list item contains two or more sentences, punctuate all list items. - If all list items are one sentence or fragments, don’t punctuate. This doesn't apply to procedural steps, which should end with punctuation. - Never put a comma or semicolon at the end of a bulleted or numbered list item. - Treat each list item as a self-contained piece of information. ---
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Lists > Punctuation in lists).

statement: - nine - one hundred - You have five orders to fulfill. Use commas for numbers with four or more digits. Avoid shortening numbers.

author: Shopify
subcategory: Grammar > Numbers, dates, and currency > Date
title: Grammar: Date
statement: Use the month’s full name. If there isn’t enough space, use 3-letter abbreviations. Don’t write dates with numerals only.

subcategory: Grammar > Numbers, dates, and currency > Don’t
title: Grammar: Don’t
statement: - December 11, ’24 - 12/11/24 Don’t use ordinal indicators, which are words representing position or rank in a sequential order (1st, 2nd, 3rd, and so on).

author: Shopify
subcategory: Grammar > Numbers, dates, and currency > Don’t
title: Grammar: Don’t
statement: January 23rd–April 1st Note: Dates, numbers, and measurements are often formatted automatically according to users’ local preferences, and they may be formatted differently in other languages. These guidelines are for manually formatting in American English, which we use as a base before translating to other languages.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Numbers, dates, and currency > Don’t).

author: Shopify
subcategory: Grammar > Numbers, dates, and currency > Time
title: Grammar: Time
statement: For all translations, the time format is automatically localized by the Intl.DateTimeFormat JavaScript object. When time must be formatted manually, follow these guidelines: - Use the 12-hour clock, followed by am or pm - Include a space after the last number. For example, “Your package will arrive at 12:35 pm.” - Use the browser time of the logged in user - To show a time range, use an en dash and include the am/pm after both times, for example, 3:00 pm–4:00 pm - If indicating both the date and time, separate them with the word “at” instead of a comma
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Numbers, dates, and currency > Time).

author: Shopify
subcategory: Grammar > Numbers, dates, and currency > Time zones
title: Grammar: Time zones
statement: - Include a time zone only if it’s necessary, such as for an event listing. - Use the time zone’s abbreviation following the am or pm, for example, 4:00 pm NZT. - If your audience is in a single time zone, then don’t include an S (for Standard) or D (for Daylight). For example, 3:00 pm PT. - If your audience is in a combination of time zones, then include the S (for Standard) or D (for Daylight) to avoid confusion. For example, 3:00 pm PDT.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Numbers, dates, and currency > Time zones).

author: Shopify
subcategory: Grammar > Numbers, dates, and currency > Don’t
title: Grammar: Don’t

author: Shopify
subcategory: Grammar > Numbers, dates, and currency > Currency

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Addressing merchants
statement: Always refer to merchants as “you.” Don’t speak for merchants with phrases that use “I” or “my.”
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Pronouns (you, us) > Addressing merchants).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Don’t
statement: Change your email address in My Profile. In some cases (such as getting merchant consent or granting permissions) you should refer to merchants as “I.”
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Pronouns (you, us) > Don’t).

author: Shopify
subcategory: Grammar > Pronouns (you, us) > Referring to Shopify
title: Grammar: Referring to Shopify
statement: Always refer to Shopify as “we,” but avoid inserting Shopify into the content as much as possible (except when a human is taking action, such as reviewing a request).
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Pronouns (you, us) > Referring to Shopify).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Do
statement: Pinterest Buyable Pins will be available in the coming weeks.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Pronouns (you, us) > Do).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Don’t
statement: We’re making Pinterest Buyable Pins available in the coming weeks. ---
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Pronouns (you, us) > Don’t).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Ampersands
statement: Don’t use ampersands (&). They attract attention to the least important part of the sentence. Spell out the word “and.”
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Punctuation > Ampersands).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Apostrophes
statement: Use apostrophes to represent omitted letters or numbers: - Omitted numbers (’40s) - Omitted letters (don’t, can’t, won’t) - Verb contractions (it’s, you’re, we’re) Use apostrophes to form possessives: - Singular nouns: add ’s, even if they end in s (merchant’s, bus’s) - Plural nouns that don’t end in s: add ’s (women’s, men’s) - Plural nouns that end in s: add an apostrophe (boxes’, customers’) Don’t use apostrophes to form possessive pronouns such as hers or his.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Punctuation > Apostrophes).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Do
statement: - Merchant’s store - Women’s clothing - Customers’ credit cards
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Punctuation > Do).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Don’t
statement: - Merchants store - Womens clothing - Customers credit cards Always use apostrophes, not vertical (straight) quotes.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Punctuation > Don’t).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Colons
statement: Avoid using colons in sentences. If you need to use one, don’t capitalize the first word after the colon unless it’s a proper noun.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Punctuation > Colons).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Do
statement: Your store accepts payments with GoCoin and Shopify Payments.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Punctuation > Do).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Don’t
statement: Your store accepts payments with: GoCoin and Shopify Payments. Don’t use colons to introduce radio buttons or checkboxes.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Punctuation > Don’t).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Do
statement: If the customer abandons their checkout, send them an email reminder to complete their order
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Punctuation > Do).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Don’t
statement: If the customer abandons their checkout, send them an email reminder to complete their order: Introduce bulleted lists with a colon.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Punctuation > Don’t).

title: Grammar: Do
statement: Correct the following payment information to continue: - The credit card verification value (CVV) doesn’t match the credit card - The billing address street doesn’t match the street for the credit card - The billing address ZIP or postal code doesn’t match the credit card address
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Punctuation > Do).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Don’t

citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Punctuation > Don’t).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Commas
statement: Use the oxford comma (also known as the serial comma) in sentences. There should be a comma after every list of 3 or more items (unless you’re using a bulleted or numbered list).
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Punctuation > Commas).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Do
statement: Kit is an app that handles your online advertising, email marketing, and social media.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Punctuation > Do).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Don’t
statement: Kit is an app that handles your online advertising, email marketing and social media. Don’t use commas to separate bulleted or numbered list items.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Punctuation > Don’t).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Do
statement: - The credit card verification value (CVV) doesn’t match the credit card - The billing address street doesn’t match the street for the credit card - The billing address ZIP or postal code doesn’t match the credit card address
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Punctuation > Do).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Don’t

citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Punctuation > Don’t).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Ellipses
statement: The ellipses (…) can be used in place of a missing piece of text (most commonly to show the deletion of words from a direct quotation). Avoid using ellipses in text. Use ellipses for: - Truncation in the center of a title bar Don’t use ellipses for: - Placeholder copy - Trailing off a sentence
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Punctuation > Ellipses).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Don’t
statement: Start typing to search for files… Always use the ellipsis character, not three periods.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Punctuation > Don’t).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Truncation
statement: Consider constraints of the space in the interface when deciding to use truncation. Think about what part of the string merchants needs most. It’s usually the beginning or end, which means you might have to truncate the middle of the string.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Punctuation > Truncation).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Ellipses button component
statement: A button with an ellipsis icon (not the same as text) is used to expand more actions. It’s typically used in cards, or for horizontal sets of actions when space is limited.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Punctuation > Ellipses button component).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: En-dashes and em-dashes
statement: Use an en dash with no spaces in between (–) for a fixed range of numbers
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Punctuation > En-dashes and em-dashes).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Don’t
statement: 2006 – 2013 Use an em dash only if you can’t make your message clearer by splitting it into two sentences. Use an em dash without a space on either side (—).
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Punctuation > Don’t).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Exclamation marks
statement: Avoid exclamation marks—only use them for really really exciting things. If you absolutely have to, limit yourself to one exclamation mark per page.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Punctuation > Exclamation marks).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Hyphens
statement: Use hyphens to: - Form compound modifiers: two words that combine to modify or describe the noun that follows
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Punctuation > Hyphens).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Do
statement: - Start your free, no-risk, 14-day trial. - This is a high-risk order. - This order is high risk. - Add weight-based shipping rates. - Add rates based on the weight of an order.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Punctuation > Do).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Don’t
statement: - Start your free, no risk, 14 day trial. - This is a high risk order. - This order is high-risk. - Add weight based shipping rates. - Join prefixes and suffixes only if there are two vowels beside each other. Never use hyphens in the words ecommerce and email.

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Periods
statement: - Don't use periods in interface copy - If text includes 2 or more sentences, it's okay to use periods
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Punctuation > Periods).

title: Grammar: Do
statement: - Use when a list item has two or more full sentences, then also add periods to the whole list - Use for the description or helper text below a bulleted or numbered list item

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Don’t
statement: - Don’t use periods when a list has only single sentences or fragments - Don’t use periods for lists of links
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Punctuation > Don’t).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Question marks
statement: Avoid question marks wherever possible. Reword into affirmative statements wherever you can, but there are exceptions: It’s okay to use question marks if you don’t know the result of the question: - “Did you forget your password?” - “Do you need to add a shipping rate?” Don’t use question marks if: - It’s the only option available: “Reset password” - It’s an on/off option: “Show quantity box”
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Punctuation > Question marks).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Quotation marks
statement: Use quotation marks to: - Define words (“growth-hacking”) - Quote text When it’s helpful to the merchant, use quotation marks to indicate input that the merchant has provided, such as a product title or file name. Use this indication only when the input appears in running text.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Punctuation > Quotation marks).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Do

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Don’t
statement: - Are you sure you want to delete cat shirt? - Nike Air Max 90.png failed to upload In general, place commas and periods inside quotation marks. When working with literal strings like typed commands or merchant inputs, place punctuation outside the quotation marks.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Punctuation > Don’t).

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Do
statement: - “I see this all the time,” said Mary. - Avoid general words like “all,” “every,” or “most.” - To remove this item, type “DELETE”.

title: Grammar: Don’t

author: Shopify
title: Grammar: Semicolons
statement: Avoid semicolons if possible. If you really need them, use semicolons to: - Connect two closely related ideas, as long as they are both independent clauses (full sentences that could stand on their own). - Replace a comma or the word “and” between two closely related ideas.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Punctuation > Semicolons).

title: Grammar: Do

citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Grammar" (Punctuation > Do).

author: Shopify

statement: Use American spelling for all external-facing Shopify content. When in doubt, check the Merriam-Webster dictionary for the preferred spelling of specific terms.

author: Shopify

author: Shopify
title: Inclusive language: {frontmatter.title}
statement: {frontmatter.description} Clear and precise language creates a better experience for all users. Everyone interacting with Shopify should feel welcome and included. Start by involving different perspectives in the planning process. Limit assumptions or biases by testing your content with a diverse audience. Recruit research participants from a variety of backgrounds, including historically excluded groups. Be aware of bias, and let those with lived experiences guide the way. ---
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Inclusive language" ({frontmatter.title}).

author: Shopify
title: Inclusive language: Writing principles
statement: Our language should reflect the diversity of Shopify merchants. Here are some principles for creating welcoming commerce experiences through writing. - When talking to people, use language that considers others’ perspectives and lived experiences - When talking about people, be descriptive only when necessary to the context, and use language preferred by the group being described - When talking about things, be clear and accurate, avoiding metaphors and idioms For more context on the etymology of terms mentioned in this guide, visit the EGAL Inclusive Terms Glossary. ---
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Inclusive language" (Writing principles).

author: Shopify
title: Inclusive language: Disability
statement: As technology advances, it’s important to remember that we continue to design for all levels of ability. Considering those with disabilities will make your content accessible and more inclusive. To write accessible content: - Center content around people, not their disabilities - Be clear and avoid metaphors, euphemisms, and idioms - Don’t imply that those with disabilities are abnormal, less than, or “suffering” - Avoid words associated with disabilities to describe objects, features, or experiences
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Inclusive language" (Disability).

author: Shopify
title: Inclusive language: Disable, disabled
statement: Don’t label actions or features using “disable” or “disabled.” This can imply that being disabled is a negative state. Alternatives include “turn off,” “inactive,” and “deactivated.” Note: Because “disabled” is a valid state for HTML elements, it’s currently considered appropriate when talking about specific element states.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Inclusive language" (Disability > Disable, disabled).

author: Shopify
title: Inclusive language: Deaf
statement: Only use this term to refer to actual deafness, not as a metaphor. Use lowercase, unless referring to the Deaf community.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Inclusive language" (Disability > Deaf).

author: Shopify
title: Inclusive language: Handicap, handicapped
statement: Don’t use this term to refer to someone’s disability. Be specific, such as: - person who requires a keyboard accessible checkout - person who uses an accessibility device
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Inclusive language" (Disability > Handicap, handicapped).

author: Shopify
title: Inclusive language: Blind
statement: Only use this term to reference actual blindness, not as a metaphor.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Inclusive language" (Disability > Blind).

author: Shopify
title: Inclusive language: Insane, crazy
statement: Avoid using these words to describe something as extreme or unbelievable.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Inclusive language" (Disability > Insane, crazy).

author: Shopify
subcategory: Inclusive language > Disability > Just, only, easy, etc.
title: Inclusive language: Just, only, easy, etc.
statement: When writing instructional content, avoid saying the task itself is easy or quick. If you imply it’s easy for everyone, it can discourage those who might struggle. While they are fine in the right context, watch out for these words: - just - only - easy - simple - quick Note: When marketing, it’s okay to use these words to communicate the value of a new product or feature.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Inclusive language" (Disability > Just, only, easy, etc.).

author: Shopify
title: Inclusive language: Race
statement: We want all merchants to feel comfortable participating in commerce. Even if unintentional, language can exclude or harm people who have been historically marginalized due to their race, ethnicity, or culture. Consider the diversity of merchants’ lived experiences and be intentional about using language that is free of bias.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Inclusive language" (Race).

author: Shopify
title: Inclusive language: Tips
statement: - Don’t treat perspectives that are different from yours as exotic or strange - Don’t use phrases or terms that denote “black” or “dark” as bad or negative, versus “white” or “light” as good or positive - Avoid metaphors and idioms since they can have racist origins or interpretations
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Inclusive language" (Race > Tips).

author: Shopify
subcategory: Inclusive language > Race > Black hat, white hat (hacking)
title: Inclusive language: Black hat, white hat (hacking)
statement: Avoid these terms since they imply that “white is good” and “black is bad.”
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Inclusive language" (Race > Black hat, white hat (hacking)).

author: Shopify
title: Inclusive language: Blacklist, whitelist
statement: Avoid these terms since they imply that “white is good” and “black is bad.”
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Inclusive language" (Race > Blacklist, whitelist).

citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Inclusive language" (Race > Do).

author: Shopify
subcategory: Inclusive language > Race > Grandfather in, grandfather clause
title: Inclusive language: Grandfather in, grandfather clause
statement: Avoid using these phrases, as they come from laws in the U.S. meant to circumvent or disenfranchise Black people’s rights.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Inclusive language" (Race > Grandfather in, grandfather clause).

author: Shopify
title: Inclusive language: Master
statement: Avoid using this term, as many associate it with the institution of slavery.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Inclusive language" (Race > Master).

author: Shopify
title: Inclusive language: Gender
statement: Gender is an important part of many people’s identity. Stereotypes and assumptions about gender can make their way into product experiences and leave people feeling excluded or misrepresented. When you do talk about gender, be intentional. Only use gendered language if it makes your content more inclusive and accurate.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Inclusive language" (Gender).

author: Shopify
title: Inclusive language: Internationalization
statement: Many languages lack ungendered options, like the English “they.” When possible, write in a way that avoids gendered language. For example, write “you” instead of a third person pronoun. You may need to work with a translator to avoid unintentionally gendering concepts. Always choose the clearest option.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Inclusive language" (Gender > Internationalization).

author: Shopify
title: Inclusive language: Recommended language
statement: Always use someone’s preferred gender and pronouns. If you’re not sure, use the pronouns “they/them.” This keeps the content inclusive, simple, and readable.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Inclusive language" (Gender > Recommended language).

author: Shopify
title: Inclusive language: Don’t
statement: Call the customer to confirm his or her address If pronouns are necessary or useful to the experience, offer users an inclusive list of options that also allows them to opt out.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Inclusive language" (Gender > Don’t).

author: Shopify
title: Inclusive language: Don’t
statement: Don’t use language that associates roles, qualities, or objects with a specific gender.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Inclusive language" (Gender > Don’t).

author: Shopify
title: Naming: Thoughtful naming
statement: Names influence how merchants and other audiences perceive and understand Shopify. A well-chosen name will: - Put clarity above creativity - Help establish a mental model for our audiences - Enhance people’s perception of our brand - Increase adoption of the product or feature - Differentiate Shopify from other products - Clarify where a product or feature fits into our brand system The naming process involves collaboration. Include different disciplines and people with different subject matter expertise in the creation of a name. ---
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Naming" (Thoughtful naming).

author: Shopify
subcategory: Naming > Does it need a branded name?
title: Naming: Does it need a branded name?
statement: Most features don’t need an official, branded name. For example, order entry is a feature that’s referred to descriptively and so doesn’t need to be capitalized. When choosing what to call a feature, pick words that describe what the feature does or represents. If there’s room, add extra context for merchants by describing the feature instead of using only the feature name. Avoid capitalizing descriptive feature names.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Naming" (Does it need a branded name?).

author: Shopify
subcategory: Naming > Does it need a branded name? > Don’t
title: Naming: Don’t
statement: - Order Entry If there‘s room, describe the feature instead of defaulting to only using the name.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Naming" (Does it need a branded name? > Don’t).

author: Shopify
subcategory: Naming > Does it need a branded name? > Do
title: Naming: Do
statement: - Display carrier calculated shipping rates to your customers at checkout.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Naming" (Does it need a branded name? > Do).

author: Shopify
subcategory: Naming > Does it need a branded name? > Using “Shopify”
title: Naming: Using “Shopify”
statement: Only Shopify can use the word “Shopify” in a name. The word “Shopify” can’t be used to name third-party products. It’s important we use the word “Shopify” consistently, and sparingly. Don’t use “Shopify” in a name unless there’s a lack of surrounding context and we want its target audience to know it’s associated with Shopify. Adding “Shopify” doesn’t add clarity in the context of other Shopify products and features. For example, merchants often confuse Shopify Shipping with the other shipping features, like shipping settings, carrier calculated shipping rates, shipping labels, and shipping zones. Our support staff have to refer to the Shopify Plan by its cost because the general name doesn’t distinguish it from the other plans. Use “Shopify” in front of a name when a product: - Is or will become a separate product or platform and we need to associate it with Shopify - Should be differentiated from other, similar products in the industry - Doesn’t justify an evocative name, but still needs to associated with Shopify Don’t use “Shopify” in a name for built in functionality features, like fraud analysis or importing products.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Naming" (Does it need a branded name? > Using “Shopify”).

author: Shopify
subcategory: Naming > Does it need a branded name? > Do
title: Naming: Do
statement: - Shopify Payments - Shopify App Store - Shopify Theme Store
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Naming" (Does it need a branded name? > Do).

author: Shopify
subcategory: Naming > Does it need a branded name? > Don’t
title: Naming: Don’t
statement: - Shopify Analytics - Shopify Discounts - Shopify Account Shopify makes apps that merchants can add to their Shopify admin. It’s okay to say “Built by Shopify” or “Made by Shopify” after the app name. Once you’ve picked the format that works for the design, use it consistently.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Naming" (Does it need a branded name? > Don’t).

author: Shopify
subcategory: Naming > Does it need a branded name? > Do
title: Naming: Do
statement: - Shopify Product Reviews - Shopify Order Printer - Shopify Shopcodes
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Naming" (Does it need a branded name? > Do).

author: Shopify
subcategory: Naming > Does it need a branded name? > Don’t
title: Naming: Don’t
statement: - Product Reviews - Order Printer - Shopcodes Apps that aren’t built by Shopify should not use the word “Shopify” in their name or say “for Shopify” after the name.
citation: Shopify. Shopify Polaris: "Naming" (Does it need a branded name? > Don’t).

author: Shopify
title: Naming: Descriptive vs evocative names
statement: There are two types of approaches to naming, the descriptive approach, or the evocative approach. Descriptive names are concrete, while evocative can be more abstract. Descriptive names are merchant friendly, and the most common. Features should always have descriptive names. Standalone products that require independent branding can use evocative names. Third-party apps and channels should have their own branded names and should never use the word “Shopify” in the name. If you’re a Shopify employee and are looking to trademark an evocative name, ask the legal department for help.
