author: GitHub
title: Typography: Hierarchy
statement: When establishing hierarchy for GitHub products, designers should remember that we stress efficient, clean reading experiences for our users. Refrain from utilizing color as a primary method of emphasis.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Typography" (Best practices > Hierarchy).

author: GitHub
title: Typography: Line height
statement: Line height —Utilize line-height tokens for proper alignment.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Typography" (Best practices > Readability).

author: GitHub
title: Typography: Line length
statement: Line length —It's considered a good practice to keep lines around 80 characters or less—W3 Page Structure Guidelines. Cases vary depending on the situation, but this serves as a general rule of thumb for designing layouts.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Typography" (Best practices > Readability).

author: GitHub
title: Typography: Type alignment
statement: Type alignment —Our content is typically left-aligned and ragged right. Be sensible in deviating from this standard, as justifying, centering, and right-aligning text is atypical of GitHub products.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Typography" (Best practices > Readability).

author: GitHub
title: Typography: Font weight
statement: Font weight —Adjust font weight to add emphasis and differentiate content hierarchy.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Typography" (Best practices > Readability).

author: GitHub
title: Typography: Letter spacing
statement: Letter spacing —Please refrain from altering letter-spacing on our products. There may be rare scenarios in which this is acceptable, but generally speaking, this should be avoided altogether.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Typography" (Best practices > Readability).

author: GitHub
title: Accessibility at GitHub
statement: GitHub's aim is to be the home for all developers. To be inclusive means we must consider accessibility at the core of how we design. 16% of the world's population has a disability (estimated by the World Health Organization), and that doesn't take into consideration those under temporary or situational disabilities. In many cases, devices that have been designed with accessibility in mind for a portion of the population end up benefiting everyone. Take the OXO brand's Good Grips line of products; although they were developed for people who have arthritis, most people found them easier to use than other product lines. When you consider accessibility from the beginning of the design process and incorporate it throughout, it becomes part of an established design process that seeks to include everyone, of all abilities, and allows everyone to achieve more. When reading through accessibility information, you might find the common abbreviation: "a11y". A11y is a shortening of the word "accessibility". It starts with the first letter, "a", uses the number 11 for the eleven characters inbetween the first and last letter, and ends with the last letter, "y".
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Accessibility at GitHub" ().

author: GitHub
subcategory: Accessibility at GitHub > What standards you must aim for
title: Accessibility at GitHub: What standards you must aim for
statement: GitHub aims for Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1 AA compliance. This includes all of WCAG 2.0 AA plus additional considerations. Currently, Section 508 (required by law in the United States) follows WCAG 2.0 AA guidelines for compliance.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Accessibility at GitHub" (What standards you must aim for).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Accessibility at GitHub > Who should you consider when designing?
title: Accessibility at GitHub: Visual:
statement: Visual: Anything that deals with sight, or technology that helps someone to see. This includes people who have different types of sight like color blindness.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Accessibility at GitHub" (Who should you consider when designing?).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Accessibility at GitHub > Who should you consider when designing?
title: Accessibility at GitHub: Cognitive:
statement: Cognitive: Concentration, memory, judgement, problem solving, logic skills.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Accessibility at GitHub" (Who should you consider when designing?).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Accessibility at GitHub > Who should you consider when designing?
title: Accessibility at GitHub: Mobility:
statement: Mobility: Anything that affects movement in a body.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Accessibility at GitHub" (Who should you consider when designing?).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Accessibility at GitHub > Who should you consider when designing?
title: Accessibility at GitHub: Hearing:
statement: Hearing: A spectrum of disabilities related to sound or audio.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Accessibility at GitHub" (Who should you consider when designing?).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Accessibility at GitHub > Who should you consider when designing?
title: Accessibility at GitHub: Permanent:
statement: Permanent: Disability does not go away.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Accessibility at GitHub" (Who should you consider when designing?).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Accessibility at GitHub > Who should you consider when designing?
title: Accessibility at GitHub: Temporary:
statement: Temporary: The disability will go away in time.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Accessibility at GitHub" (Who should you consider when designing?).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Accessibility at GitHub > Who should you consider when designing?
title: Accessibility at GitHub: Situational:
statement: Situational: The environment someone is in plays a huge factor in how they interact with web content.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Accessibility at GitHub" (Who should you consider when designing?).

author: GitHub
title: Accessibility at GitHub: Support
statement: Accessibility is a priority for GitHub. If you ever encounter accessibility related issues when using github.com, please don’t hesitate to get in touch via email support@github.com with your concerns. For information about the accessibility compliance of GitHub products, please refer to the VPAT report, outlining §508 accessibility information for GitHub.com, GitHub Enterprise, and GitHub Desktop.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Accessibility at GitHub" (Support).

author: GitHub
title: Alternative text for images: Overview
statement: Text alternatives are a primary way for making information accessible because they can be rendered through any sensory modality (for example, visual, auditory, or tactile) to match the needs of the user. Providing text alternatives allows the information to be rendered in a variety of ways by a variety of user agents. For example, a person who cannot see a picture can have the text alternative read aloud using synthesized speech. Source: https://www.w3.org/TR/UNDERSTANDING-WCAG20/text-equiv-all.html
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Alternative text for images" (Overview).

author: GitHub
title: Alternative text for images: Why?
statement: Images can make the web user experience better and more pleasant, especially for users with cognitive and learning disabilities. Not all images used in websites are accessible, and that can be a major barrier. Accessible images are beneficial for everyone, especially for people using screen readers and other assistive technologies, as well as search engine optimization (SEO). When screen readers come across images, graphs, and icons without an alt attribute, by default the screen reader will speak the name of the file, which most of the time can be unhelpful (for example: final-final-truly-final-V2.jpg). You can read more about why alternative text for images is important in the Web Accessibility Tutorials Guidance on how to create websites that meet WCAG .
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Alternative text for images" (Why?).

author: GitHub
title: Assistive technology announcements: Overview
statement: These guidelines will help you determine when assistive tools should output a message.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Assistive technology announcements" (Overview).

author: GitHub
title: Assistive technology announcements: Always: Announce location changes
statement: Always: Announce location changes — Help users understand where they are on a page. Maintain positional awareness.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Assistive technology announcements" (Guidelines).

author: GitHub
title: Assistive technology announcements: Always: Announce results of user actions
statement: Always: Announce results of user actions — Give feedback about the success or failure directly following a user action.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Assistive technology announcements" (Guidelines).

author: GitHub
title: Assistive technology announcements: Sometimes: Announce other changes
statement: Sometimes: Announce other changes — Explore case-by-case when changes are disconnected from the user’s place and the success or failure of the user’s actions. For example:
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Assistive technology announcements" (Guidelines).

author: GitHub
title: Color considerations: Overview
statement: This guidance covers considerations that can't automatically be integrated into Primer. It supplements accessibility guidance given in the Color portion of our Foundations documentation.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Color considerations" (Overview).

author: GitHub
title: Color considerations: Determining contrast
statement: WebAIM's Contrast Checker tool is the recommended way to calculate color contrast ratios.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Color considerations" (Overview > Determining contrast).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Color considerations > Overview > Level AA support
title: Color considerations: Level AA support
statement: GitHub is required to honor WCAG AA-level compliance. This means that WCAG Success Criterion levels A and AA are both observed. An example level A Success Criterion is SC 1.4.1 Use of Color. An example level AA Success Criterion is SC 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum).
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Color considerations" (Overview > Level AA support).

author: GitHub
title: Color considerations: Compliance
statement: The following guidance is based on one or more normative Web Content Accessibility Guidelines ( WCAG ) success criterion. This means that the guidance is based on objective requirements with implications that affect MAS-C compliance efforts, as well as international laws regarding accessibility. An example of the difference between non-normative and normative considerations would be the difference between the overall choice of color used, and then the actual value of the color.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Color considerations" (Compliance).

author: GitHub
title: Color considerations: Non-normative choices
statement: A design could use a dark shade of purple as the background color as a non-normative aesthetic choice. Reasons for going with dark purple could be: - The team prefers how it looks over dark blue, dark green, dark gray, etc., - The dark purple is a subtle reference to a brighter purple that is a core part of main palette, - The dark purple is part of a new branding update, - Etc.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Color considerations" (Compliance > Non-normative choices).

author: GitHub
title: Color considerations: Normative requirements
statement: The normative requirement for going with dark purple would be comparing the final computed color value used for the dark purple background color against the color value used for text.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Color considerations" (Compliance > Normative requirements).

author: GitHub
title: Color considerations: The APCA
statement: The Advanced Accessible Perceptual Contrast Algorithm ( APCA ) is a proposal and is not normative. In terms of WCAG, and therefore, MAS-C compliance, this means that color contrast is valid only if it meets WCAG 2.1 criteria. A color value that is APCA-compliant might not be WCAG-compliant until APCA is integrated into WCAG 3.0. WCAG 3.0 is still a work in progress and currently does not have an anticipated release date.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Color considerations" (Compliance > The APCA).

author: GitHub
title: Color considerations: Visual themes
statement: GitHub offers two parent themes: 1. Day (light), and 2. Night (dark). Each parent theme has a default appearance, and then a suite of sub-themes. Sub-themes include considerations for high and low contrast experiences, as well as certain vision conditions. It is possible to set GitHub to use a dark sub-theme when a parent Day theme has been set, and vice-versa. This allows a user to have a fine-grained control over their experience.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Color considerations" (Visual themes).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Color considerations > Visual themes > Default theme
title: Color considerations: The default Day (light) theme
statement: The default Day (light) theme when a user visits the site in a logged out state and their operating system is set to light mode.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Color considerations" (Visual themes > Default theme).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Color considerations > Visual themes > Default theme
title: Color considerations: The default Night (dark) theme
statement: The default Night (dark) theme when a user visits the site in a logged out state and their operating system is set to dark mode.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Color considerations" (Visual themes > Default theme).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Color considerations > Visual themes > Non-default themes
title: Color considerations: Non-default themes
statement: All Day and Night sub-themes do not need to meet WCAG color contrast requirements, provided all default Day and Night theme content is accessible. This guidance is derived from WCAG 2.1 Technique G174. Certain themes are specifically designed to create a low contrast effect, notably the Dark Dimmed sub-theme. In this use case, a user selecting this theme is likely intentionally expressing a desire for an experience with less visual contrast. Like other theme selections, this may be to satisfy: 1. Aesthetic sensibilities, 2. Access needs that are derived from visual conditions that make a higher contrast experience unusable, or 3. A combination of both. In the case of access needs, a higher contrast experience may actually be less accessible for the user. The availability of the Dark Dimmed theme treatment allows users to customize their GitHub experience without having to resort to browser extensions or other user-hosted modifications. Of note is the portability of this theme, in that it will automatically be available across multiple sessions, browsers, and devices. GitHub should strive to ensure all themes that don't specifically deal with an intentionally-lowered contrast experience are color contrast compliant. While this is not a normative requirement, it proactively helps an unknown number of users with unknown access needs.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Color considerations" (Visual themes > Non-default themes).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Color considerations > Visual themes > High contrast themes, high contrast mode, and forced colors mode
title: Color considerations: High contrast themes, high contrast mode, and forced colors mode
statement: GitHub offers two high contrast sub-themes: 1. Light High Contrast, and 2. Dark High Contrast. In addition some, but not all operating systems offer forced color and high contrast mode experiences.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Color considerations" (Visual themes > High contrast themes, high contrast mode, and forced colors mode).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Color considerations > Visual themes > High contrast themes
title: Color considerations: High contrast themes
statement: These are provided by GitHub. High contrast themes can be enabled with or without forced color and high contrast modes enabled. Some users may be unaware of, or unable to access these modes. Other users may not need them.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Color considerations" (Visual themes > High contrast themes).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Color considerations > Visual themes > High contrast mode
title: Color considerations: High contrast mode
statement: This is not provided by GitHub. A high contrast mode is a signal to the operating system to increase the visual distinction between different UI elements. On the web, it is a flag that can be targeted with a media query. The presence of an enabled high contrast mode experience does not guarantee a high contrast web experience is generated—that is an experience the website has to intentionally provide. GitHub currently does not auto-opt a user into its high contrast themes if a user has enabled high contrast mode on their device.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Color considerations" (Visual themes > High contrast mode).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Color considerations > Visual themes > Forced colors mode
title: Color considerations: Forced colors mode
statement: This is not provided by GitHub. Forced color mode is another media query. Unlike high contrast mode, forced colors mode automatically adapts all operating system content. This includes all web content. A forced color mode will update all GitHub content's visual presentation regardless of what theme a user has selected. It uses a suite of heuristics to determine content meaning and then assign a dynamic color keyword value to it. Forced color mode content presentation should not be overridden to satisfy aesthetic desires. Instead, it should only be lightly adjusted to ensure maximum legibility and accuracy of applied color keywords.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Color considerations" (Visual themes > Forced colors mode).

author: GitHub
title: Color considerations: Inputs and buttons
statement: Different kinds of UI have their contrast compliance determined in different ways. This is because different parts of them are visually significant for understanding purpose. The difference between inputs and buttons may be confusing. Understanding the difference between the two types of UI helps to understand why they are evaluated differently for color contrast purposes. At a high-level: - Buttons perform a predetermined action when pressed. Examples of this are submitting form input, triggering a dialog, or saving user-entered content. - Inputs collect information for eventual submission. Examples of this are single and multiline text-entry areas, checkbox selections/radio choices, and comboboxes. Inputs and buttons are combined to form data collection and transmission experiences such as a contact form or a Pull Request submission.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Color considerations" (Inputs and buttons).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Color considerations > Inputs and buttons > Inputs
title: Color considerations: Inputs
statement: Being able to perceive the boundaries of an input is vital. Meeting WCAG color contrast requirements helps to ensure the widest possible range of users can perform the data entry required to operate GitHub successfully.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Color considerations" (Inputs and buttons > Inputs).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Color considerations > Inputs and buttons > Input considerations
title: Color considerations: Input considerations
statement: Broadly-speaking, there are four overall considerations for input contrast: 1. Text, 2. Borders, 3. Selected state, and 4. Validation state. Combined, meeting contrast requirements allow a user to understand: 1. What the input is for, 2. What area of the input a user can interact with, 3. What information a user has entered into the input, and 4. What state the input is in. If a computed color value in any of the four considerations is not compliant, it may endanger one or more portions of user understanding and operation of the input.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Color considerations" (Inputs and buttons > Input considerations).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Color considerations > Inputs and buttons > Input text contrast
title: Color considerations: Input text contrast
statement: Text portions of an input must meet a contrast ratio of 4.5:1 for "normal text", or 3:1 for "large text". This applies to both an input's visible label and its user-provided text content. The majority of GitHub input text size is "normal text". Both "normal text" and "large text" are WCAG-specific terms. More information about this can be found on the Key Terms subsection of SC 1.4.3: Contrast (Minimum).
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Color considerations" (Inputs and buttons > Input text contrast).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Color considerations > Inputs and buttons > Input border contrast
title: Color considerations: Input border contrast
statement: Borders communicate the boundaries of an input, and are considered non-text contrast. This includes inputs that allow for freeform user input such as text, and also pre-specified inputs such as checkboxes. Borders of an input must meet a contrast ratio of 3:1. This is calculated by the border's computed color value compared to the computed background color the input is placed on. The contrast of the input's border color compared to the input's background color does not need to meet a contrast ratio. The color of the input's text against its background color still needs to be compliant, however. Inputs without visible borders must use their background color instead. In this case, the required contrast ratio is 3:1, with the computed input background color and the color of the background of what the input is placed on.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Color considerations" (Inputs and buttons > Input border contrast).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Color considerations > Inputs and buttons > Input selected state contrast
title: Color considerations: Input selected state contrast
statement: Selection state communicates if a user has chosen an input option, and is considered non-text contrast. Examples of this are a checkbox's check or a radio's dot. Selected state of an input such as a checkbox must meet a contrast ratio of 3:1. This is calculated by the border's computed color value compared to the computed background color the input is placed on.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Color considerations" (Inputs and buttons > Input selected state contrast).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Color considerations > Inputs and buttons > Input validation state contrast
title: Color considerations: Input validation state contrast
statement: Validation state communicates if the content a user has submitted meets the intake requirements or not. Examples of this are an inline error message with a text input, or a checkmark icon to indicate password criteria have been met. Validation state must not rely on color as the sole way of determining if an input is valid. Accompanying text or icons can help accomplish this. - If the validation message is only text, it must meet a contrast ratio of 4.5:1 for "normal text", or 3:1 for "large text". - If the validation message is only an icon, it must meet a contrast ratio of 3:1. - If the validation message is both text and an icon, it must meet a contrast ratio of 4.5:1 for "normal text", or 3:1 for "large text". In this context the icon is considered decorative. It is still encouraged to make the icon meet a 3:1 contrast ratio, however. Contrast for validation state is calculated by the text or icon's computed color value compared to the computed background color the input is placed on.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Color considerations" (Inputs and buttons > Input validation state contrast).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Color considerations > Inputs and buttons > Buttons
title: Color considerations: Buttons
statement: Being able to perceive the name or icon of a button is vital. Meeting WCAG color contrast requirements helps to ensure the widest possible range of users can perform the actions required to operate GitHub successfully.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Color considerations" (Inputs and buttons > Buttons).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Color considerations > Inputs and buttons > Button considerations
title: Color considerations: Button considerations
statement: Broadly-speaking, there are four overall considerations for button contrast: 1. Text, 2. Icons, 3. Borders, and 4. Disabled state. Combined, meeting contrast requirements allow a user to understand: 1. What the button is for, and 2. What area of the button a user can interact with.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Color considerations" (Inputs and buttons > Button considerations).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Color considerations > Inputs and buttons > Button text contrast
title: Color considerations: Button text contrast
statement: The visible text portion that communicates the button's purpose must meet a contrast ratio of 4.5:1 for "normal text", or 3:1 for "large text". The majority of GitHub input text size is "normal text". Both "normal text" and "large text" are WCAG-specific terms. More information about this can be found on the Key Terms subsection of SC 1.4.3: Contrast (Minimum).
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Color considerations" (Inputs and buttons > Button text contrast).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Color considerations > Inputs and buttons > Button icon contrast
title: Color considerations: Button icon contrast
statement: Icons can either be: 1. Functional, or 2. Decorative. Functional icons If the icon is the sole means of determining a button's purpose, it is considered functional. An example of this is an IconButton. Functional icons must meet a contrast ratio of 3:1. This is calculated by the icon's computed color value compared to the computed background color the input is placed on. Beyond the scope of normative WCAG guidance, a further consideration is if the icon's meaning has cultural considerations or represents abstract functionality a user may not be familiar with. Decorative icons Buttons with a text label that also have an accompanying icons can consider their icons as decorative. Decorative icons do not need to meet WCAG-compliant contrast ratios. The reason for this is that the text label communicates the input's purpose, provided its computed color value is WCAG compliant. The icon in this circumstance reinforces the text label. An example of this is a button with both a trash Octicon and a text label of "Delete". Beyond the scope of normative WCAG guidance, a further consideration is if making a decorative icon color contrast compliant is useful for aiding in facilitating understanding, even if it is not required to be.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Color considerations" (Inputs and buttons > Button icon contrast).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Color considerations > Inputs and buttons > Button border contrast
title: Color considerations: Button border contrast
statement: The contrast of a button's border color compared to the input's background color does not need to meet a contrast ratio. Only the button's text or functional icon does.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Color considerations" (Inputs and buttons > Button border contrast).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Color considerations > Inputs and buttons > Button disabled state contrast
title: Color considerations: Button disabled state contrast
statement: Broadly-speaking, buttons should not be disabled until form validation criteria has been met. An example of behavior to avoid is disabling a submit button until a user has filled out all required fields. If a button needs to be placed in a disabled state, it does not need to be color contrast compliant. Other WCAG criteria may affect this treatment, however. Beyond the scope of normative WCAG guidance, a further consideration is there are other ways to visually communicate a disabled button, or to design the system in such a way that a button cannot circumstantially be placed in a disabled state. While a button's disabled state is exempt from normative compliance, consider that the control may be invisible or unpredictably disappear from the perspective of a user experiencing low vision conditions.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Color considerations" (Inputs and buttons > Button disabled state contrast).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Color considerations > Patterns that might be confusing
title: Color considerations: Patterns that might be confusing
statement: Following are examples of unique GitHub UI that are worth specifically documenting:
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Color considerations" (Patterns that might be confusing).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Color considerations > Patterns that might be confusing > GitHub's search
title: Color considerations: GitHub's search
statement: GitHub's search visually looks like an input, but is coded as a button. Use of this approach is discouraged. The following documentation communicates how normative WCAG color contrast rules apply. This is because it triggers the dialog that displays the full search interface—a user cannot directly enter text into a faux-input field. Because of this, it is treated like a button in terms of normative color contrast evaluation. When the search dialog is displayed, the input that a user types in is treated as a text input for color contrast purposes.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Color considerations" (Patterns that might be confusing > GitHub's search).

author: GitHub
title: Descriptive buttons: Overview
statement: In order for a button’s purpose to be clear to all users, it must have a meaningful name.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Descriptive buttons" (Overview).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Descriptive buttons > Overview > What is a meaningful name?
title: Descriptive buttons: What is a meaningful name?
statement: A meaningful name describes the button’s purpose: the action that occurs when the button is activated (for example: removing a list item), and the action’s associated context (for example: the specific item to be removed). To avoid unnecessary verbosity, button names should be as succinct as possible while still being descriptive and unique. Refer to Identifying GitHub comments below for an example of a succinct, unique name. To explore how meaningful names can be set in code, refer to the examples below.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Descriptive buttons" (Overview > What is a meaningful name?).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Descriptive buttons > Overview > Why is a meaningful name necessary?
title: Descriptive buttons: Why is a meaningful name necessary?
statement: Clear and consistent labels set user expectations for button actions, giving users confidence that activating a button will have the outcome they expect. Screen readers (for example: VoiceOver) provide overlays to enable users to jump to specific types of elements, including buttons. Elements are listed by their names. When buttons don’t have meaningful names, it’s not possible to determine which action will be performed when selecting them from the list.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Descriptive buttons" (Overview > Why is a meaningful name necessary?).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Descriptive buttons > How to test names
title: Descriptive buttons: How to test names
statement: When reviewing buttons on a page, ensure the following are true: - Each button has a non-empty name. Refer to ACT 97a4e1: Button has non-empty accessible name. - When buttons perform the same action, they have the same name. - When buttons perform different actions, they don’t have the same name.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Descriptive buttons" (How to test names).

author: GitHub
title: Descriptive buttons: For designers
statement: - When including an unlabeled, icon-only button in a design, recommend an accessible name. - When including multiple buttons that peform the same function in a design, use the same label for each.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Descriptive buttons" (Guidelines > For designers).

author: GitHub
title: Descriptive buttons: For engineers
statement: - When a button doesn’t have a visible label (for example: an IconButton), provide an accessible name. Refer to ARIA 14: Using aria-label to provide an invisible label where a visible label cannot be used. - Because aria-label doesn’t supplement visible labels but rather supplants them, when a button has a visible label, include that label in its accessible name. A good practice is to have the text of the label at the start of the name. - Don’t use aria-label when its content would be identical to a button’s visible label. - Don’t reuse the same (visible) label or (invisible) name for buttons which perform different actions.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Descriptive buttons" (Guidelines > For engineers).

author: GitHub
title: Focus management: Overview
statement: Managing focus within a page or application is essential for users to successfully navigate, complete actions, and understand where they are. A focus indicator is usually seen visually as a blue outline around an interactive element when that element has focus.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Focus management" (Overview).

author: GitHub
title: Focus management: Why?
statement: Not all users are able to use a mouse to navigate a web page or application. Keyboard-only and screen reader users rely on navigating and using a web page with only a keyboard, so they will be unable to perform certain actions if they cannot navigate to all elements. To meet WCAG Guideline 2.1 (Keyboard Accessible), all interactive elements need to be accessed and activated by a keyboard alone.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Focus management" (Why?).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Focus management > How to test focus management
title: Focus management: How to test focus management
statement: To verify proper focus management, try using the feature or page with only a keyboard. Use the Tab key to navigate forward and Shift + Tab to move backwards. Some elements will use the arrow keys for keyboard navigation, such as toolbars and dropdowns. While using the feature, you should make sure that: - You can navigate to every interactive element (for example: buttons, form fields, links) - You see a visual focus indicator for every element (for example: a blue outline) - The tabbing order is logical based on the page structure and content - You are not trapped anywhere, and focus is never lost (for example: when deleting a comment, focus is returned to a logical place) - If you can trigger a new element (for example: a modal), focus is moved to that modal when opened, and returned to the page when closed
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Focus management" (How to test focus management).

author: GitHub
title: Focus management: For designers
statement: In your designs, annotate how the focus should move through various states of a feature, if applicable, for the user. Include where the focus should be when: an item is deleted, an item is added, an action triggers a page refresh, a modal is opened, a modal is closed, etc. Keep in mind high-contrast mode, dark mode, and light mode. Ensure the focus indicator meets the minimum color contrast ratio.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Focus management" (Guidelines > For designers).

author: GitHub
title: Focus management: For engineers
statement: Most interactive elements will have a focus indicator automatically. For example, if you use a element, it should automatically receive focus when using a keyboard. If you need to create your own focus indicator, you can do so with the CSS pseudo-class :focus. You may also need to add/remove a class with JavaScript to apply/remove the focus indicator. A common complaint when using :focus is that when a user clicks on a button, for example, they see the focus indicator which isn't always necessary for a mouse user. This may lead to an engineer removing the outline entirely — never remove the focus indicator unless you are replacing it with a border or some other visual indicator. Using :focus-visible will prevent the focus indicator from being seen for mouse users, but show it for keyboard users. You may need to programmatically determine where the focus should be when an event happens. For example, when you open a modal, you will need to programmatically move focus to an element inside of it. One way of doing this is by setting document.activeElement to the element you want to have focus. See the Primer Behaviors repo for existing behaviors related to focus, such as focus trapping.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Focus management" (Guidelines > For engineers).

author: GitHub
title: Accessibility guidelines
statement: For official guidance, always refer to the WCAG 2.1 W3C documentation. You can find failure examples for each WCAG standard, and techniques for fixing them in How to Meet WCAG (Quick Reference).
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Accessibility guidelines" ().

author: GitHub
subcategory: Accessibility guidelines > It starts with you
title: Accessibility guidelines: It starts with you
statement: Accessible experiences start with designers. Tacking on accessibility after a design is implemented costs businesses time and money, and it muddies the original design, leading to a poor user experience for people with and without disabilities. When we consider accessibility from the beginning, we design for everyone from the start. Consider how different people will experience your design. For an informative list on real-life disability situations, check An Alphabet of Accessibility Issues, published in The Pastry Box Project.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Accessibility guidelines" (It starts with you).

author: GitHub
title: Accessibility guidelines: Feature checklist
statement: If you're designing a feature or experience in GitHub, use the following checklist to assess your design for accessibility: - [ ] Have you annotated the headings on your feature? - [ ] Have you defined the focus/tabbing order on your feature? - [ ] Have you added screen reader labels for elements that are not focusable? (Dynamic content changes, images and their alt text) - [ ] If this is a new page outside the GitHub monolith, are the landmarks annotated? - [ ] Does the text meet color contrast? - [ ] Do graphic objects meet color contrast? - [ ] With color removed, can you still understand the design? - [ ] Can all revealable information (hover card, tooltips, accordions) be accessed with a keyboard or a mouse? - [ ] If the user increases the text size to 200%, is the page still usable? - [ ] When the screen reduces in size (down to 320px wide), is everything usable without scrolling horizontally? (There are a few exceptions to this rule: check 1.4.10 - Reflow for details)
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Accessibility guidelines" (Feature checklist).

author: GitHub
title: Accessibility guidelines: Basic visual considerations
statement: WCAG 2.1 includes more nuanced considerations than what is listed here, but these basic considerations will give you a strong foothold into accessible design.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Accessibility guidelines" (Basic visual considerations).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Accessibility guidelines > Basic visual considerations > Contrast
title: Accessibility guidelines: Normal text (14pt)
statement: Normal text (14pt) : 4.5:1 minimum contrast
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Accessibility guidelines" (Basic visual considerations > Contrast).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Accessibility guidelines > Basic visual considerations > Contrast
title: Accessibility guidelines: Large text (14pt bold + , 18pt +)
statement: Large text (14pt bold + , 18pt +) : 3:1 minimum contrast
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Accessibility guidelines" (Basic visual considerations > Contrast).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Accessibility guidelines > Basic visual considerations > Contrast
title: Accessibility guidelines: Graphical objects and user interface components
statement: Graphical objects and user interface components : 3:1 minimum contrast
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Accessibility guidelines" (Basic visual considerations > Contrast).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Accessibility guidelines > Basic visual considerations > Use of color
title: Accessibility guidelines: Use of color
statement: The main point in the guideline 1.4.1 Use of Color is to make sure that color isn't the sole identifier. If you have an important transition that is only a change in color, make sure that color change has a 3:1 contrast ratio. A great way to test for this is to navigate that experience in greyscale mode. Use color and a different shape to indicate issue status Don't use only color to indicate issue status
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Accessibility guidelines" (Basic visual considerations > Use of color).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Accessibility guidelines > Basic visual considerations > Links
title: Accessibility guidelines: Links
statement: Assistive technology users will frequently browse a list of links for easy navigation. For this reason, make sure that the link text is meaningful and unique. There should be as few duplicated references as possible to prevent confusion. For more detail on accessible links, read the W3C's Understanding 2.4.4 - Link Purpose. { Find out more about GitHub Enterprise pricing . } Make links meaningful and easy to understand { To find out more about GitHub Enterprise pricing, click here . } Don't create links that give no indication to the user
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Accessibility guidelines" (Basic visual considerations > Links).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Accessibility guidelines > Basic visual considerations > Forms
title: Accessibility guidelines: Forms
statement: - All form inputs should have a visible label - Don't use placeholder text for titles, hints, or other important information. Why? Visible labels determine the purpose for inputs, and screen readers can read this information without extra code. If placeholder text contains important information and that information disappears when one starts to type, those with cognitive disabilities will have difficulty completing the form.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Accessibility guidelines" (Basic visual considerations > Forms).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Accessibility guidelines > Basic visual considerations > Content on hover or focus
title: Accessibility guidelines: Dismissible
statement: Dismissible : Be able to dismiss tooltips without moving the pointer or keyboard focus (unless it's an input error or does not cover other content).
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Accessibility guidelines" (Basic visual considerations > Content on hover or focus).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Accessibility guidelines > Basic visual considerations > Content on hover or focus
title: Accessibility guidelines: Hoverable
statement: Hoverable : Pointer can move over the hover content without the content disappearing.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Accessibility guidelines" (Basic visual considerations > Content on hover or focus).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Accessibility guidelines > Basic visual considerations > Content on hover or focus
title: Accessibility guidelines: Persistent
statement: Persistent : The tooltip doesn't dismiss itself without user action.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Accessibility guidelines" (Basic visual considerations > Content on hover or focus).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Accessibility guidelines > Basic visual considerations > Text
title: Accessibility guidelines: Text
statement: People using the web should be able to increase font size to 200% without losing content or functionality. If you'd like to go the extra mile and meet AAA guidelines, you can make sure that: - The width of text doesn't exceed 80 characters or glyphs - Text isn't justified (align text to the left and right) Read Primer's typography guidelines for more detail about using type on GitHub.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Accessibility guidelines" (Basic visual considerations > Text).

author: GitHub
title: Accessibility guidelines: Keyboard accessibility
statement: All interactive elements need to be accessed and activated by a keyboard alone (2.1 Keyboard Accessible). - Tabbing should be used to access standalone controls (buttons, links, widgets), and arrow keys should be used to navigate within a composite control (group of standalone controls, list of checkboxes). - Some assistive technologies have keyboard combinations that override those of a web page, so don't rely on keyboard shortcuts as the only alternative to mouse actions. - Focus must be visible for all interactive elements. Read more about focus management
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Accessibility guidelines" (Keyboard accessibility).

author: GitHub
title: Headings: Overview
statement: Headings play a critical role in communicating the structure of a page. Heading levels range from to .
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Headings" (Overview).

author: GitHub
title: Headings: Best practices
statement: - Avoid skipping heading levels. should be followed by and so on. - Do not use heading elements solely for resizing text. - Avoid setting more than one per page. should be reserved to describe the page as a whole, similar to a page . (Dialog headings are excepted from this rule.)
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Headings" (Overview > Best practices).

author: GitHub
title: Headings: Why?
statement: A correct heading structure is critical for enabling users to navigate quickly within a page. Headings are by far the most common navigation technique for screen reader users. 67.7% of surveyed screen reader users responded that they are first likely to navigate via the headings when trying to find information on a lengthy web page. A proper heading structure also allows sighted users to visually scan and find what they want on a page quickly. An improper heading structure can cause a confusing navigation experience.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Headings" (Why?).

author: GitHub
title: Headings: For designers
statement: In your designs, annotate the heading level. Properly labeled headings are one of the most important things a designer can do for developer handoff.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Headings" (Guidelines > For designers).

author: GitHub
title: Headings: For engineers
statement: As you're developing a page, use tools like Accessibility Insights and HeadingsMap to verify the heading structure. You may also inspect the DOM structure of your page using the browser inspector, but using an extension will surface heading levels more easily.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Headings" (Guidelines > For engineers).

author: GitHub
title: Links: Overview
statement: Links are user interface elements that navigate you to a new place or new content. Contrast this with buttons, which are designed to activate a feature.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Links" (Overview).

author: GitHub
title: Links: Why?
statement: Links can do things like help with page context, reference similar items of interest, and allow for endless connected information surfing through sites like Wikipedia. Links play a key part in your experience on the web, but without proper consideration they can be frustrating to use, skipped over, or completely unnoticed. For screen reader assistive technology, links and buttons are expected to function differently from each other. If a link is activated and does not do what was expected, that can be disorienting and frustrating. A common way a screen reader might navigate the page is by going through a list of all the links on the page. Without context, "read more" or "click here" links are not helpful. People who have low or colorblind vision may have trouble identifying links that just use color to distinguish them from plain text, this is why keeping the underline styling on links within body text is important for identification.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Links" (Why?).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Links > How to test links > Functionality and purpose
title: Links: Functionality and purpose
statement: A link's function is to navigate to a different page or new content. If instead a feature on the page is activated, use a . Learn when to use a link or button. A link's purpose must be obvious from the link text alone. If you can't get an idea of where a link will take you based on the link text without reading the sourrounding text, the link text should be updated. Learn how to write good link text. This is important because screen readers allow users to browse through a list of links, where the link text is the only clue of where a link will take you.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Links" (How to test links > Functionality and purpose).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Links > How to test links > Visual distinction & contrast
title: Links: Visual distinction & contrast
statement: Like normal text, a link must have a 4.5:1 contrast against the background color that it is placed on. Use a contrast checker to validate that your link meets this required contrast. If a link is sourrounded by text, it must be underlined or pass a 3:1 contrast against the sourrounding text as well. Alternativly an icon, a background shape or an outline can demarcate a link. Some examples of this are: - links within body text - a headline and subline which both are individual links - issue numbers or usernames within a commit line
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Links" (How to test links > Visual distinction & contrast).

author: GitHub
title: Links: For designers
statement: - Visually demarcate your links by using: - the accent.fg color in combination with fg.default for the sourrounding text on any of the canvas.[...] colors - an underline for the link text - an icon before or after the link text - using a background shape behind the link - using a link color that has a 3:1 contrast against the sourrounding text color AND a 4.5:1 against the background color - Make sure a link's purpose can be understood from the link text alone, without needing the surrounding context. - Links should look like links, not buttons, except in rare circumstances, like calls to action. Be descriptive with your links so that they can stand alone and be understood. Don't use generic terms like 'click here' that can't be understood out of context. Underline links in paragraphs and sentences Don't use underlines for non-link highlights or forget to demarcate links Use a link color that has a 3:1 contrast against the text color Don't use a color that has less than a 3:1 contrast against the text color for links Use an icon or a background shape to demarcate a link Don't use text styles like italic or bold to demarcate links
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Links" (Guidelines > For designers).

author: GitHub
title: Links: For engineers
statement: - Use Primer link components: - Rails component - React component - Don't override the link styling provided in the components - Make sure links receive our global focus indicator styling when navigating the page with a keyboard (reference: Focus management) - Don't use the title attribute - Content within a title is inaccessible for many users, such as touch-only and keyboard-only users. If additional content needs to be associated with a link consider using a tooltip or alternatives to a tooltip. - Avoid adding side effects to link click events. Links should navigate, not affect the page. - Don't force links to open in a new tab/window by setting the target property. - Links should always open in a new window when clicking while holding Command/Control.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Links" (Guidelines > For engineers).

author: GitHub
title: Links: Common mistakes
statement: - Only adding an underline to a link when it has focus or is hovered over - Underlining every link on the page. For example, a navigation list is a list of links but navigational links don't have to be underlined because the intent is understood and an underline is not needed to identify the interactive nature of the control.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Links" (Common mistakes).

author: GitHub
title: Placeholders: Overview
statement: Placeholders are hint text placed inside of an input. They are used to help suggest what kind of input should be provided, but have some accessibility considerations to be aware of.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Placeholders" (Overview).

author: GitHub
title: Placeholders: Best practices
statement: - Avoid using placeholders if at all possible. - Instead, use a caption to communicate this information. - If you must use a placeholder, be sure that the input also has a concise, descriptive label.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Placeholders" (Overview > Best practices).

author: GitHub
title: Placeholders: Why?
statement: Placeholders are typically styled using a light text treatment to visually communicate that they are suggestions, and not pre-filled input. However, this often means they are too light to be color contrast compliant. If the placeholder color treatment is darkened to be compliant, it risks being visually interpreted as pre-filled input. Placeholder length is also constrained by the width of the input it is used in. This means important information may be truncated, especially if the user relies on an increased font size. Additionally, activating an input that has a placeholder will cause the placeholder to disappear. If the placeholder contains important information, such as formatting requirements, it will no longer be able to be referenced. Compare this to a caption, which is always shown to the user. Placeholder information also cannot contain interactive information such as support links, or buttons that trigger tooltips. Unlike a placeholder, a caption can contain these pieces of information. placeholder attribute values can also factor into accessible name computation if a programatically associated label does not accompany the input. Although placeholder is not intended to be used this way, it can serve as last-ditch technique used by some assistive technology to try and determine the purpose of the input the placeholder declaraction is applied to. This can be confusing if the placeholder's content does not communicate the purpose of the input (ex: "No numbers or special characters").
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Placeholders" (Why?).

author: GitHub
title: Placeholders: For designers
statement: Use techniques like explanatory paragraphs and input captions to explain the content in a way that is always visually persistent. Also ensure a visible label for the input is also utilized, and that the label has a concise, descriptive name that communicates the input's purpose.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Placeholders" (Guidelines > For designers).

author: GitHub
title: Placeholders: For engineers
statement: Ensure that the label uses the label element, with a for attribute that references an id declared on the associated input. The placeholder color value should also be controlled by a design token to ensure it visually renders appropriately across different themes.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Placeholders" (Guidelines > For engineers).

author: GitHub
title: Semantic HTML: Overview
statement: Semantic HTML provides meaning to the content of a web page. It involves using the correct HTML element for the job. Semantic HTML breaks the page up into meaningful sections.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Semantic HTML" (Overview).

author: GitHub
title: Semantic HTML: Why?
statement: Many groups of people benefit from properly used semantic HTML. Using the correct elements allows assistive technology to accurately convey the purpose of the content to the user. Without it, they will not be able to navigate easily. Other benefits of using semantic HTML are SEO and code readability.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Semantic HTML" (Why?).

author: GitHub
title: Semantic HTML: For designers
statement: In your designs, annotate what HTML elements should be used for various parts of the design, if appropriate. Understand that most designs are achievable with CSS alone, agnostic of the HTML elements used.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Semantic HTML" (Guidelines > For designers).

author: GitHub
title: Semantic HTML: For engineers
statement: Think about the content that will populate an element in order to determine what HTML element should be used. Are you building a navigation? Use the element instead of nested elements. You may need to add interactivity to more complex elements, such as . Some elements may require additional ARIA attributes to convey things such as state, but be careful to use these only when necessary.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Semantic HTML" (Guidelines > For engineers).

author: GitHub
title: Semantic HTML: Common mistakes
statement: - Using improper elements to achieve the desired visual style - Example: using an tag for a heading that should be an because the visual style of the is desired - Solve: use CSS for visual styling - Using the title attribute - It is inaccessible for many users, such as touch-only and keyboard-only users. Do not use. - Using improper markup - Example: placing text in a instead of a - Solve: use the proper element to depict the content that is inside - Using incorrect ARIA - Example: using an aria-label on a non-interactive element such as a - Solve: only use ARIA when necessary, and if you can use a native HTML element, you should. More information on ARIA - Duplicate IDs - Example: two elements on the page with id="anchor" - Solve: use unique IDs for every element on the page - Decorative elements not marked as decorative - Example: an element not being marked as decorative - Solve: add role="presentation" or aria-hidden="true" to elements that are for decorative purposes only
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Semantic HTML" (Common mistakes).

author: GitHub
title: Semantic HTML: Reading order
statement: Screen readers and other assistive technologies convey the information to the user in the order that it is marked up in the code, not necessarily how it looks on the page. Ensure the order matches a logical order of information presented. One way to verify this is to view the page without styles and see if the order of content is logical.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Semantic HTML" (Reading order).

author: GitHub
title: Text resize and respacing: Overview
statement: Users should be able to resize text and use custom text spacing without text being clipped, truncated, or obscured. In addition, interactive controls should not break.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Text resize and respacing" (Overview).

author: GitHub
title: Text resize and respacing: Why?
statement: People with low-vision may rely on the browser's zoom functionality or update the font-size of a page to read content. Additionally, people with low-vision and people with dyslexia may increase text spacing with custom CSS to improve readability. When sites are built without adequate considerations around responsiveness (for example: setting fixed width and height, using non-relative font sizing), sites may become completely unreadable and unusable for some users.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Text resize and respacing" (Why?).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Text resize and respacing > How to test > Text resizing
title: Text resize and respacing: Text resizing
statement: Most modern browsers support full-page zoom, while some also support text-only zoom (for example: Firefox). While WCAG does not specify how text should be resized, it is best practice for your page to be readable with full-page zoom and text-only zoom. Aside from using the browser zoom, some users may also resize text through browser font-size setting. Test your page by using browser zoom with magnification of up to 200%. Confirm that the text content does not overflow, overlap, or become truncated, and that interactive controls still work. Learn more about resize testing techniques at TheA11yProject: Resize text.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Text resize and respacing" (How to test > Text resizing).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Text resize and respacing > How to test > Text spacing
title: Text resize and respacing: Text spacing
statement: Modify text spacing according to the WCAG text spacing testing guidelines. You can do this by changing the CSS using the browser inspector or by using a tool like Steve Faulkner: text spacing bookmarklet. Confirm that text is contained within the bounds of its container without overlapping or being cutoff.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Text resize and respacing" (How to test > Text spacing).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Text resize and respacing > Guidelines > For designers
title: Text resize and respacing: For designers
statement: When creating a design, ensure that font sizes and element sizes are annotated with proper resizing techniques before handing it off to an engineer. There are a variety of techniques that can be employed to ensure responsive text and space resizing. This includes avoiding setting fixed height on a container to allow text content to expand, and using relative units such as em and rem instead of px. Learn more about the techniques at: WCAG Resize text techniques and WCAG Text spacing techniques.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Text resize and respacing" (Guidelines > For designers).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Text resize and respacing > Guidelines > For engineers
title: Text resize and respacing: For engineers
statement: As you're developing a feature, make sure to test the page using the resize techniques described in How to test. Ensure that WCAG Resize text techniques and WCAG Text spacing techniques are employed.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Text resize and respacing" (Guidelines > For engineers).

author: GitHub
title: Accessibility tools
statement: A selection of tools to help product designers design accessibly.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Accessibility tools" ().

author: GitHub
subcategory: Accessibility tools > On testing color contrast
title: Accessibility tools: On testing color contrast
statement: When testing contrast be wary of tools that use color pickers. The picked color may differ depending on your color space settings and other factors. Always prefer direct value input.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Accessibility tools" ( > On testing color contrast).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Accessibility tools > System tools > Sim Daltonism (MacOS)
title: Accessibility tools: Sim Daltonism (MacOS)
statement: Free application in the Mac App Store that can simulate various color blindness disorders. How does this help? When you're designing something that uses color (yes, that's everything), you can use this app to see the design as someone who has color blindness would see it, and check if it still makes sense.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Accessibility tools" (System tools > Sim Daltonism (MacOS)).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Accessibility tools > System tools > Colour Simulations (Windows)
title: Accessibility tools: Colour Simulations (Windows)
statement: Free application for Windows that is comparable to Sim Daltonism on Mac.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Accessibility tools" (System tools > Colour Simulations (Windows)).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Accessibility tools > Web tools > WebAIM Contrast Checker
title: Accessibility tools: WebAIM Contrast Checker
statement: The WebAIM contrast checker is the golden standard and does a good job explaining what the result means. At GitHub the WebAIM contrast checker is the standard that has to be met. There is also a link contrast checker.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Accessibility tools" (Web tools > WebAIM Contrast Checker).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Accessibility tools > Web tools > Color Review
title: Accessibility tools: Color Review
statement: Color review is fantastic if you're looking for help finding an accessible color in an existing palette.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Accessibility tools" (Web tools > Color Review).

author: GitHub
title: Tooltips: Overview
statement: Tooltips are often used to convey information. However, tooltips are rarely appropriate, and their misuse can result in a myriad of accessibility issues. Always consider not using a tooltip for an improved user experience.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Tooltips" (Overview).

author: GitHub
title: Tooltips: Why?
statement: - Tooltips are hidden by default making it easy to miss, so they should never be used to convey critical information. - Tooltips are never accessible on mobile devices. - Tooltips should never be set on non-interactive elements (for example, div, span, p), and should only ever be set on interactive elements (for example, button, a). Tooltips on non-interactive elements are not accessible to keyboard users and screen reader users.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Tooltips" (Why?).

author: GitHub
title: Tooltips: For designers
statement: - Reserve tooltips for components like icon buttons. - Keep your tooltip text minimal. - Only include tooltips on other components as a last resort. - Never include tooltips on non-interactive components (div, span, p). Use a tooltip to give a text label to an icon button Don't use tooltips on non-interactive elements Annotations If you have an appropriate tooltip in your design, annotate the tooltip carefully with the preferred type (whether it's a label or description) to ensure proper semantics.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Tooltips" (Guidelines > For designers).

author: GitHub
title: Tooltips: For developers
statement: If you come across a design or a page with a tooltip on a static element (for example, div, span, p), remove it. Consult a designer for an alternative way of conveying the information. If you determine that tooltips are appropriate for your use case, make sure to carefully follow guidelines set in Primer ViewComponents: Tooltip component.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Tooltips" (Guidelines > For developers).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Adding new components > On-ramp from product to Primer
title: Adding new components: On-ramp from product to Primer
statement: The process starts with a new component being introduced as a custom React component in a feature team's app and becoming a Primer component once it matures and gets more usage. This guidance is intended for GitHub staff members who are introducing design patterns that are not yet supported by Primer components. Contributions from Primer consumers who don't work at GitHub are welcome and encouraged, but these steps assume the reader is working on a feature team at GitHub.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Adding new components" (On-ramp from product to Primer).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Adding new components > On-ramp from product to Primer > 1. Exists and is discoverable
title: Adding new components: 1. Exists and is discoverable
statement: Your component should have: - A name - A description - At least 1 Storybook story This is the least refined phase of a new component: it just needs to exist. If you've already decided that this is a component worth sharing with other teams, it just needs to be discoverable and pass basic accessibility checks. For guidance on what makes a pattern worth sharing, check out the documentation: Handling new patterns.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Adding new components" (On-ramp from product to Primer > 1. Exists and is discoverable).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Adding new components > On-ramp from product to Primer > 2. Meets basic design quality checks
title: Adding new components: 2. Meets basic design quality checks
statement: Check the design against the criteria in the pattern design checklist. The criteria in the pattern design checklist ensure your pattern is sturdy enough to be used in production and easily picked up by other designers or engineers. For a more detailed quality check, you can refer to the product design checklist (GitHub staff only).
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Adding new components" (On-ramp from product to Primer > 2. Meets basic design quality checks).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Adding new components > On-ramp from product to Primer > 3. Has documentation
title: Adding new components: 3. Has documentation
statement: The most basic documentation your component should have: - Storybook stories demonstrate all of the pattern's features and options - At least meets the MVP component documentation criteria Documentation makes your pattern easier for others to use, and helps the team understand how your pattern could be adopted into Primer. Resources for writing documentation: - Component documentation criteria - Primer documentation guidelines
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Adding new components" (On-ramp from product to Primer > 3. Has documentation).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Adding new components > On-ramp from product to Primer > 4. Is accessible
title: Adding new components: 4. Is accessible
statement: Your component likely meets basic accessibility requirements if it passes axe checks and follows the guidance in the Product Accessibility Checkpoints (GitHub staff only) in our accessibility playbook. It would be even better if your component has gone through an a11y design review and a a11y engineering review. Every new component we add to Primer goes through rigorous testing by the accessibility team, so your component will be better prepared for adopting and releasing in Primer.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Adding new components" (On-ramp from product to Primer > 4. Is accessible).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Adding new components > On-ramp from product to Primer > 5. Ready to upstream
title: Adding new components: 5. Ready to upstream
statement: Now your component has satisfied enough criteria that it's well on it's way to being at the “Alpha” maturity status! From here, your team or the Primer maintainers will be in a good position to adopt your component and iterate on it until it reaches the “Alpha” maturity status.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Adding new components" (On-ramp from product to Primer > 5. Ready to upstream).

author: GitHub
title: Adding new components: Avoiding duplication
statement: New components should never have the same name as an existing Primer component - especially if it's distinctly different from the existing component. The only exception is if you're introducing the React implementation of a component that has already been created in Primer ViewComponents. If you're creating a modified version of an existing component, try to modify it in Primer first. If your changes are rejected by Primer, you can iterate on a "fork" of the component with a new name until it can be upstreamed. See the flowchart in the "Handling new patterns" guidelines.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Adding new components" (Avoiding duplication).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Adding new components > Upstreaming to Primer
title: Adding new components: Upstreaming to Primer
statement: Primer has a strict process for adding new components to ensure they meet certain quality criteria and are accessible. Initiated by Primer: If a component gains enough traction that it's being regularly used by multiple feature teams, the Primer maintainers will create and prioritize an issue to upstream it. Initiated by a feature team: If a feature team feels that the component is ready to be upstreamed to Primer, anybody is welcome to create an issue to review the component with Primer maintainers. During that review, the Primer will decide whether or not the component is a good candidate for upstreaming. Use the Primer pattern proposal issue template.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Adding new components" (Upstreaming to Primer).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Adding new components > Upstreaming to Primer > How do Primer maintainers arrive at a decision to upstream?
title: Adding new components: How do Primer maintainers arrive at a decision to upstream?
statement: - Is the pattern frequently used by multiple feature teams? - Is this a pattern we want to encourage because it does a good job solving a particular design, engineering, or accessibility problem? - Will there be any negative consequences from adding this new component? For example, a negative impact on performance - Does it fit in with a “theme” of any existing Primer components? For example, a new data input component would fit in nicely with our existing form components and other patterns for data input - Is the time we'd have to invest in owning and maintaining the component worth it?
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Adding new components" (Upstreaming to Primer > How do Primer maintainers arrive at a decision to upstream?).

author: GitHub
subcategory: Adding new components > Upstreaming to Primer > Who are the decision makers and stakeholders involved?
title: Adding new components: Who are the decision makers and stakeholders involved?
statement: The Primer maintainers (designers and engineers) will decide if a component should be upstreamed using input from feature teams and the criteria described above.
citation: GitHub. GitHub Primer Design System: "Adding new components" (Upstreaming to Primer > Who are the decision makers and stakeholders involved?).

title: Adding new components: How do Primer maintainers vet components once they're upstreamed?

Once a component meets “Alpha” criteria it's considered safe to be use in production, but consumers can expect breaking changes as it matures to “Beta”. We aim to get all or most components to the “Stable” level of maturity criteria.

Finally, consider where a pattern will live in the context of a system. A pattern designed for a specific context is not likely to be considered a reusable component.

subcategory: Documentation > Documenting components > Minimum-viable component documentation
title: Documentation: Minimum-viable component documentation
statement: One of the strategies to help Primer documentation become self-serve is to accurately represent the breadth of patterns and components we have available through our documentation. To do this, we are increasing our coverage to include 100% of available-for-use components temporarily in the primer/design repository. Executing on this plan requires us to be practical and concise in terms of the depth of the documentation. In order to ensure we can reach 100% coverage, we're using a "minimum-viable documentation" approach. Minimum-viable documentation should be: - Accurate - Informative but concise - Visible

title: Documentation: Minimum-viable component documentation structure
